The availability of large, high-quality parallel corpora is a cornerstone of statistical machine translation (SMT) systems (Koehn et al., 2003; Och and Ney, 2004). Traditionally, constructing such resources has been a laborious and expensive undertaking, typically relying on human translators or meticulously curated collections of multilingual documents from international organizations like the United Nations and the European Parliament. While these resources have driven significant progress in MT, their limited size and specific domain focus restrict the generalization capabilities of trained models. Consequently, the development of methods for automatically acquiring parallel data has become a crucial area of research. Existing approaches to parallel data acquisition largely fall into two categories: comparable corpus mining and web mining. Comparable corpus mining (e.g., Resnik and Smith, 2003; Potthoff and Skibski, 2003; Freitag and Al-Onaizan, 2007) leverages collections of non-parallel texts in different languages that cover similar topics. Techniques often involve identifying translational equivalents through word alignment, document structure comparison, or topic modeling. This approach is relatively straightforward but suffers from inherent noise, as the documents are not direct translations of each other, and relies heavily on the accuracy of the identification process. A more direct, albeit significantly more challenging, approach is to mine parallel data directly from the Web. The Web is a vast repository of multilingual content, and potentially contains numerous instances of naturally occurring translations. However, extracting high-quality parallel sentences from this noise requires overcoming several hurdles. The sheer scale of the Web necessitates efficient and targeted search strategies. Furthermore, identifying true translations amidst the vast amount of unrelated content, near-misses, and machine-translated outputs demands robust filtering techniques. Previous work in this area (e.g., Munteanu and Fraser, 2005; Nakayama et al., 2009; Erdos et al., 2012) has explored various techniques for web mining of parallel data, often focusing on identifying bilingual websites or leveraging anchor text to retrieve translations. However, many existing web mining approaches rely on heuristics or hand-engineered features to identify potential translations, which can be brittle and require substantial adaptation for different language pairs and domains. Furthermore, the evaluation of these systems is often limited by the difficulty of ensuring the quality of the mined data. In this paper, we present an empirical study on web mining of parallel data that addresses these challenges through a novel, end-to-end approach. We formulate the problem of identifying relevant web pages as a learning-to-rank task, enabling us to leverage machine learning to optimize search query generation. Subsequently, we employ IBM Model 1 (Brown et al., 1993) alignment to filter noisy document pairs, focusing on those exhibiting strong translational correspondences at the sentence level. Critically, we demonstrate that this process not only yields a substantial amount of high-quality parallel data but also directly improves the performance of a statistical machine translation system, providing a clear demonstration of the utility of our approach.

## Towards More Variation in Text Generation: Developing and Evaluating Variation Models for Choice of Referential Form Natural Language Generation (NLG) systems are increasingly capable of producing fluent and grammatical text. However, a common criticism remains that generated text often lacks the stylistic variation characteristic of human writing (Gatt et al., 2018; Li et al., 2016). This lack of variation manifests in numerous ways, including limited lexical choice, repetitive sentence structures, and, crucially, a uniformity in the way entities are referred to. While a single, unambiguous referential form is often sufficient for comprehension, human communication consistently exhibits a preference for varied referencing strategies – employing full names, pronouns, definite descriptions, and nicknames in a dynamically shifting pattern. This variation is not merely stylistic; it contributes to discourse coherence, reader engagement, and a more natural flow of information (Brennan et al., 1996; Artstein & Poesio, 2008). The challenge lies in modeling this inherent variability. Traditional NLG approaches often prioritize determinism, focusing on generating *a* correct referring expression rather than *a range* of plausible options. This deterministic approach leads to predictable, and ultimately less engaging, text. Recent work has explored methods for introducing controlled stochasticity into generation, but often relies on hand-crafted rules or pre-defined paraphrases (Clement et al., 2008; Stent et al., 2004). These methods, while effective, are limited in their scalability and ability to capture the subtle nuances of human referencing behaviour. This paper addresses the problem of variability in text generation by focusing specifically on the choice of referential form. We propose a nondeterministic approach to Referring Expression Generation (REG) – the task of generating descriptions that uniquely identify entities within a discourse context – that moves beyond deterministic selection and actively models the probability of different referring expressions. We investigate two distinct approaches for modeling this variation: a probabilistic Naive Bayes model, leveraging established features from the REG literature, and a more expressive Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) model, capable of learning complex contextual dependencies. Our work differs from previous studies in several key aspects. First, we explicitly model the *distribution* over possible referring expressions, moving away from simply selecting the single most likely option. Secondly, we evaluate our models not only on the traditional task of REG accuracy, but also on the downstream impact of variability on the perceived coherence and comprehensibility of generated text in a more realistic NLG setting. Specifically, we leverage the VaREG corpus (Belz & Gatt, 2009) for initial model training and evaluation, and subsequently integrate the best-performing model into a pipeline generating text from the GREC-2.0 corpus (Dale & Reiter, 2005), assessing human judgements of text quality. Through these evaluations, we aim to demonstrate that incorporating variation models for referential form can lead to more engaging and human-like generated text, contributing towards a more nuanced and adaptable NLG landscape.

Event extraction (EE) – the task of identifying event triggers and their associated arguments from unstructured text – is a core component of many information extraction pipelines, with applications ranging from news monitoring and crisis management to knowledge base construction. While substantial progress has been made in extracting events from formal text sources like news articles (Hovy et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2015), adapting these techniques to social media content presents unique challenges. Social media messages are often characterized by their brevity, noisy nature, informal language, and a severe lack of contextual information. This sparsity hinders the performance of traditional event extractors, which rely heavily on well-formed sentences and comprehensive linguistic cues. For instance, a tweet like “explosion downtown!” lacks explicit verb phrases indicating an event trigger, and requires external knowledge to fully understand the type of event (e.g., a bomb detonation, a gas leak explosion, or perhaps even a metaphorical “explosion” of excitement). Existing approaches to event extraction on social media have largely focused on adapting supervised learning methods trained on news corpora (e.g., via domain adaptation techniques) or leveraging distant supervision (Yao et al., 2011; Nguyen and Grishman, 2016). However, domain adaptation can be plagued by negative transfer, where models trained on formal data perform *worse* on informal social media text. Distant supervision, while reducing annotation costs, introduces noise due to the imperfect alignment between knowledge bases and social media mentions. Furthermore, these methods predominantly treat each social media message in isolation, failing to exploit potentially valuable contextual information available from other sources. In this work, we propose a novel approach to cross-genre event extraction that addresses the shortcomings of existing methods by strategically incorporating knowledge from more verbose and contextually rich sources, specifically leveraging news articles. Our key insight is that events occurring in the real world are often reported across multiple genres. By connecting social media messages to related news reports, we can enrich the sparse contextual information inherent in social media text and improve event extraction accuracy. We don’t rely on explicitly linking messages and articles; instead, we utilize shared entity mentions as an anchor for knowledge transfer. This allows us to project event-related patterns observed in news articles onto social media content, even in the absence of direct correspondence between the two. Specifically, we propose a knowledge enrichment framework that leverages pre-trained event extraction models on news data to generate pseudo-labels for social media messages based on shared entity mentions. These pseudo-labels, representing potential event types and arguments, are then incorporated as additional features into a social media event extractor. This allows the model to “see” events in a broader context, mitigating the effect of linguistic sparsity and informality. We demonstrate through extensive experiments that our approach significantly improves event extraction performance on a benchmark social media dataset, achieving a 15% absolute F-score improvement over the state-of-the-art without requiring any additional annotations. The results highlight the effectiveness of cross-genre knowledge enrichment for tackling the challenges of event extraction in the social media domain.

The increasing globalization of communication has led to the widespread phenomenon of code-switching, where texts incorporate elements from multiple languages. This is particularly evident in modern Chinese writing, especially in informal contexts such as emails, online forums, and Internet literature, where English words are frequently embedded within Chinese sentences. This linguistic mixture presents significant challenges for Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks, particularly Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging, a fundamental component of many downstream applications like machine translation, information extraction, and syntactic parsing. Traditional POS tagging systems, typically trained on monolingual corpora, struggle to accurately analyze Chinese-English mixed texts. The primary difficulty lies in correctly identifying the POS tags for the interspersed English words. Without specialized training data, these words are often mislabeled with a generic “foreign word” tag, resulting in a loss of valuable linguistic information. While this approach avoids outright errors, it dramatically reduces the utility of POS tagging for tasks requiring detailed syntactic or semantic analysis. The “foreign word” label provides no information about the word’s function within the sentence – whether it’s a noun, verb, adjective, or other part of speech. Existing approaches to handling code-switching often rely on creating large, manually annotated corpora of mixed texts. However, the cost and effort involved in such annotation projects are substantial, making this solution impractical for many scenarios. Furthermore, the rapidly evolving nature of code-switching – new English words are continually adopted into Chinese writing – means that even meticulously annotated corpora can quickly become outdated. Therefore, there is a pressing need for methods that can effectively handle English words within Chinese text *without* requiring extensive and continuously updated training resources. This paper addresses this challenge by presenting a novel method for POS tagging of Chinese-English mixed texts that leverages *dynamic features*. Instead of relying solely on static, pre-defined features, our approach incorporates characteristics derived from the context surrounding the English word, allowing the system to infer the most likely POS tag based on the interplay between Chinese and English linguistic structures. We argue that capturing these dynamic dependencies is crucial for accurately tagging English words in mixed text environments. We demonstrate through experimentation that our method significantly outperforms traditional sequence labeling techniques, such as Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) and Conditional Random Fields (CRFs), when applied to mixed texts. Moreover, surprisingly, we also find that incorporating this dynamic feature approach improves the performance of POS tagging even for *pure* Chinese texts, suggesting a general benefit in capturing contextual information. This improvement indicates that the features developed are broadly applicable to Chinese POS tagging, and aren't simply effective due to the presence of English words. The rapid growth of microblogging platforms like Twitter has created a wealth of data reflecting public opinion, emerging trends, and individual interests. Analyzing this data offers valuable insights for a diverse range of applications, including personalized recommendation systems, real-time event detection, and social science research. Topic modeling, a powerful unsupervised machine learning technique, has emerged as a key approach to uncovering the thematic structure within large text corpora, and, in particular, within the often-noisy stream of Twitter data. Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) (Blei et al., 2003) is arguably the most widely used topic model, providing a probabilistic framework for identifying latent topics and assigning them to documents. When applied to Twitter data, a common approach is to treat all tweets from a given user as a single document, effectively representing a user's overall topical profile. However, user interests are rarely static; they evolve over time in response to current events, personal experiences, and shifting preferences. Traditional LDA, being a batch learning method, struggles to capture these dynamics effectively. While it can provide a snapshot of a user’s interests at a particular point in time, it requires retraining the model from scratch each time new data becomes available, making it computationally expensive and lacking responsiveness to rapidly changing trends. Recent work has highlighted the benefits of modeling each tweet individually as a distinct document, assuming a single dominant topic per tweet. Twitter-LDA (Röder et al., 2011) represents a significant step in this direction, demonstrating improvements in topic semantic coherence compared to traditional LDA approaches applied to aggregated tweet collections. By focusing on the finer granularity of individual tweets, Twitter-LDA better reflects the diverse range of topics discussed within a user’s timeline. However, a critical limitation of Twitter-LDA is its inability to perform online inference. This means that as new tweets are posted, the model cannot update its understanding of user interests and topic trends incrementally, again necessitating costly retraining. This paper addresses these limitations by extending Twitter-LDA to support online learning and to more accurately model the generative process of tweets. We propose a novel approach that incorporates two key innovations. First, we introduce a method for estimating the ratio between topic-specific words and general, non-topic-specific words for each user. This allows the model to better distinguish between a user’s core interests and transient discussions. Second, and crucially, we integrate the principles of the Topic Tracking Model (TTM) (Hu et al., 2009), originally developed to model consumer purchase behavior, to enable online estimation of both user interest dynamics and evolving topic trends. This permits the model to adapt continuously to the incoming stream of tweets, providing a more responsive and accurate representation of the underlying topical landscape on Twitter. Abstractive text summarization aims to generate concise and fluent summaries that capture the core meaning of a source document. While significant progress has been made in this field, effectively representing and reasoning about *events* remains a key challenge, particularly in the context of news summarization. News articles frequently revolve around specific events – such as political debates, natural disasters, or economic shifts – and a successful summarization system should accurately identify, represent, and articulate these events. Simply stringing together salient sentences, as many extractive methods do, often fails to provide a coherent narrative of the underlying event structure. Previous approaches to event representation for summarization have largely relied on predefined event schemas or manually curated knowledge bases (Barzilay & Lapata, 2008; Chen & Chen, 2016). However, these methods are limited by their dependence on external resources and their inability to adapt to new or evolving event types. More recent work has explored learning event representations directly from data, often leveraging Open Information Extraction (OpenIE) techniques to identify relation triples that implicitly represent events (Miller et al., 2016; Nadeau et al., 2013). These triple-based approaches, while promising, can sometimes struggle to capture the nuances of complex events involving multiple participants and intricate relationships. In this work, we propose a novel approach to event representation based on *patterns* of grammatical utterances. We envision events as clusters of patterns, where each cluster represents a specific event type (e.g., “marriage”, “protest”, “election”), and each pattern within the cluster represents a distinct linguistic realization of that event (e.g., “X married Y”, “X and Y tied the knot”, “protesters gathered in front of Z”). This framework allows for a more flexible and expressive representation of events than simple triple-based approaches, capturing both the semantic roles and the syntactic patterns associated with each event type. A crucial aspect of our approach lies in how these event patterns are extracted. We compare three distinct techniques: a heuristics-based method, a compression-based method, and a novel *memory-based* method. The heuristics-based method leverages existing linguistic resources and rules to identify likely event patterns, similar to techniques used in prior work on multi-document abstraction (Galanis et al., 2011). The compression-based method, inspired by information bottleneck principles, aims to identify patterns that are both informative and concise. However, the key innovation in this paper is the memory-based method. This method stores a large collection of parse trees derived from a corpus of known grammatical utterances and then efficiently searches this “memory” to identify patterns that match sentences in the input document. While intuitively appealing, the memory-based approach faces a significant computational challenge: the search space of potential patterns is vast, encompassing hundreds of millions of parse trees. To address this, we introduce a novel data structure and search algorithm that allows for efficient extrapolation of parse sub-trees, enabling rapid matching against the stored utterances. We demonstrate that the memory-based method, despite its computational demands, generates significantly more grammatical and informative sentences compared to the other two techniques, ultimately leading to improved abstractive summarization performance. We believe that this work represents a significant step towards bridging the gap between linguistic structure and semantic understanding in abstractive summarization.

Narratives form the backbone of human communication and understanding, serving as the primary means through which we convey experiences, share knowledge, and construct our worldview. At their core, narratives aren’t simply sequences of events; they adhere to underlying structures – *schemas* – that dictate the expected order and relationships between these events. Recognizing these schemas is crucial for tasks ranging from story comprehension and question answering to event prediction and commonsense reasoning. For instance, understanding the schema associated with a “crime” narrative automatically suggests the probable involvement of participants like ‘police officers’ and ‘suspects’, and a likely sequence of events including an ‘arrest’ followed by a ‘trial’. Traditionally, the study of narrative schemas, often manifested as *frames* in the linguistic literature (Fillmore, 1982), has relied heavily on manually curated resources like FrameNet (Baker et al., 1998) and PropBank (Palmer et al., 2005). While invaluable, these resources are painstakingly constructed, limiting their scalability and adaptability to new domains. More recent approaches have leveraged supervised machine learning techniques, requiring large annotated corpora to train models for event structure or semantic role labeling (e.g., Ruppert et al., 2016; Goldberg et al., 2014). However, reliance on labeled data presents a significant bottleneck, especially when dealing with diverse and evolving narrative structures. This paper introduces a novel, entirely *unsupervised* system for learning narrative schemas and the semantic roles of their participants directly from raw text. Our approach departs dramatically from previous work by eschewing the need for supervised signals, hand-built knowledge bases, or predefined event or role categories. Instead, we exploit the inherent statistical regularities present in narrative text – specifically, the consistent co-occurrence of arguments surrounding verbs within coherent discourse. Our core insight is that arguments which corefer within chains of verbs are indicative of underlying narrative structures. By tracking these coreferring arguments, our algorithm simultaneously learns both the event sequences (schemas) and the semantic roles filled by those arguments. This is a crucial distinction; many existing unsupervised methods tackle event structure learning and semantic role induction as separate tasks. We argue that jointly addressing both leads to significantly improved performance on both fronts, inducing richer and more meaningful frame-specific semantic roles. For instance, rather than simply identifying ‘agent’ and ‘patient’ roles, our system learns roles specific to a 'legal proceeding' schema, such as ‘judge’ or ‘prosecutor’. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our system on a corpus of news articles, showcasing its ability to discover coherent narrative schemas and to learn participant roles defined over words – roles that align well with intuitive interpretations and demonstrate improvements over prior unsupervised frame learning methods. This work represents a significant step towards automatically building robust and adaptable representations of narrative knowledge directly from textual data. Fillmore, C. J. (1982). The ability for machines to comprehend natural language, to the extent of successfully answering questions about a given text, remains a pivotal, yet largely unrealized ambition within the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP). While substantial progress has been made in areas like machine translation and sentiment analysis, truly understanding a document – extracting not just surface-level information but also nuanced meaning, relationships, and inferences – continues to present a formidable challenge. A significant barrier to achieving this goal is the chronic scarcity of large, high-quality, human-annotated datasets required for training robust machine learning systems. The creation of such datasets is expensive, time-consuming, and often requires specialized linguistic expertise. Recently, Hermann et al. (2015) proposed a novel approach to address this data bottleneck, introducing a large-scale reading comprehension task based on articles from CNN and the Daily Mail news sources. Their method leverages the inherent summarization structure present in these articles – specifically, matching news articles with their corresponding bullet-point summaries – to automatically generate over a million training examples. This dataset, and the neural network models trained upon it, demonstrated promising performance, suggesting a viable path towards scaling up reading comprehension capabilities. However, the implicit assumption underpinning this approach – that success on this task equates to genuine language understanding – warrants careful scrutiny. It is crucial to ascertain *what kind* of linguistic understanding is actually required to perform well on the CNN/Daily Mail task. Is it indicative of deep reasoning and inference, or can reasonably good performance be achieved through more superficial pattern matching and lexical overlap? This paper undertakes a thorough examination of the CNN/Daily Mail reading comprehension task, with the primary goal of dissecting its demands on language understanding. We adopt a dual-pronged approach. First, we delve into a detailed, manual analysis of a representative subset of the questions and their corresponding articles, meticulously identifying the linguistic cues and reasoning processes necessary for accurate answer selection. This provides a qualitative understanding of the task’s intricacies. Second, we challenge the notion that complex neural architectures are *necessary* for strong performance. We demonstrate that relatively simple, yet carefully engineered systems – specifically designed to exploit specific characteristics of the dataset – can attain accuracies of 72.4% and 75.8% on the CNN/Daily Mail datasets, respectively. These results surpass current state-of-the-art performance by a substantial margin of over 5%, and, importantly, approach what we believe represents an upper bound on achievable performance given the inherent limitations of the task itself. Through this combined analysis, we aim to provide a clearer understanding of the capabilities and limitations of current approaches to reading comprehension and to guide future research towards truly intelligent systems. Recommendation systems have become increasingly prevalent in a wide range of applications, from e-commerce and online entertainment to news aggregation and social networking. Traditionally, these systems have relied heavily on collaborative filtering (CF) and matrix completion techniques, which leverage observed user-item interaction data – such as ratings, purchases, or clicks – to predict preferences for unobserved pairs. While effective, these methods often suffer from the cold-start problem, struggling to provide accurate recommendations for new users or items with limited interaction history. Furthermore, they largely ignore the rich textual information often associated with users and items, particularly in the form of reviews and comments. A natural avenue for enhancing recommendation systems is to incorporate insights derived from analyzing this textual data. Opinion mining and sentiment analysis offer techniques to extract subjective information from text, potentially revealing user preferences and item characteristics. However, existing opinion mining approaches often focus on identifying sentiment polarity or extracting specific features, rather than providing direct, readily usable representations for building comprehensive user and item profiles suitable for a recommendation task. These methods frequently require hand-engineered features or operate on a feature-by-feature basis, lacking a holistic understanding of the underlying semantic relationships within the text. In this work, we propose a novel approach to learning distributed representations of both users and items directly from the text of their reviews and associated comments. Our core idea is to construct vector embeddings – distributed representations – that encapsulate the semantic essence of each user and item, allowing us to capture nuanced preferences and characteristics beyond simple rating patterns. Unlike traditional methods, our approach operates within a unified framework that maximizes the likelihood of observed words, effectively learning representations that reflect the underlying generative process of textual feedback. This allows us to bypass the need for explicit feature engineering and capture complex relationships between users, items, and their textual descriptions. Crucially, these learned vector representations are then utilized for a downstream recommendation task: predicting scores for unobserved user-item interactions solely based on their corresponding embeddings, without requiring access to the original text during prediction. This addresses a key limitation of many existing text-based methods, which often rely on computationally expensive text analysis at prediction time. We develop effective and efficient learning algorithms capable of scaling to massive text archives, making our approach practical for real-world applications. Through extensive empirical evaluation on benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that our recommendation-aware distributed representation approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baseline systems, showcasing the power of leveraging textual information in a unified and scalable manner. Anaphora resolution, the task of identifying what expressions in text refer to, is a core problem in natural language processing with implications for numerous downstream applications including machine translation, information extraction, and discourse understanding. While traditional anaphora resolution has largely focused on identifying coreference – instances where different expressions refer to the same entity – a significant challenge lies in resolving *associative anaphora*. Unlike coreference, associative anaphora does not involve identical reference; rather, the anaphor and its antecedent are related through a non-identity association, often representing a characteristic or typical instance. This phenomenon is particularly salient in languages like Japanese, where pronouns are frequently omitted, leading to instances of both zero anaphora (pronoun ellipsis) and associative anaphora relying heavily on contextual relationships. Consider the following example (translated from Japanese): “I bought a car. The insurance was expensive.” Here, "the insurance" is an associative anaphor, linked to "a car" through a typical association – cars require insurance. Crucially, “the insurance” does *not* refer to the same entity as “a car”; it refers to something intrinsically related to it. Resolving this relationship demands understanding of common-sense knowledge and contextual cues, presenting a substantial hurdle for existing anaphora resolution techniques designed primarily for coreference. Existing approaches to associative anaphora often rely on hand-crafted rules or manually annotated knowledge bases, making them brittle and difficult to generalize across domains. Furthermore, treating associative anaphora as distinct from other anaphoric phenomena can lead to fragmented modeling and sub-optimal performance. This paper proposes a novel probabilistic framework for resolving associative anaphora in Japanese, grounded in the observation that it shares crucial characteristics with zero anaphora. Specifically, we treat associative anaphora as a form of implicit anaphora – akin to zero anaphora – and leverage a unified probabilistic model for their simultaneous resolution. Our model employs automatically acquired lexical knowledge – statistical associations between words gleaned from large corpora – to model the likelihood of anaphor-antecedent relationships. By framing both zero and associative anaphora resolution within a shared probabilistic framework, we benefit from synergistic effects, allowing the model to exploit shared contextual cues and effectively disambiguate subtle anaphoric relationships. We demonstrate, through rigorous experimentation on a Japanese text corpus, that our model achieves strong performance in resolving associative anaphora, and that incorporating simultaneous zero anaphora resolution consistently improves the results. This work contributes a principled and data-driven approach to resolving a challenging facet of anaphora, with potential implications for enhancing the robustness and accuracy of Japanese natural language understanding systems. Taxonomies, or hierarchical classifications of concepts, are fundamental to human cognition and play a crucial role in many Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications. From information retrieval and question answering to knowledge representation and reasoning, the ability to understand the ‘is-a’ relationship between concepts – a core component of taxonomy induction – is essential. Traditionally, constructing these taxonomies has been a manual, labor-intensive process, often relying on expert lexicographers. However, the vastness and dynamism of language necessitate automated methods for building and maintaining large-scale taxonomies. Recent advances in distributional semantics (Turney & Pantel, 2010; Miller, 1994) offer a promising avenue, leveraging the statistical properties of language to infer taxonomic relations. Existing approaches to automated taxonomy induction can broadly be categorized into those that focus on hypernymy detection – identifying ‘is-a’ relationships between individual concept pairs – and those that aim to construct entire taxonomic structures directly. While pairwise hypernymy detection can be relatively accurate, scaling this to a complete taxonomy requires resolving inconsistent or conflicting relationships and grappling with the combinatorial complexity of structure learning. Previous work explored the use of patterns extracted from large corpora (Hearst, 1998) or distributional similarity measures (Widdows & Dorow, 2002) to build taxonomies, however, these approaches often suffer from limited scope or a lack of robustness. More recent work has begun to leverage structured prediction to address these limitations (Navigli & Ponzetto, 2012; Spohr et al., 2014). However, previous structured learning approaches often rely on simplified models that fail to fully exploit the rich relational evidence available. Specifically, they typically focus solely on hypernymy relations, neglecting the crucial information encoded in siblinghood – the ‘sister’ relationships within a taxonomy. A robust taxonomy should not only accurately represent hypernyms but also capture the nuanced relationships between concepts at the same level of abstraction. In this paper, we present a novel structured learning approach for inducing hypernym taxonomies. We formulate the problem as probabilistic graphical model that incorporates both hypernymy and siblinghood relations, utilizing a heterogeneous set of semantic features derived from Web n-grams and Wikipedia abstracts. A key innovation of our approach is the inclusion of *non-hypernym-factored* sibling features – features that directly model the relationship between siblings, rather than deriving it solely from hypernymic connections. To handle the computational challenges of inference over complex taxonomy structures, we employ loopy belief propagation alongside a directed spanning tree algorithm, ensuring efficient and scalable learning. We train our model discriminatively by extracting sub-structures from WordNet and optimizing to reproduce them, utilizing adaptive subgradient stochastic optimization. Our experimental results demonstrate a significant improvement over baseline methods, achieving a 51% error reduction compared to a chance baseline and a 15% reduction attributable specifically to the inclusion of sibling features. Furthermore, we demonstrate a relative error reduction of up to 29% over previous state-of-the-art work on ancestor F1 score, validating the effectiveness of our approach.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has rapidly become the dominant paradigm in machine translation, surpassing traditional Phrase-Based Statistical Machine Translation (PBSMT) approaches in both performance and fluency (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Sutskever et al., 2014; Luong et al., 2015). The success of NMT is largely attributable to its ability to learn complex, non-linear relationships between source and target language sequences using deep neural networks, coupled with the attention mechanism which allows the model to focus on relevant parts of the input sequence during decoding. However, standard NMT models operate solely on textual data, ignoring potentially valuable information available from other modalities. In many real-world translation scenarios, visual context is crucial for accurate and fluent translation. Consider the task of translating a sentence describing a scene depicted in an image. Without access to the image, the translation may be ambiguous or miss key details. For example, the sentence “The man is on the left” is meaningless without knowing what the ‘left’ refers to, and an image can provide this crucial information. Multi-modal machine translation, which integrates both textual and visual data, offers a promising approach to address these challenges and improve translation quality. Prior work in multi-modal translation has explored various methods for incorporating visual information into NMT models (Fukushima and Takei, 2016; Cakici et al., 2017; Nguyen et al., 2017). These approaches generally fall into two categories: those that focus on local, object-level visual features obtained through object detection (Cakici et al., 2017) and those that utilize global, scene-level features extracted from pre-trained Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) (Fukushima and Takei, 2016; Nguyen et al., 2017). While local features can provide fine-grained information about the objects present in an image, they often require computationally expensive object detection models and may not capture the overall context of the scene. Global features, on the other hand, offer a more holistic representation of the image and can be readily obtained using pre-trained CNNs, making them a more efficient and practical option. However, the optimal way to integrate these global features into the NMT framework remains an open question. In this paper, we investigate different strategies for incorporating global visual features into attention-based NMT models. Specifically, we explore three approaches: (i) treating global image features as additional “words” in the source sentence, (ii) using global features to initialize the encoder hidden state, and (iii) initializing the decoder hidden state with global features. We evaluate these strategies on both English-to-German and English-to-English translation tasks using the Multi30k dataset (Koehn et al., 2015). Furthermore, we explore the benefits of augmenting the training data with synthetic multi-modal, multilingual data. Our results demonstrate that the proposed methods significantly improve translation performance and, importantly, allow a purely neural model to surpass a strong PBSMT baseline on all evaluated metrics – a first for this dataset.

Recent advances in natural language processing have demonstrated the effectiveness of leveraging large-scale, unlabeled textual data through the use of pre-trained word embeddings (Mikolov et al., 2013;Pennington et al., 2014). These embeddings, learned from tasks like predicting surrounding words or sentence completion, capture semantic and syntactic relationships present in the corpus, and can significantly boost performance when transferred to downstream tasks. Commonly, these pre-trained embeddings are employed in two primary ways: either as initializations for the embedding layer of a task-specific neural network, or as fixed word representations throughout the training process. While both approaches have proven successful, they often represent a compromise. Initializing with pre-trained embeddings allows the model to benefit from prior knowledge, but the embeddings themselves remain static, potentially hindering the model's ability to learn task-specific nuances. Conversely, fine-tuning the embeddings during training allows for adaptation to the specific task, but can lead to catastrophic forgetting of the general semantic information captured during pre-training. In this work, we propose a novel approach that seeks to bridge this gap by simultaneously optimizing both task-specific performance and the quality of learned word representations. We introduce word-level loss extensions, where we augment the primary task loss function with an unsupervised auxiliary loss directly operating on the word embeddings themselves. This auxiliary loss encourages the embeddings to retain more general linguistic properties while simultaneously adapting to the demands of the target task. By jointly optimizing both objectives, we aim to create word representations that are both semantically informative and finely tuned for the specific classification problem at hand. We evaluate our approach on the challenging task of neural temporal relation classification, focusing specifically on narrative containment relation extraction from clinical records. Temporal relation extraction—identifying the temporal relationships between events described in text—is crucial for various information extraction tasks, particularly in domains like healthcare, where understanding the chronological order of medical events is vital for accurate diagnosis and treatment (Compton et al., 2007; Poon et al., 2009). Clinical narratives, however, pose unique challenges due to their complex language, specialized terminology, and often unstructured nature. Our experiments are conducted on the THYME dataset (Kim et al., 2010), a widely used benchmark for temporal relation extraction. We demonstrate that our approach, which continues training the embeddings on an unsupervised objective alongside the supervised task objective, yields significant improvements over state-of-the-art performance. Notably, we achieve these gains while relying solely on a general-domain part-of-speech tagger as a linguistic resource, highlighting the robustness and generalizability of our method. We believe this work provides a valuable contribution to the field by offering an effective strategy for harnessing the power of pre-trained embeddings while maintaining their semantic richness and adapting them for specialized NLP tasks. Determining the semantic similarity between sentences is a fundamental task in natural language processing with applications spanning information retrieval, question answering, and text summarization. Unlike tasks focused on document-level semantics, sentence similarity (SS) presents unique challenges due to the inherent sparsity of word occurrences within the data unit – the sentence itself. A single sentence contains a limited number of words, making robust modeling of each constituent word crucial for capturing the complete semantic picture and achieving accurate similarity assessments. Consequently, even minor inaccuracies in the representation of individual words can significantly impact the overall sentence embedding and, ultimately, the computed similarity score. Traditional approaches to sentence similarity often rely on distributed word representations (e.g., word2vec, GloVe) aggregated to form sentence embeddings. While these methods have shown considerable success, they often struggle to adequately capture the nuanced meanings of words in specific contexts, particularly in shorter texts like sentences. A key limitation lies in their relatively impoverished lexical semantics – their inability to effectively distinguish between different senses of a word or recognize relationships between words beyond simple distributional similarity. For instance, the word “bank” can refer to a financial institution or the side of a river; a robust semantic model must differentiate between these meanings to accurately assess sentence similarity. We hypothesize that improvements in modeling lexical semantics will directly translate to advancements in sentential semantics and, subsequently, enhanced performance on SS tasks. This paper explores this hypothesis by incorporating both corpus-based and knowledge-based lexical semantic information into a novel latent variable model. Specifically, we leverage selectional preference (SP) – statistical information derived from large corpora about the typical arguments a verb or predicate expects – to better contextualize word meanings. This allows us to understand *how* a word is used within a sentence, and not just *that* it is used. Complementing this corpus-based approach, we integrate knowledge-based lexical semantics by incorporating similar words extracted from external dictionaries and lexical resources. This provides a broader semantic understanding of each word, accounting for synonyms and related terms that may not be explicitly present in the training corpus. Our latent variable model elegantly integrates these distinct sources of lexical information, learning a shared representation that captures both contextualized word usage and inherent semantic relationships. This architecture allows the model to disambiguate word senses, effectively handle synonymy, and build more robust sentence embeddings. We evaluate our approach on two publicly available sentence similarity datasets and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance among unsupervised systems, confirming the effectiveness of our proposed method. The increasing adoption of Electronic Health Records (EHRs) presents a unique opportunity to leverage the wealth of clinical information for improved healthcare outcomes. However, a significant portion of this information resides within unstructured clinical notes, hindering its effective utilization. Extracting structured information from these notes – specifically, identifying medical events (e.g., diagnoses, treatments, adverse reactions) and their associated attributes – is a critical step towards unlocking the full potential of EHR data. This process, often framed as a sequence labeling task, forms the foundation for numerous downstream applications in health informatics, including pharmacovigilance, drug surveillance, clinical decision support, and population health management. Entity Linking (EL) – the task of grounding mentions of entities in unstructured text to their corresponding entries in a structured knowledge base (KB) – is a core problem in natural language processing, crucial for downstream applications like question answering, information extraction, and knowledge graph completion. A robust EL system must navigate the inherent ambiguity of natural language, disambiguating entity mentions that could refer to multiple candidates within a KB. Achieving high accuracy necessitates a deep understanding of entities, which extends beyond simple surface form matching. This understanding encompasses an entity’s definition, the contexts in which it is typically mentioned, and its relationships to other entities as formalized through its type within the KB. Existing approaches to entity linking can broadly be categorized into feature-based and neural methods. Early feature-based systems (e.g., Mihalcea & Cucerzan, 2007; Hoffart et al., 2011) relied heavily on hand-engineered features, such as string similarity, context similarity, and prior probability derived from the KB. While effective to a degree, these systems suffer from significant limitations. Feature engineering is a laborious process, often requiring substantial domain expertise, and features designed for one domain may not generalize well to others. Moreover, these systems typically treat different sources of information – description, context, type – largely independently, failing to capture the complex interplay between them. Recent advancements in deep learning have spurred the development of neural EL systems. These models often leverage distributed representations (embeddings) to encode entities and mentions, and employ different architectures like convolutional neural networks (CNNs) (e.g., Yamada et al., 2016) or recurrent neural networks (RNNs) (e.g., Gu et al., 2018) to model contextual information. However, even these neural approaches often focus on a limited set of information sources, or combine them in a relatively shallow manner. For example, some models primarily focus on comparing mention contexts with entity descriptions, neglecting the valuable structural information provided by entity types. Furthermore, a critical challenge in EL is domain adaptation. Most EL systems are trained on specific datasets originating from particular domains (e.g., Wikipedia, news articles). Performance often degrades substantially when applied to texts from different domains without further training. The need for domain-specific data is a major bottleneck, as acquiring labeled data is expensive and time-consuming. Finally, the ability to handle entities *new* to a KB – often referred to as “nil entity” or “novel entity” detection – is an important, yet often overlooked, aspect of EL. A system should be able to identify mentions that do not correspond to any existing entry in the KB and, ideally, create a meaningful representation for these entities, allowing for linking of future mentions. In this work, we introduce a novel neural, modular entity linking system designed to address these challenges. Our system learns a unified, dense representation for each entity by jointly encoding its description, surrounding mention contexts, and fine-grained KB types. We specifically design our architecture to facilitate effective interaction between these different information sources. Crucially, our system achieves competitive or state-of-the-art performance across multiple EL datasets *without* relying on any domain-specific training data or hand-engineered features. We further demonstrate that our model can effectively embed new entities, accurately linking their subsequent mentions even if they were not present during training. Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has rapidly become the dominant paradigm for machine translation, achieving remarkable progress in recent years (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Sutskever et al., 2014; Vaswani et al., 2017). However, standard NMT models typically process sentences independently, neglecting the rich contextual information present within a document. This poses a significant limitation, as coherent and fluent translation often requires understanding relationships between sentences, resolving discourse phenomena like coreference, and maintaining consistency in terminology and style across the document. Early attempts to incorporate document-level context in NMT focused on concatenating source sentences or using document-level embeddings (Shen et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2016). More recently, attention mechanisms have been adapted to leverage contextual information from preceding sentences (Tu et al., 2016; Rocktäschel et al., 2016). These methods typically augment the standard sentence-level attention with a document-level attention, allowing the decoder to attend to relevant parts of previous sentences. While effective, these approaches often treat document context as a flat collection of information, lacking a structured way to capture hierarchical relationships between sentences. Furthermore, simply adding context can sometimes disrupt the internal dynamics of the NMT model itself. The decoder's hidden states represent a sophisticated encoding of the source sentence, and injecting external context naively can dilute this information and hinder translation quality. It is therefore crucial to integrate contextual information in a manner that complements, rather than overwrites, the existing representations learned by the NMT model. In this paper, we propose a novel Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN) for document-level NMT. Our model introduces a hierarchical structure to capture context in a more organized and dynamic manner. The core idea is to condition the standard NMT model not directly on preceding sentences, but on an abstract representation of the document context generated by a hierarchical attention mechanism. This attention mechanism operates at two levels: a sentence-level attention to identify important sentences within the document context, and a word-level attention within each selected sentence. Crucially, the hierarchical attention is integrated as *another level of abstraction*, conditioning on the NMT model’s own previous hidden states, and allowing the model to selectively integrate context based on its current translation state. We demonstrate through extensive experiments on a standard machine translation task that our hierarchical attention model significantly improves translation quality, achieving a substantial gain in BLEU score over a strong NMT baseline and surpassing state-of-the-art context-aware methods. Our analyses reveal that both the encoder and decoder benefit from document-level context, but in complementary ways. The encoder leverages context to better understand the source document, while the decoder uses context to generate more coherent and fluent translations. This work highlights the importance of structured contextual representation for document-level NMT and provides a promising direction for future research.

The ability to automatically infer opinions expressed in text is a core goal of sentiment analysis and opinion mining. Traditional approaches have largely focused on identifying the sentiment polarity – positive or negative – expressed towards entities (e.g., “The battery life of this phone is excellent.”). However, a more nuanced form of opinion expression centers around *events* that have effects, either positive or negative, on entities. We refer to these as +/-effect events. For example, “The company’s acquisition of the startup boosted its stock price” expresses a positive effect of the acquisition event on the company, while “The oil spill devastated the local ecosystem” details a negative effect of the spill on the ecosystem. Inferring opinions in these contexts requires identifying not just sentiment, but also the event itself and its inherent effect polarity. This paper addresses a critical component in enabling such +/-effect-based opinion inference: the construction of a lexicon of events annotated with their inherent effect polarity at a sense-level granularity. Existing sentiment lexicons, like SentiWordNet (Baccianella et al., 2010), tend to provide sentiment scores for word *senses*, but rarely explicitly delineate whether specific event senses have positive or negative effects. Furthermore, many words denoting events are highly polysemous, exhibiting different effect polarities across senses. For example, “raise” can describe a positive effect (e.g., “raise funds”) or a negative one (e.g., “raise concerns”). Acquiring a sense-level lexicon of +/-effect events is therefore crucial for accurate opinion inference. Building such a lexicon presents several challenges. Manual annotation is costly and time-consuming. While distant supervision approaches (e.g., using patterns to automatically label events) are possible, they are prone to noise and may miss subtle effect polarity cues. Moreover, leveraging existing lexical resources like WordNet efficiently requires addressing the inherent complexity of semantic relations and sense disambiguation. Our work tackles these challenges by developing a novel approach that combines a graph-based method utilizing WordNet’s rich relational structure with a supervised classifier leveraging the informative glosses associated with each sense. The intuition behind the graph-based method is that senses with similar meanings (as indicated by WordNet relations) are likely to share similar effect polarities. The classifier, on the other hand, attempts to directly predict the effect polarity based on the textual definition of each sense. By integrating these complementary approaches, we aim to maximize lexicon coverage and accuracy. We present extensive experiments demonstrating that a hybrid method, combining the strengths of both approaches, achieves the best results. Importantly, we also show that the model isn’t simply recapitulating the seed lexicon; it provides effective guidance for manual annotation, surfacing +/-effect senses that were not initially included in our seed set, thereby illustrating its potential for iterative lexicon expansion. This paper contributes a new resource for +/-effect opinion inference and demonstrates a practical methodology for automatically constructing such resources at a sense-level granularity.

Sentence compression, the task of shortening a sentence while preserving its key information, has emerged as a valuable technique in natural language processing (NLP) with applications ranging from text summarization and machine translation to information retrieval and mobile computing. Traditionally, sentence compression has been largely investigated as a monolingual problem, focusing on reducing redundancy and streamlining sentence structures within a single language. However, the increasingly globalized nature of information and the growing demand for multilingual NLP systems necessitate exploring compression methods that can leverage cross-lingual information. This paper addresses the challenge of *parallel sentence compression* – the task of simultaneously compressing a pair of parallel sentences (i.e., sentences that are translations of each other) to obtain a new pair of compressed, yet semantically equivalent, parallel sentences. The potential benefits of parallel sentence compression are numerous. For machine translation, compressing the source sentence *before* translation can reduce computational complexity and potentially improve translation quality by focusing the translation model on essential information. Conversely, compressing the target sentence *after* translation can provide a more concise and readable output. Further applications lie in creating parallel corpora for low-resource languages, where compressing readily available larger corpora in high-resource languages can generate more manageable training sets. In multilingual summarization, parallel compression offers a means to generate summaries that maintain cross-lingual coherence and consistency. A key question in parallel sentence compression is how to effectively integrate information from both languages. Simply applying monolingual compression techniques independently to each sentence in the parallel pair may lead to inconsistencies or a loss of translational equivalence. Thus, maintaining semantic correspondence across languages during the compression process is crucial. In this work, we investigate two distinct approaches to incorporate bilingual information during sentence compression. The first approach utilizes cross-lingual alignment techniques to identify corresponding phrases and dependencies between the two sentences, guiding the compression process to preserve these relationships. The second approach leverages machine translation models to ensure that the compressed sentences remain accurate translations of each other. We rigorously compare the performance of these methods on a parallel corpus of news articles, evaluating both compression rates and the preservation of semantic content through automatic metrics and human evaluation. Our goal is to determine which strategy offers a more effective balance between compression efficiency and translational fidelity, paving the way for robust and reliable parallel sentence compression systems. Section 3 details the two proposed approaches to parallel sentence compression. Section 4 presents the experimental setup, data, and evaluation metrics. The task of syntactic analysis – encompassing word segmentation, part-of-speech (POS) tagging, and dependency parsing – remains a central challenge in natural language processing. While English benefits from well-defined word boundaries and relatively straightforward morphological structures, Chinese presents unique difficulties. The lack of explicit delimiters between words necessitates accurate word segmentation, a task frequently complicated by ambiguity and the potential for various valid segmentations. Furthermore, Chinese POS tagging is complicated by the relatively limited number of morphological features, demanding reliance on contextual information. Finally, dependency parsing, which aims to reveal the grammatical relationships between words in a sentence, is inherently dependent on the accuracy of both segmentation and tagging. Traditionally, these tasks have been addressed using pipeline approaches, where the output of one stage serves as input to the next. For instance, a word segmentation module might first identify word boundaries, followed by a POS tagger to assign grammatical tags, and finally a dependency parser to construct the syntactic tree. However, pipeline models suffer from a critical limitation: error propagation. An error made in an early stage, such as incorrect word segmentation, can cascade through subsequent stages, leading to a significant degradation in overall performance. Recent advances in neural networks have offered promising avenues for addressing these challenges, particularly through the development of joint models. By learning to perform segmentation, tagging, and parsing simultaneously, joint models can leverage dependencies between these tasks to improve accuracy and mitigate error propagation. Prior work in neural joint modeling for Chinese syntactic analysis has begun to explore this potential, but has often struggled to effectively integrate word-level information. Existing neural approaches frequently rely on pre-trained word embeddings, which, while effective for dependency parsing in isolation, can be suboptimal in a joint setting where unseen words or segmentation errors can lead to poorly represented input features. This paper introduces a novel neural joint model for transition-based Chinese syntactic analysis. Our work represents the first neural approach to fully joint Chinese analysis that explicitly aims to prevent error propagation by considering all three tasks concurrently. A key contribution lies in our proposal to utilize embeddings of *character strings* in addition to traditional word embeddings. Character-level embeddings prove crucial for handling out-of-vocabulary words – a common issue in Chinese due to its large lexicon and frequent creation of new terms – and for capturing sub-word information that aids in both segmentation and POS tagging. Our experiments demonstrate that our models achieve state-of-the-art performance on standard Chinese syntactic analysis benchmarks, outperforming existing systems in both word segmentation and POS tagging, and achieving competitive accuracy in dependency parsing. Furthermore, we investigate simplified bi-LSTM architectures with reduced feature sets, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach even with limited model complexity. We believe this work provides a significant step towards more robust and accurate Chinese syntactic analysis through the power of neural joint modeling. ‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍‍

Ontologies serve as formal representations of knowledge within a specific domain, meticulously organizing concepts and their relationships. They are foundational components in a wide array of applications, including semantic search, data integration, and knowledge-based reasoning. However, the development of ontologies is often a decentralized process, leading to the creation of multiple, independent ontologies for the same domain. This proliferation of “parallel” ontologies necessitates the establishment of correspondences, or *alignments*, between their entities – mapping equivalent or related concepts across different knowledge structures. This process, known as ontology matching, is a critical step in enabling interoperability and knowledge sharing. Traditional ontology matching approaches have relied heavily on linguistic similarity measures, logical reasoning, and structural analysis of the ontologies themselves (Euzenat & Shvaiko, 2013). More recently, representation learning techniques, particularly those leveraging distributional semantics, have emerged as promising alternatives. The core idea is to embed ontological entities into a vector space, where semantically similar entities are positioned closely together, thus facilitating the identification of alignments. Early work often utilized pre-trained word embeddings (e.g., Word2Vec, GloVe) as entity representations, assuming that the semantic meaning captured in these general-purpose embeddings transfers well to the specific context of ontology matching. However, these pre-trained embeddings are often trained on large text corpora that differ significantly in domain and scope from the ontologies being matched. Consequently, they may not accurately capture the nuanced semantic distinctions crucial for identifying correct alignments. Furthermore, they lack explicit awareness of the ontological context – the relationships and definitions within the ontologies themselves. Directly applying these generic embeddings can therefore limit matching performance. In this paper, we present DeepAlignment, a novel and entirely unsupervised entity alignment method designed to address these limitations. DeepAlignment refines pre-trained word vectors specifically for the ontology matching task, without requiring any labeled alignment data or external knowledge sources. The refinement process leverages the inherent structure of the ontologies – the relationships between entities and their textual descriptions – to adjust the embeddings, creating representations more tailored to the domain and the matching objective. Crucially, this refinement is achieved in an unsupervised manner, allowing DeepAlignment to be applied to any pair of ontologies without the need for costly manual annotation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DeepAlignment through extensive experiments on established ontology matching benchmarks. Our results show significant performance improvements over state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the advantages of refining word embeddings to better capture the semantic nuances relevant to ontology matching. This work contributes to the growing body of research demonstrating the power of representation learning in the semantic web and paves the way for more accurate and scalable ontology matching solutions. The increasing digitization of healthcare has led to a proliferation of clinical notes, unstructured text documents created by clinicians during patient encounters. These notes contain rich information about a patient’s medical history, symptoms, diagnoses, and treatments. Accompanying these notes are medical codes – standardized alphanumeric designations representing diagnoses, procedures, and other aspects of patient care. These codes are crucial for billing, reimbursement, research, and public health surveillance. However, the process of assigning these codes is often manual, labor-intensive, prone to human error, and expensive. Furthermore, a significant limitation of current coding systems is the lack of explicit annotation linking specific sections of the clinical text to the assigned codes. This hinders understanding *why* a particular code was assigned, obscuring the clinical reasoning behind diagnoses and treatments, and limiting the utility of the data for tasks requiring interpretability. Automating medical code prediction from clinical text offers a potential solution to these challenges. Machine learning models can assist coders, reduce errors, and potentially identify patterns within the data that may be missed by manual review. However, simply achieving high predictive accuracy is insufficient in the medical domain. Clinicians require transparency and the ability to understand *how* a model arrived at a particular prediction to build trust and ensure patient safety. A “black box” model, while potentially accurate, may be unsuitable for clinical adoption if its reasoning cannot be scrutinized. In this work, we present an attentional convolutional network designed to address both the accuracy and interpretability requirements of medical code prediction. Our approach leverages the power of deep learning to automatically extract relevant features from clinical text and predict the appropriate medical codes. Specifically, we employ a convolutional neural network (CNN) to aggregate information across the document, capturing important contextual relationships. Crucially, we integrate an attention mechanism which selectively focuses on the most informative segments of the clinical note for each specific code being predicted. This allows the model to highlight the portions of the text that most strongly support its prediction. The result is a model that achieves state-of-the-art performance on a challenging medical code prediction task, demonstrating strong predictive accuracy – surpassing prior methods with a precision@8 of 0.71 and a Micro-F1 of 0.54. However, our primary contribution extends beyond mere accuracy. Through a rigorous interpretability evaluation conducted in collaboration with a practicing physician, we demonstrate that the attention mechanism effectively identifies meaningful textual evidence explaining each code assignment. These “attention maps” appear to align with clinical reasoning, providing a transparent and justifiable rationale for the model’s predictions. We believe this combination of accuracy and explainability represents a significant step forward in the development of clinically useful natural language processing systems for healthcare. The proliferation of smartphones and voice assistants has spurred a dramatic increase in voice search, particularly for tasks like local business directory assistance (LBDA). Users increasingly rely on voice commands to locate nearby businesses – “Find me a pizza place nearby,” or “Call the closest gas station.” While significant advances have been made in Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) technology, a persistent challenge remains: accurately recognizing business listing names. These names, often proper nouns and containing unique or uncommon terms, frequently fall outside the vocabulary and statistical patterns captured by traditional, broadly trained ASR models. This leads to lower recognition rates for business names compared to general conversational speech, resulting in frustrating user experiences and abandoned search queries. Existing approaches to improve business name recognition in voice search often rely on manually curated lists of business names, or adapting nationwide language models with limited local context. While these methods offer some improvement, they suffer from several limitations. Manually maintained lists are expensive to create and require constant updates to reflect changes in the business landscape. Nationwide language models, even when augmented with local business names, struggle to distinguish between commonly used words and infrequently mentioned business names, especially in areas with a high density of businesses. Moreover, generating and deploying specialized language models for each user’s current location dynamically is computationally expensive and introduces latency, hindering real-time responsiveness crucial for a seamless voice search experience. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to address these challenges: geo-centric language models for local business voice search. Our algorithm dynamically generates language models tailored to a user’s geographic location, leveraging the principle that the probability of encountering a specific business name is heavily influenced by proximity. Crucially, our system is designed to provide coverage for *any* user location, solving the cold-start problem inherent in localized models. Furthermore, we adapt the geographic scope of the language model to the local business density; densely populated areas necessitate smaller, more specific models, while sparsely populated areas benefit from broader coverage. This adaptive granularity optimizes recognition accuracy without sacrificing efficiency. A key advantage of our approach is the ability to pre-compile these geo-centric language models, enabling rapid deployment and minimizing recognition latency – a critical factor for voice-based interactions. We achieve this by strategically partitioning geographic space and pre-computing language models for each partition. At runtime, the system simply selects the appropriate pre-compiled language model based on the user’s location. We evaluate our algorithm using a dataset of spoken business listing name queries collected from a real-world business directory assistance service. Our experimental results demonstrate a substantial 16.8% absolute improvement in recognition accuracy compared to a baseline nationwide language model. Significantly, we also achieve a 3-fold speedup in recognition time, highlighting the efficiency of our pre-compilation strategy. These findings suggest that geo-centric language models represent a promising solution for enhancing the performance and usability of local business voice search applications.
