WordNet: A lexical database. *Communications of the ACM, 38*(11), 39–41.

Domain adaptation – the task of generalizing a model trained on a source domain to perform well on a different, but related, target domain – has become increasingly important in natural language processing. Real-world applications often encounter scenarios where labeled data is plentiful for one domain (e.g., news articles) but scarce or unavailable for another (e.g., medical reports, customer service dialogues). This discrepancy in data availability can severely limit the performance of machine learning models when applied to the target domain. Traditional approaches to domain adaptation often rely on feature engineering and careful selection of domain-invariant features (Ben-David et al., 2010). However, the rise of deep learning and dense, real-valued feature representations presents new challenges and opportunities. While deep neural networks have demonstrated impressive performance across a range of NLP tasks, they are often sensitive to domain shifts and can suffer significant performance degradation when deployed in unseen environments. One significant line of work in domain adaptation revolves around techniques for aligning feature distributions or learning domain-invariant representations (Glorot et al., 2011; Ganin et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2018). These methods typically aim to minimize the distance between source and target domain features in some embedded space. Another fruitful approach, pioneered by Daumé III (2009), centers on feature augmentation – specifically, explicitly modeling the domain as a feature and learning domain-specific models. Daumé III’s work demonstrated strong results, particularly in the context of sparse, binary-valued features and Conditional Random Fields (CRFs). However, a key gap remains: extending these effective, yet traditionally feature-engineering focused, methods to the realm of dense, real-valued features utilized by modern neural networks. Simply applying the original feature augmentation technique to neural networks is often suboptimal, as it doesn’t fully leverage the representational capacity of these models. Furthermore, the application of other established domain adaptation frameworks, such as the shared structure learning approach originally proposed by Ando and Zhang (2005), has not been fully explored within a neural network setting. In this paper, we bridge this gap. We propose simple, yet effective, neural network extensions of Daumé III’s feature augmentation method and the shared structure learning framework of Ando and Zhang. Specifically, we introduce a neural architecture that utilizes K+1 Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks: one LSTM learns global patterns across all K domains, while the remaining K LSTMs capture domain-specific information. We also present a novel application of the Ando and Zhang framework for domain adaptation, formulating it as a neural learning problem. Our experiments, conducted on the challenging slot tagging task across 17 diverse domains, demonstrate that our neural extensions consistently outperform the original Daumé III approach when applied with feature-rich CRFs. The results highlight the effectiveness of these simple neural adaptations in exploiting domain-specific information and achieving robust performance across a wide range of domains. We find that the performance gains are, perhaps surprisingly, substantial given the simplicity of the proposed methods—a fact that inspires the paper’s title: “Frustratingly Easy Neural Domain Adaptation”.

Document-level sentiment analysis remains a significant challenge in Natural Language Processing, particularly when nuanced opinions and contextual dependencies play a critical role in determining the overall sentiment expressed. While sentence-level sentiment analysis has achieved considerable success (Pang et al., 2002; Socher et al., 2013), aggregating these local sentiment scores to obtain a coherent document-level prediction often proves insufficient. This is largely due to the inherent complexity of discourse – the ways in which ideas are connected and contrasted – and the subtle shifts in subjectivity that occur throughout a text. Effective document-level analysis necessitates a fine-grained understanding of *where* and *why* sentiment changes, moving beyond simply identifying positive or negative sentences. Traditional approaches to incorporate such nuance have relied on manually annotated datasets providing detailed subjectivity information (Wilson et al., 2006; Choi and Cardie, 2008). However, the creation of these resources is both expensive and time-consuming, severely limiting their scalability and applicability to diverse domains and languages. Recognizing this bottleneck, recent work has explored modeling subjectivity as a *latent* variable, inferring the underlying subjective state of the text without explicit annotations (e.g., Brody and Lapata, 2010; Li et al., 2014). These latent variable models offer a promising pathway to leverage the benefits of fine-grained subjectivity without the laborious annotation process. However, current latent variable approaches, while demonstrating encouraging results, often operate as a “black box,” failing to fully exploit readily available linguistic knowledge. A crucial, yet largely untapped, source of this knowledge lies in *discourse connectives* – words and phrases like “because,” “but,” “however,” and “therefore” – which explicitly signal relationships between clauses and segments of text. These connectors serve as vital cues to shifts in argumentation, opinion, and subjectivity, effectively outlining the logical flow and semantic connections within a document. For instance, the connective “although” immediately signals a potential contrast in sentiment, while “because” often introduces a justification for a preceding opinion. In this paper, we argue that integrating discourse connectives into latent variable subjectivity modeling holds the key to substantial improvements in document-level sentiment analysis. We present a novel method that injects linguistic knowledge about discourse structure into a latent variable framework. Specifically, we introduce connector-augmented transition features that allow the model to learn the relevance of specific discourse connectors for predicting changes in the latent subjective state. Crucially, this is achieved *without* requiring any explicit subjectivity annotations. The model learns to associate connectors with subjectivity transitions directly from the sentiment analysis task itself. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on both English and Spanish datasets, showcasing significant performance gains over existing methods. Furthermore, we propose a simple, yet effective, heuristic for automatically identifying discourse connectors even in the absence of a predefined list, enabling broader application of our technique.

Machine Translation (MT) has rapidly advanced in recent years, becoming an indispensable tool for cross-lingual communication. However, not all translations are created equal – the quality of MT output can vary significantly depending on factors like language pair, domain, and sentence complexity. Consequently, knowing *whether* to trust a particular translation is as important as the translation itself. This has spurred a growing field of research in Quality Estimation (QE), aiming to predict the quality of MT output *without* access to reference translations. Traditionally, QE focused on system-level evaluation, predicting the quality of translations produced by a specific MT system. More recently, the focus has shifted to sentence-level QE, predicting the quality of individual sentences. This is crucial for applications like interactive MT, where users need immediate feedback on translation quality, and post-editing, where human translators need to prioritize sentences requiring more attention. Sentence-level QE has seen a proliferation of approaches, ranging from traditional feature-based models like Support Vector Regression (SVR) and Ridge Regression, to more modern neural network-based methods. While neural models have demonstrated strong performance, the landscape of QE models is diverse, and a comprehensive comparison is lacking. Existing studies often focus on a limited subset of models or evaluation datasets. Furthermore, the robustness of these models – their ability to generalize across different data distributions – remains largely unexplored. A model that performs well on one dataset might falter when presented with data from a different domain or with subtle variations in input characteristics. In this paper, we undertake a thorough evaluation of a wide range of advanced sentence-level QE models. We compare the performance of SVR, Ridge Regression, various Neural Network (NN) architectures, Gaussian Processes (GPs), Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs), Deep Kernel Learning (DKL), and Deep Gaussian Processes (DGPs). Beyond simply reporting accuracy metrics, our primary concern revolves around the *robustness* of these models. We investigate how their behavior changes depending on the characteristics of the feature space – specifically, whether the dimensionality is small, medium, or large – and crucially, how performance shifts when evaluating on data from the same domain used for training versus data from an out-of-domain setting. Our findings reveal that QE models do not uniformly perform across different conditions. We demonstrate that the optimal model choice is contingent on the feature space dimensionality and the data distribution of the test set. We identify specific models that exhibit greater stability and generalization ability, offering practical recommendations for choosing a QE model based on the intended application and available resources. Ultimately, our work highlights the significant challenges in building robust and reliable QE systems, and lays the groundwork for future research towards more adaptive and trustworthy MT pipelines. Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) is a semantic formalism designed to capture the meaning of a sentence in a graph-based structure (Banarescu et al., 2013). Unlike traditional syntactic representations, AMR focuses solely on *what* is being expressed, rather than *how* it is being expressed, making it a valuable resource for semantic parsing, information extraction, and, crucially, text generation. The task of AMR-to-text generation aims to automatically produce natural language text from a given AMR graph, effectively reversing the semantic parsing process. This task presents significant challenges, requiring models to not only understand the complex relational information encoded in the graph but also to fluently and grammatically realize that information as coherent text. Recent advances in neural sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models have shown considerable success in AMR-to-text generation (Li et al., 2016; Song et al., 2018). These approaches typically linearize the AMR graph into a sequential representation – often using a depth-first traversal – and then feed this sequence into an encoder-decoder framework, commonly employing Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. While effective, this linearization process inherently disrupts the graph structure, potentially leading to a loss of important relational information, particularly in larger and more complex AMR graphs. A sequence LSTM, despite its ability to model long-range dependencies, can struggle to capture the holistic graph semantics when faced with lengthy linearized sequences. This limitation becomes more pronounced as the size of the AMR graph increases, resulting in diminished generation quality. The inherent challenges with representing graph structures using sequential models have motivated exploration of alternative approaches. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) offer a promising avenue, directly operating on the graph structure and leveraging message-passing mechanisms to encode the relationships between nodes. However, directly applying GNNs to text generation can be complex, as the output text requires a sequential structure. In this work, we propose a novel neural *graph-to-sequence* model for AMR-to-text generation. Our model eschews the explicit linearization step, instead employing a specialized LSTM architecture designed to directly encode graph-level semantics. This architecture incorporates a graph attention mechanism, allowing the model to dynamically attend to relevant nodes and edges within the AMR graph during the encoding process. By leveraging this approach, we aim to preserve the crucial structural information inherent in the AMR graph while simultaneously facilitating the generation of fluent and accurate text. We demonstrate through experiments on a standard AMR-to-text benchmark that our graph-to-sequence model consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the benefits of directly encoding graph semantics for this challenging task. The key contribution of this work lies in the development of a novel LSTM architecture that effectively bridges the gap between graph-structured input and sequential text output, offering a more robust and accurate solution for AMR-to-text generation. Automatic summarization has become increasingly important with the explosive growth of online information. The core objective of summarization is to condense a source text – be it a single document or a collection – into a shorter, coherent version that retains the most important information. Early approaches to summarization largely focused on extracting salient sentences based on features like term frequency, sentence position, and cue words (Luhn, 1958; Edmundson, 1969). While these methods offer a degree of automation, they often result in summaries that lack coherence and readability, appearing as a disjointed collection of important, yet unrelated, sentences. More recent work has attempted to address the coherence problem. These approaches often incorporate rhetorical structure theory (RST) to identify relationships between sentences (Marcu, 2000) or utilize graph-based models to represent the relationships between text segments (Wan and Li, 2008; Mihalcea and Dascalu, 2009). Graph-based methods, in particular, have proven effective, often representing sentences as nodes and semantic relationships between them as edges. However, many such systems still primarily prioritize salience, viewing coherence as a secondary concern addressed through post-processing steps or limited relational features. This paper argues that coherence should be a fundamental component of the summarization process, interwoven with informativeness from the outset. We propose a novel graph-based method that explicitly leverages *text links* – inherent relational cues within and between documents – to simultaneously optimize for both coherence and informativeness. Our approach differs from existing graph-based summarization techniques in its emphasis on identifying a cohesive sequence of sentences, guided not only by content similarity but also by the presence of explicit and implicit textual connections. We model the multi-document corpus as a heterogeneous graph, where nodes represent sentences and edges denote various types of relationships: semantic similarity, coreference, and crucially, textual links indicative of discourse relations. Utilizing this graph structure, we formulate the summarization task as a path-finding problem, aiming to discover a sentence sequence that maximizes a combined score reflecting both content relevance (informativeness) and path coherence. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we conducted experiments on the Document Understanding Conference (DUC) 2004 summarization task dataset. Our results demonstrate that the summaries generated by our system achieve competitive performance in terms of the standard ROUGE metric (Lin, 2004), mirroring the precision and recall of existing state-of-the-art methods. More importantly, human evaluations reveal a significant improvement in the readability and overall coherence of our summaries compared to those produced by baseline systems. This suggests that explicitly modeling and leveraging text links offers a promising avenue for generating more natural and informative multi-document summaries. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews related work in multi-document summarization and graph-based approaches. Section 3 details our proposed method, including the graph construction process and the sentence selection algorithm. Section 4 presents the experimental setup, results, and analysis. Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper and discusses future research directions.

Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) has emerged as a dominant paradigm in machine translation, achieving remarkable progress in recent years (Koehn et al., 2003; Chiang, 2005). However, the performance of SMT systems remains heavily reliant on the availability of large, high-quality parallel corpora—text paired with its translation in the target language. This dependency poses a significant challenge, particularly for low-resource language pairs where such data is scarce or nonexistent. A persistent issue within SMT, exacerbating the problem of limited parallel data, is the presence of untranslated words – words in the source sentence that do not appear in the training vocabulary (Papineni et al., 2002). These out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words disrupt the translation process and contribute significantly to translation errors. Various approaches have been explored to address the data sparsity and OOV problems. One popular technique involves data augmentation through pivoting – leveraging a third, pivot language to translate from the source to the pivot language, and then from the pivot to the target language (Ueffing & Ney, 2003; Suzuki et al., 2008). While effective, pivoting introduces its own complexities, including error propagation and the need for additional parallel corpora between the source/target and the pivot language. This requirement limits the applicability of pivoting in scenarios where resources are already constrained. Recent research has also investigated the utilization of monolingual data, recognizing its potential to enrich the language model component of SMT systems (Schmidhuber, 2003). However, directly incorporating monolingual data into the translation model itself remains a challenge. A promising avenue for achieving this is through the generation of paraphrases – alternative formulations of the same meaning. Leveraging monolingual paraphrases effectively expands the training data, providing additional contexts for rare words and improving the overall fluency and adequacy of translations. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to SMT augmentation based on *monolingually-derived paraphrases*. Instead of relying on pivoting, we leverage distributional semantic similarity measures applied to large monolingual corpora to identify paraphrases within a single language. This allows us to tap into significantly larger training resources, including comparable and even entirely unrelated monolingual text, circumventing the need for additional parallel data. Furthermore, we present a novel integration of this paraphrasing technique with a state-of-the-art, end-to-end SMT system, specifically focusing on addressing the problem of untranslated words through a collocational approach. Our experimental results demonstrate substantial improvements in translation quality, particularly in a low-resource setting, confirming the effectiveness of our proposed method. Task-completion dialogue systems aim to assist users in achieving specific goals, such as booking a restaurant or finding a movie. Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) have shown promising results in learning dialogue policies (Li et al., 2016; Zhao & Eskenazi, 2016; Wen et al., 2017). However, training DRL agents for dialogue management typically requires a substantial number of interactions with real users, which is often costly and time-consuming. To alleviate this sample inefficiency problem, planning-based methods have gained attention as a way to learn more efficiently from limited real-world experience. A particularly promising approach is Dyna-Q (Sutton, 1990), which augments standard Q-learning by learning a model of the environment and using this model to generate simulated experiences for planning. Recently, Deep Dyna-Q (DDQ) (Wang et al., 2020) extended this framework by leveraging deep neural networks to represent the Q-function and the environment model, enabling it to effectively handle complex dialogue states and actions. DDQ demonstrates significant improvements over standard DRL methods in sample efficiency and task completion rate. However, a key challenge with planning-based methods like DDQ is their reliance on the quality of the simulated experiences. The environment model learned by DDQ can be inaccurate, leading to the generation of unrealistic or suboptimal simulated transitions. This can negatively impact the learning process, as the agent may learn to exploit flaws in the model rather than developing a robust policy for interacting with real users. In essence, "garbage in, garbage out": poor simulation data leads to poor planning and ultimately, a weaker policy. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach called Discriminative Deep Dyna-Q (D3Q). D3Q builds upon DDQ by incorporating a discriminator network based on recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to explicitly differentiate between simulated and real user experiences. This discriminator is then used to weight or filter the simulated experiences used for planning, effectively controlling the quality of the training data. By prioritizing simulated experiences that are more similar to real interactions, D3Q can mitigate the negative effects of an inaccurate environment model and learn more robust dialogue policies. Our key contribution lies in the integration of a discriminative model within the Dyna-Q framework. This allows us to selectively leverage simulated data, improving the stability and convergence of the learning process. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of D3Q in a domain extension setting, where the agent must adapt to a changing environment with new user intents and dialogue states. This showcases the robustness of our approach and its ability to generalize beyond the initial training distribution. Experiments in a simulated restaurant booking domain show that D3Q significantly outperforms DDQ, achieving considerably higher task completion rates. Event pattern extraction, the task of identifying mentions of event types and their arguments in text, is a cornerstone of information extraction with applications ranging from news analysis and crisis management to knowledge base population. A major challenge in this field is the inherent variability in how events are expressed linguistically – the same event can be described using a multitude of different paraphrases. For instance, a “company acquisition” might be reported as “X acquires Y,” “Y is bought by X,” or “X completes takeover of Y.” Identifying these diverse surface realizations as instances of the same underlying event pattern is crucial for high-recall event extraction. Traditional approaches to event pattern learning often rely on manually crafted rules or distantly supervised learning with heuristics based on lexical overlap or co-occurrence statistics (e.g., Hoffmann et al., 2016; Schoenick et al., 2017). While effective to a degree, these methods struggle to generalize to novel paraphrases and often require substantial manual effort for pattern refinement. More recent work has explored neural network architectures for learning event pattern representations, leveraging large labeled datasets or carefully engineered features (e.g., Nguyen and Grishman, 2018; Lai et al., 2019). However, creating such large, high-quality labeled datasets is expensive and time-consuming, and feature engineering demands significant domain expertise. In this paper, we introduce IDEST (Inferring Distributed Representations for Event Patterns), a novel approach for learning event pattern paraphrases that minimizes the reliance on explicit supervision. IDEST leverages a unique form of weak supervision inherent in news data: the assumption that news articles published on the same day and referencing the same real-world entities frequently describe related events. This allows us to create noisy but readily available training data without requiring costly manual annotations. At the heart of IDEST is a novel neural network architecture designed to learn distributed representations of event patterns directly from these weakly supervised examples. Our key contribution lies in demonstrating that IDEST can effectively capture semantic similarity between event patterns using only this weak supervision signal. The learned representations are robust and generalize well across extractions from different dates, enabling the model to identify paraphrases it has never encountered during training. This generalization capability is particularly valuable for capturing representations of rare event patterns, which often suffer from data sparsity. We empirically evaluate IDEST on a challenging event extraction dataset and demonstrate its ability to achieve comparable performance to state-of-the-art systems when trained on a small dataset. Furthermore, we show that IDEST’s generalization capabilities allow it to effectively leverage larger amounts of weakly supervised data, leading to substantial improvements in event pattern extraction quality. We believe IDEST represents a significant step towards more robust and scalable event pattern learning with minimal manual effort. Semantic parsing – the task of mapping natural language utterances to formal meaning representations – has witnessed significant advances in recent years, largely fueled by the proliferation of neural network architectures and large-scale datasets. However, despite these gains, accurately capturing the semantic nuances of natural language remains a considerable challenge. A prevailing paradigm in semantic parsing relies heavily on syntactic structure as a crucial intermediate representation. The rationale is intuitive: the hierarchical organization of a sentence, as revealed by its parse tree, often mirrors the compositional structure of its meaning. Consider syntactic alternations, such as the causative-inchoative alternation in English (“John broke the window” vs. “The window broke”), control phenomena (where a verb governs the interpretation of a pronoun in a subordinate clause), or raising constructions (where a subject appears to be governed by two different verbs). These structures, while central to the formal study of syntax, introduce complexities that obscure the direct relationship between syntactic form and semantic content. They represent surface-level variations that do not fundamentally alter the underlying semantic relationships within a sentence. A truly effective semantic parser, therefore, should ideally operate on a representation that is less burdened by these purely syntactic intricacies. By “deeper” syntax, we refer to a structural organization of the sentence that prioritizes semantic relationships and minimizes the impact of surface syntactic variations. This abstraction results in a representation more closely aligned with the target semantic structure, facilitating a more direct and accurate mapping from form to meaning. We investigate this concept through experiments conducted on a French corpus annotated with semantic frames, utilizing a frame-based semantic parsing approach. Our findings demonstrate that incorporating a deep syntactic input significantly boosts the performance of a semantic parser, achieving notable gains over systems relying on traditional syntactic analysis. We present a methodology for constructing this deep syntactic representation and detail the empirical evidence supporting its effectiveness. This work offers a novel perspective on the interplay between syntax and semantics and provides a promising avenue for further research in semantic parsing and natural language understanding. Machine comprehension (MC), the task of automatically answering questions about a given text passage, has witnessed substantial progress in recent years, fueled by the advent of large-scale datasets like SQuAD (Rajpurkar et al., 2016) and the development of powerful neural network architectures (Wang et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2017). However, a key limitation of current MC models is their reliance on extensive labeled data – specifically, question-answer pairs – for training. Obtaining such datasets is costly and time-consuming, hindering the application of MC to new domains where labeled data is scarce or unavailable. This presents a significant challenge for real-world deployment, as the need to adapt to diverse information sources is paramount. The problem of transferring knowledge learned in one domain (source domain) to another (target domain) is a central issue in machine learning known as transfer learning. In the context of MC, this often manifests as training a model on a large, annotated dataset like SQuAD and then attempting to apply it, without further training, to a new dataset like NewsQA (Trischler et al., 2019) or HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018). While direct transfer can yield some results, performance often degrades significantly when the target domain differs substantially from the source domain in terms of content, style, or question types. Existing approaches to address this domain gap include fine-tuning the pretrained model on a small amount of labeled data from the target domain (Wang et al., 2019), domain adaptation techniques focusing on aligning feature distributions (Gulcehre et al., 2017), or generating synthetic training data (Luan et al., 2020). However, leveraging labeled data directly often defeats the purpose of truly zero-shot transfer, while domain adaptation can be complex and may not effectively capture the nuances of question answering. Synthetic data generation requires careful design to avoid introducing biases or inaccuracies. In this paper, we introduce a novel technique for transfer learning in MC that avoids the need for any labeled target domain data. Our method leverages a two-stage synthesis network (SynNet) designed to generate plausible question-answer pairs within the target domain, using a pretrained MC model as a core component. The key idea is to first synthesize questions from the target domain text, and then use the pretrained model to *answer* those synthesized questions, effectively creating a self-training loop. This allows the model to bootstrap itself in the new domain without requiring human annotations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SynNet by applying it to the challenging NewsQA dataset, using a model pretrained on SQuAD as our foundation. Our results show that SynNet achieves an F1 score of 46.6% on NewsQA, approaching the performance of models trained directly on the NewsQA dataset (F1 score of 50.0%) and significantly outperforming a baseline that applies the pretrained model *without* synthesis (F1 score of 39.0%). This work represents a significant step towards robust and adaptable MC systems capable of reasoning about diverse textual content in a truly zero-shot manner.

Humans rarely process text uniformly; rather, our attention is drawn to specific concepts, entities, and topics that pique our curiosity and warrant further exploration. Identifying these “interesting” elements within a document is a core challenge with broad implications for information retrieval, text summarization, and personalized recommendations. While traditional approaches often rely on metrics like term frequency or centrality, these fail to capture the nuanced, subjective nature of user interest. What one individual finds compelling, another may deem irrelevant. Recent advances in user modeling and behavioral data collection provide new avenues for understanding and predicting this personalized interest. In this work, we address the problem of predicting “interestingness” – specifically, the level of interest a user has in various spans of text within a document. Unlike approaches that attempt to define interestingness *a priori*, we learn it directly from user behavior, leveraging naturally occurring “interest signals” derived from web browsing patterns. We hypothesize that transitions between web pages – specifically, clicks from one page to another – represent a strong indication of user interest. A user is more likely to click on a link that represents a concept or topic they wish to learn more about. Our approach casts this prediction problem as a discriminative learning task, leveraging features extracted from both the textual context surrounding potential interest spans and the semantic content of the documents involved in the transition. The textual context features capture local cues that might signal relevance, while the semantic features provide a broader understanding of the underlying concepts. A key innovation lies in our development of a novel, unsupervised approach to learning these semantic features. We employ probabilistic inference over a graphical model to discover a latent joint topic space shared by the source and target documents of each transition. This allows us to represent the semantic relationship between the pages, and consequently, the likely interest of a user in exploring that relationship. We evaluate our models on a large-scale dataset constructed from millions of real-world transitions between Wikipedia documents, as observed from anonymized web browser session logs. This provides a robust and realistic testbed for assessing the effectiveness of our approach. Our experimental results demonstrate significant improvement over a variety of baselines, highlighting the value of both our discriminative learning framework and the incorporation of latent semantic modeling. This work offers a promising step toward building systems that can dynamically identify and prioritize information based on individual user interests, ultimately enhancing the online reading and learning experience. The automatic identification of semantic classes within text is a core task in natural language processing with applications ranging from information extraction and text categorization to dialogue systems and question answering. Traditionally, achieving high performance on semantic tagging tasks requires large, manually-annotated datasets – a costly and time-consuming undertaking, particularly when targeting specialized domains. The creation of such datasets often necessitates expert knowledge, further increasing the barrier to entry for new domains or rapidly evolving fields. This reliance on substantial labeled data presents a significant bottleneck for adapting NLP systems to niche areas where annotation resources are scarce. Recent work has explored techniques for reducing the annotation burden. Distant supervision (Mintz et al., 2009; Hoffmann et al., 2011), for instance, leverages existing knowledge bases to automatically label data, albeit often introducing noisy labels. Bootstrapping methods (Yarowsky, 1995; Collins and Singer, 1999) iteratively refine a classifier using its own predictions, starting from a small set of seed examples. While promising, these approaches often struggle with generalization and can be sensitive to the quality of the initial seeds. This paper introduces a novel approach to inducing domain-specific semantic class taggers from minimal supervision. Our central tenet is that, given a collection of text from a target domain and a small set of seed words for each semantic class, we can leverage contextual information to learn robust classifiers *without* relying on large, pre-existing labeled datasets. We aim to approach the problem of semantic tagging from “almost nothing,” minimizing the need for manual effort. Our method proceeds in two key phases. First, we induce an initial contextual classifier for each semantic class, relying solely on features derived from the surrounding text and the provided seed words. This forces the classifier to generalize beyond the limited seed examples, effectively capturing the broader contextual patterns associated with each class. The classifier’s predictions are then used to expand and diversify the training set, creating a larger and more representative dataset. Second, we employ a cross-category bootstrapping process. This simultaneous training of classifiers for multiple semantic classes leverages the inherent distinctions between categories. Positive instances identified for one class are actively utilized as negative instances for all others, fostering a more discriminative learning environment and promoting a mutual refinement of the class boundaries. Furthermore, we introduce a heuristic that leverages the common assumption of one primary semantic class per discourse unit – a phrase or sentence. This constraint is incorporated into the learning process to further improve accuracy. Finally, we demonstrate how the induced classifiers can be dynamically used to generate new semantic features, enhancing the overall system performance. We evaluate our approach by inducing six semantic taggers from a collection of veterinary medicine message board posts. This domain presents a challenging, specialized vocabulary and requires understanding of complex concepts. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in generating surprisingly accurate taggers with minimal supervision, highlighting the potential for rapid adaptation of NLP systems to new and emerging domains.

Dependency parsing is a fundamental task in natural language processing, serving as a crucial component in numerous downstream applications such as machine translation, information extraction, and question answering. The goal of dependency parsing is to analyze the grammatical structure of a sentence, establishing relationships between individual words – specifically, identifying the head (governor) and dependent (modifier) for each word in the sentence, ultimately forming a connected tree structure. Over the past decades, significant advances have been made in dependency parsing, leading to highly accurate systems, largely driven by the adoption of machine learning techniques. However, despite these advancements, achieving consistently high performance across diverse datasets and languages remains a considerable challenge. It is increasingly recognized that not all dependencies are created equal; some grammatical relations are readily learned from relatively small training datasets, while others prove remarkably difficult, requiring vast amounts of annotated data or sophisticated modeling approaches. This disparity suggests an inherent heterogeneity in the “learnability” of different dependency types. Existing research has largely focused on improving parsing accuracy through architectural innovations (e.g., graph-based vs. transition-based parsers), feature engineering, or novel learning algorithms. While effective, these efforts often lack a fine-grained understanding of *why* certain dependencies are more challenging than others. A deeper understanding of these challenges would not only allow for a more principled evaluation of parsing systems, but also inform strategies to specifically address the more difficult cases. Furthermore, a quantitative analysis of dependency difficulty could be highly valuable in assessing the quality and utility of cross-lingual projection approaches, where parsers trained on resource-rich languages are applied to lower-resource languages. In this work, we address this gap by introducing a novel suite of metrics designed to quantify the inherent learning challenges associated with different dependency relations. We aim to move beyond simple accuracy scores and provide a more nuanced picture of parser performance, revealing specific weaknesses and highlighting areas where improvements are most needed. Our metrics are designed to capture aspects such as the frequency of a dependency type, its structural context, and the ambiguity associated with its attachment. By analyzing these factors, we gain valuable insights into the characteristics that contribute to parsing difficulty. We demonstrate the utility of these metrics through a comprehensive comparison of several state-of-the-art dependency parsers, and illustrate their effectiveness in characterizing the information transferred by cross-lingual parsers. The aim is to arm the NLP community with tools for a more detailed analysis of dependency parsing challenges and ultimately, to drive further progress in this critical area of NLP. Named Entity Recognition (NER) – the task of identifying and classifying named entities in text – is a fundamental component of many Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications, including information extraction, question answering, and machine translation. Accurate NER systems are crucial for enabling machines to understand and process unstructured text effectively. While significant progress has been made in NER for languages like English, applying these techniques directly to morphologically rich languages poses substantial challenges. Turkish, in particular, presents unique difficulties due to its agglutinative structure, where suffixes are liberally appended to roots to express grammatical relations and semantic nuances. This results in a vast number of possible word forms, making it difficult for traditional NER approaches relying on limited vocabulary or surface form patterns to generalize effectively. Current state-of-the-art NER systems often leverage machine learning techniques, with Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) proving particularly successful (Lafferty et al., 2001). CRFs offer a probabilistic framework for modeling sequential data, allowing for the incorporation of a wide range of features to capture contextual information and dependencies between entities. However, the inherent complexities of Turkish require careful consideration of feature engineering to effectively exploit the language’s rich morphological information. Previous attempts at Turkish NER have yielded promising, but ultimately limited, results. Early work often relied heavily on manually crafted rules and gazetteers (Türetken et al., 2004; Oflazer, 2005), which proved brittle and lacked robustness when applied to unseen data. More recent studies have explored the use of machine learning, predominantly Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) and Maximum Entropy Models (MEMs), but these approaches have struggled to fully capture the subtle patterns present in Turkish text (Dermeval et al., 2008; Yılmaz et al., 2012). This paper presents an initial exploration into the application of CRFs to the task of Turkish NER, specifically focusing on the detection of Person, Location, and Organization entities in general news texts. We hypothesize that by carefully integrating features that leverage the morphological richness of Turkish, alongside the utilization of generative gazetteers, we can significantly improve upon existing NER performance. We provide a detailed analysis of previous studies, highlighting their strengths and weaknesses, and present a comparative evaluation of our approach against established benchmarks. Critically, we report results achieving state-of-the-art performance – reaching 95% accuracy in the MUC evaluation metric and 92% in the CoNLL metric – demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed methodology and paving the way for further advancements in Turkish NER. This work serves as a foundational step towards building more robust and accurate NLP systems for the Turkish language. References: Lafferty, J., McCallum, A., & Pereira, F. (2001). The ability to understand language goes far beyond simply recognizing words and parsing their syntactic structure. A crucial component of human language understanding involves *lexicosyntactic inference* – the process of drawing conclusions based on the interplay between the meanings of words (lexical semantics) and the way those words are combined grammatically (syntax). For instance, understanding that “John promised Mary to visit her” implies John will visit Mary requires integrating the semantic constraints of ‘promise’ (which necessitates a future event) with the syntactic structure indicating Mary as the recipient of the action. While recent advances in neural network models have led to impressive performance on various natural language processing tasks, a fundamental question remains: to what extent do these models genuinely *capture* and reason with these subtle, yet essential, lexicosyntactic inferences? Existing neural language models often achieve high accuracy by leveraging massive datasets and statistical correlations. However, this success does not necessarily equate to genuine understanding. It is possible for a model to perform well without explicitly representing or reasoning about the underlying semantic and syntactic constraints that humans readily employ. Examining the systematic errors made by these models can reveal gaps in their ability to perform lexicosyntactic inference. In this work, we directly address the question of how well current neural models capture lexicosyntactic inferences. We focus on *event factuality prediction* – determining whether an event described by a clause is likely to actually occur – as a probing task. This task is particularly well-suited for revealing lexicosyntactic understanding, as factuality is frequently determined by the specific lexical item governing the event and its surrounding syntactic context. For example, the verb ‘believe’ generally indicates a non-factual event (someone *believes* something, but that doesn't make it true), while ‘confirm’ suggests a factual event. To facilitate this investigation, we introduce a novel, publicly available dataset designed to specifically test lexicosyntactic inference abilities. The dataset consists of factuality judgments for all English clause-embedding verbs (verbs that take another clause as an argument), presented across a diverse set of syntactic constructions. This ensures a comprehensive evaluation of a model’s ability to handle varying grammatical structures alongside lexical nuances. We then probe the behavior of several state-of-the-art neural models on this dataset. Our analysis reveals systematic error patterns demonstrating that, despite their overall language capabilities, these models often struggle with nuances in event factuality driven by lexicosyntactic information. By highlighting these shortcomings through the lens of factuality prediction, we aim to provide insights into the limitations of current neural approaches and motivate future research towards more robust and genuinely understanding models of language. The demand for natural language generation (NLG) systems capable of producing fluent and coherent text across multiple languages is steadily increasing. Applications such as machine translation post-editing, dialogue systems, and automated content creation all necessitate robust and adaptable sentence generation modules. While significant progress has been made in statistical NLG, many current approaches remain limited by their reliance on syntactically annotated corpora, and, crucially, a single-stage projection from underlying representations to surface text. This presents a bottleneck for applications operating from semantic representations, which are increasingly prevalent in modern NLG pipelines. Traditionally, full-fledged text generation begins with semantic structures – often predicate-argument representations – outlining the ‘what’ to be said, before proceeding through intermediate stages of sentence planning, linearization, and finally, morphological realization to produce well-formed sentences. To effectively address these multiple levels of the generation process, stochastic generators require correspondingly multi-level annotated corpora, enabling them to learn the complex relationships between semantic content and surface form. The scarcity of such comprehensive datasets has historically hindered the development of truly deep and versatile NLG systems. However, the landscape is changing. Multilevel annotated corpora, encompassing semantic, syntactic, and morphological information, are becoming increasingly available for a growing number of languages, fueled by ongoing research in semantic parsing and cross-linguistic annotation efforts. This availability unlocks the potential to build more sophisticated and linguistically informed sentence realizers. In this paper, we capitalize on this trend and propose a multilingual, deep stochastic sentence realizer designed to mirror the advancements in semantic parsing research. Our system is uniquely structured to address the complexities of multi-level generation. Rather than a monolithic projection, we employ a modular approach, decomposing the generation process into a series of sequential decoders. Specifically, for each pair of adjacent annotation levels – for example, semantic to syntactic, or syntactic to morphological – a separate decoder is trained using a Support Vector Machine (SVM) learning algorithm. This allows each module to specialize in a distinct aspect of the generation process, promoting greater accuracy and control. We have evaluated our realizer’s performance across four diverse languages: Chinese, English, German, and Spanish, demonstrating its adaptability and broad coverage. Our preliminary results indicate a significant potential for improving the fluency and coherence of generated text when compared to traditional single-stage approaches. This work represents a step towards building truly multilingual NLG systems capable of adapting to the intricacies of different languages and efficiently realizing complex semantic content into natural-sounding text. Part-of-speech (POS) tagging is a fundamental task in natural language processing, serving as a crucial preprocessing step for a wide range of downstream applications, including parsing, machine translation, and information extraction. While state-of-the-art POS taggers achieve high accuracy on standard benchmark datasets, their performance often degrades significantly when applied to text from different domains or genres than those on which they were trained – a phenomenon known as domain shift. This sensitivity to domain shifts limits the practical applicability of these systems and motivates the development of more robust tagging models. Recent work in machine learning, particularly in areas like robust generalization (Ben-David et al., 2010) and adversarial training (Goodfellow et al., 2014), has highlighted the importance of explicitly accounting for potential distribution shifts during model training. These approaches aim to learn models that are less vulnerable to perturbations in the input data distribution, thereby improving their generalization performance on unseen data. Inspired by these insights, we introduce a novel approach to training structured perceptrons for POS tagging that is specifically designed to enhance robustness to domain shifts. Our core idea is to minimize the average loss under a set of plausible distribution shifts, rather than solely optimizing performance on the training distribution. This is achieved through a carefully crafted objective function that considers mixtures of the source (training) data distribution and random Zipfian distributions. Zipf’s Law (Zipf, 1935) describes the frequency distribution of words in natural language, exhibiting a power-law relationship where a small number of words occur very frequently, while the vast majority occur rarely. By introducing Zipfian noise, we simulate shifts in word frequencies likely to occur across different text domains. Specifically, we assume that under distribution shifts, the input data occurs following a probability distribution where the likelihood of a particular word is proportional to 1/rank(word), where rank(word) indicates the word's frequency rank in the corpus. The key contribution of this work is a practical algorithm for minimizing this average loss under Zipfian corruptions. We demonstrate that training with this objective function leads to significant improvements in POS tagging accuracy on both the English Web Treebank and the Danish Dependency Treebank. Our experiments show an average error reduction of 4.4% across these datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach in enhancing the robustness of POS tagging models to domain shifts. This work represents a step towards building more reliable and adaptable NLP systems that can perform effectively in real-world scenarios characterized by diverse and evolving data distributions. The human brain’s capacity to represent and process conceptual knowledge is a cornerstone of cognitive function, enabling us to understand and interact with the world around us. A crucial area of research focuses on how this conceptual knowledge is grounded in neural activity, and whether computational models of semantics can effectively capture and predict this neural representation. Recent advances in neuroimaging techniques, coupled with the increasing availability of large-scale textual corpora, have opened new avenues for exploring this relationship. A particularly influential study by Mitchell et al. (2008) demonstrated a striking correlation between patterns of brain activity, measured using functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI), and semantic information extracted from corpora. Specifically, they showed that vector-space models trained on large text datasets could successfully predict which concept a participant was currently thinking about, as evidenced by their fMRI activation patterns. This work suggested a powerful methodology – using corpus-derived semantic models as a proxy for understanding neural representations of concepts. However, fMRI, while providing excellent spatial resolution, suffers from limitations that hinder its widespread use in cognitive neuroscience research. These limitations include its high cost, the need for specialized equipment, and significant constraints on the experimental environment – participants must remain largely motionless within a scanner. This makes it challenging to conduct large-scale experiments, explore dynamic cognitive processes, and investigate individual differences. Moreover, fMRI data suffers from relatively poor temporal resolution, making it difficult to pinpoint the precise timing of neural events. Electroencephalography (EEG), in contrast, offers excellent temporal resolution, is comparatively inexpensive, and allows for more flexible experimental setups. While EEG traditionally has lower spatial resolution than fMRI, recent advances in signal processing and analysis techniques are enabling researchers to extract increasingly detailed information from EEG data. Previous research has indicated that EEG activation patterns *do* encode conceptual information; for example, studies have shown the ability to discriminate broad conceptual categories based on EEG signals. Building upon these advancements, we investigate whether corpus-based semantic representations can predict EEG activation patterns, mirroring the success of the fMRI studies by Mitchell et al. (2008). Our work aims to demonstrate the feasibility of using EEG as a more accessible and flexible tool for evaluating computational models of conceptual knowledge. Furthermore, we evaluate the performance of different corpus-based semantic models – varying in their approaches to capturing semantic relationships – in predicting EEG responses. By comparing the predictive power of these models, we aim to gain insights into which aspects of semantic knowledge are most strongly reflected in neural activity as measured by EEG. This research ultimately contributes to a deeper understanding of the neural basis of conceptual representation and the validity of using corpus linguistics to model human semantic cognition. Multiword expressions (MWEs) pose a significant challenge to natural language parsing. These expressions, ranging from idioms like “kick the bucket” to collocations like “strong tea,” are frequently encountered in everyday language, yet their behavior often defies straightforward compositional analysis. A key difficulty lies in their inherent ambiguity: MWEs can possess both an idiomatic, non-compositional meaning and a literal, compositional interpretation, leading to increased syntactic ambiguity during parsing. For example, the phrase “white elephant” can refer to a costly but useless possession (idiomatic) or literally to a pale-colored elephant (compositional). Traditional parsing approaches often struggle to resolve this ambiguity effectively, resulting in a proliferation of possible parse trees and increased computational cost. This issue is particularly pronounced in formal grammar frameworks like Tree Adjoining Grammars (TAGs), which, while offering greater expressive power than context-free grammars, can suffer from combinatorial explosion when faced with ambiguous structures. The core complexity of TAG parsing originates from the inherent ambiguity stemming from the multiple adjunction operations possible within a given sentence. However, a crucial observation can mitigate this problem for certain types of MWEs. Empirically, many MWEs exhibit a strong preference for their idiomatic interpretation in typical contexts. While not universally true for *all* MWEs, this skew towards idiomaticity provides a valuable heuristic that can be leveraged to guide the parsing process. This paper exploits this tendency by introducing a promotion heuristic within an A TAG parser. Our approach doesn’t aim to definitively *resolve* MWE ambiguity, but rather to intelligently *prioritize* parse trees that align with the likely idiomatic reading. We achieve this by strategically altering the parsing agenda, effectively “promoting” analyses that involve recognizing the MWE as a single, non-compositional unit. This promotion translates to assigning higher scores to these analyses during the search process, encouraging the parser to explore them more aggressively. The key benefit of this heuristic is its efficiency. By focusing the parser’s attention on the most probable analyses, we significantly reduce the size of the search space when a true MWE is encountered. Furthermore, the design is robust to errors. Even in cases where a phrase is incorrectly identified as an MWE (a false positive), the promotion doesn’t lead to parsing failures; it simply results in the exploration of a potentially suboptimal parse tree, without preventing the discovery of a correct, compositional analysis. We present experimental results demonstrating substantial improvements in parsing speed and accuracy through this simple yet effective promotion strategy, suggesting a promising direction for handling MWEs within TAG-based parsing frameworks. Lexical taxonomies, representing hierarchical relationships between concepts, are fundamental to knowledge representation and reasoning. These structures, often resembling graphs, provide a formal framework for organizing semantic information, and serve as the backbone for numerous knowledge graphs and natural language processing applications. The ‘is-a’ relation, or hypernymy – representing a broader category encompassing a more specific one (e.g., ‘dog’ is a hyponym of ‘animal’, and ‘animal’ is a hypernym of ‘dog’) – is particularly crucial in establishing this semantic structure. While substantial efforts have been devoted to constructing lexical taxonomies, most approaches either rely on manual curation, which is expensive and time-consuming, or leverage existing resources like WordNet (Miller, 1995), which may lack coverage for specialized domains or evolving terminology. Recent trends in knowledge graph construction advocate for large-scale, automatically acquired taxonomies. Distributional semantic models (DSM), which represent word meaning based on their contextual occurrences, have emerged as a promising avenue for automatically discovering hypernymic relations (Snow et al., 2003; Lin et al., 2015). These methods generally operate on the principle that hypernyms exhibit broader distributional patterns and appear in more diverse contexts than their hyponyms. However, applying DSMs to hypernym discovery presents significant challenges. Primarily, word sense ambiguity complicates the interpretation of distributional similarities. A single word form can represent multiple concepts, and relationships discovered without considering sense distinctions may be spurious. Furthermore, DSMs are inherently sensitive to the training data they are built upon; models trained on general corpora may not perform optimally when applied to specialized domains with unique terminologies and semantic patterns. In this paper, we propose a supervised distributional framework for hypernym discovery that addresses both the sense-level disambiguation and domain adaptation challenges. Our approach operates at the level of word senses, leveraging pre-trained sense embeddings. By exploiting the inherent semantic regularities between hyponyms and hypernyms in embedding spaces – specifically, the expectation that hypernym embeddings will reside in a region representative of the distribution of their hyponym embeddings – we construct a supervised learning model for hypernym prediction. Crucially, we integrate a domain clustering algorithm to enhance the model's sensitivity to the target data. This allows the model to adapt its internal representations to capture domain-specific semantic nuances. We evaluate our approach extensively, training with information derived from both a manually curated knowledge base (specifically, a subset of WordNet) and hypernymic relations automatically extracted by Open Information Extraction (OIE) systems (e.g., ReVerb; Fader et al., 2011). Our findings demonstrate that incorporating both sources of knowledge yields the best overall results, as assessed through both automatic evaluation metrics and human judgement across ten distinct domains. This result suggests that combining the precision of manually curated resources with the broad coverage of OIE systems offers a robust strategy for building comprehensive and accurate lexical taxonomies. The contributions of this work lie in the demonstration of a scalable, supervised approach to hypernym discovery that effectively tackles the challenges of sense ambiguity and domain adaptation, paving the way for the automatic construction of large-scale, disambiguated taxonomies for diverse applications.

Narrative understanding is a cornerstone of human cognition, deeply intertwined with our ability to predict, explain, and engage with stories. A crucial element underpinning this understanding is the capacity to reason about the relationships between events within a narrative – specifically, understanding *why* events occur and what consequences they are likely to produce. This reasoning relies heavily on identifying discourse relations, connections that signal how subsequent events relate to those previously described. Among these, the CONTINGENT relation holds particular significance, indicating that one event happens *because* of another, or that one event is a plausible consequence of the preceding one (Mann and Thompson, 1988). Modeling this relation, and the broader capacity for anticipating narrative flow, is therefore a fundamental challenge in Natural Language Processing (NLP). Previous work in NLP has approached this challenge from various angles. Some researchers have focused on directly inferring the CONTINGENT discourse relation, framing it as a classification problem where systems must determine if a causal or consequential link exists between two text segments (e.g., Pitler and Nenkova, 2008; Lapata et al., 2014). Others have explored modeling expectation as a form of common-sense causal reasoning, leveraging knowledge graphs and probabilistic inference to predict plausible event sequences (e.g., Chambers et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2019). These approaches often rely on meticulously curated datasets or large-scale knowledge bases, which can be expensive to create and may not generalize well to novel narratives. This paper pursues a complementary approach, focusing on *unsupervised induction* of contingent event pairs directly from narrative text. We hypothesize that even without explicit labels or external knowledge, patterns of co-occurrence in narratives can reveal likely contingent relationships. By analyzing a corpus of film scene descriptions, we aim to identify pairs of events that frequently occur together in a sequence suggestive of a causal or consequential link. Our work builds on the idea that narrative structure provides implicit signals about event dependencies. Film scene descriptions offer a particularly rich source of data, as they often concisely summarize the core actions and consequences within a scene. We explore several unsupervised methods for learning these event pairs, moving beyond simple co-occurrence statistics to incorporate measures of semantic similarity and contextual relevance. Crucially, we refine our automatically extracted event pairs by leveraging web search counts as a proxy for real-world plausibility; if a predicted contingent event pair frequently appears in web search snippets, it suggests a degree of common-sense validity. We evaluate our approach through human judgments of contingency, demonstrating that incorporating web search information significantly improves the accuracy of our learned event pairs. Our results indicate that this refinement step boosts performance substantially, achieving an average accuracy of 85.64% – a significant improvement over a baseline of 50% and a gain of over 10% compared to our best method without web search augmentation. This work represents a step towards building more robust and generalizable narrative understanding systems that can infer event expectations from minimal supervision.

The demand for high-quality paraphrases continues to grow alongside advances in natural language generation (NLG) and text manipulation tasks. Paraphrases, sentences that express the same meaning using different wording, play a vital role in applications such as text summarization (Mani, 2001), machine translation (Koehn, 2009), and question answering (Jurafsky and Martin, 2008). Traditionally, paraphrase acquisition has relied on monolingual corpora, employing techniques like synonym substitution, back-translation, or identifying sentences with high lexical overlap (Jurafsky and Martin, 2008; Ganitkevitch et al., 2007). However, the emergence of large-scale bilingual parallel corpora—collections of sentence pairs that are translations of each other—has opened up a promising new avenue for paraphrase extraction. While initial work focused on extracting *phrasal* paraphrases from bitexts, leveraging the correspondence between source and target language phrases (Qasimi & Diab, 2008; Bannard & Callison-Burch, 2008), a critical question remained: are bitexts adequately suited for identifying more complex *sentential* paraphrases? Previous approaches have largely focused on lexical alignment and phrase-level substitutions, which may not capture the rich structural re-organizations characteristic of true sentential paraphrases. Sentential paraphrases often involve deeper linguistic transformations, such as changes in voice (active to passive), argument structure (dative shift), or information focus (topicalization), and their acquisition may better be accomplished using monolingual techniques. This paper challenges that assumption. We demonstrate that bilingual parallel corpora *can* be effectively utilized to extract sophisticated sentential paraphrases, even those involving non-trivial syntactic alterations. Our work extends existing bilingual paraphrase extraction methods to incorporate syntactic information, enabling the learning of a diverse range of paraphrastic transformations. We present a model capable of identifying and applying generalizations like passivization, dative shift, and topicalization – transformations that go beyond simple lexical substitutions. Furthermore, we discuss how this paraphrase model is remarkably adaptable to various text-to-text generation tasks. Rather than remaining a standalone resource, our model serves as a building block, and we detail how its feature set, development data, and parameter estimation routine can be tailored to specific applications. To illustrate this adaptability, we focus on the task of sentence compression, demonstrating that augmenting a compression system with our learned paraphrases yields results competitive with current state-of-the-art performance. This highlights the potential for bitext-derived paraphrases to improve a wide array of NLG tasks, establishing bilingual corpora as valuable resource for both paraphrase acquisition and downstream applications. The rapid and continuous expansion of scientific literature presents a significant challenge to researchers aiming to stay abreast of developments within their fields. This exponential growth necessitates the development of effective automated tools capable of not only indexing and retrieving information, but also of *analyzing* the nuanced rhetorical structure underlying scientific writing. Traditional approaches to scientific text analysis have often focused on content-based methods, such as keyword extraction and topic modeling. However, a deeper understanding requires recognizing how knowledge is presented, justified, and positioned within the broader scientific discourse – in essence, the *rhetoric* of scientific communication. Scientific writing is fundamentally argumentative. Researchers don’t simply present findings; they construct arguments to support their claims, critique existing work, and establish the significance of their contributions. This argumentative character is often manifested through specific rhetorical strategies, influencing choices in discourse structure, citation practices, and overall presentation of information. While previous work has explored rhetorical aspects of scientific publications – such as identifying discourse categories (e.g., background, method, results) or classifying citation functions (e.g., supporting, contrasting) – a crucial link remains largely unexplored: the explicit connection between the *argumentative structure* of a paper and its observable rhetorical features. This paper directly addresses this gap. We hypothesize that a deeper understanding of a scientific paper’s argumentative components – its claims, evidence, and reasoning – can significantly enhance our ability to automatically analyze its rhetorical characteristics. To investigate this hypothesis, we undertake two key steps. First, we enrich an existing corpus of scientific publications annotated with detailed rhetorical information. This enrichment involves annotating the corpus with explicit argumentative structures, identifying argumentative components and their relationships. Second, we explore novel neural multi-task learning architectures designed to simultaneously extract argumentative components and perform various rhetorical classification tasks. Our approach leverages the power of multi-task learning, a paradigm that allows models to share representations across related tasks, potentially improving performance on all tasks involved. By coupling rhetorical classifiers (predicting discourse categories and citation contexts) with an argument extraction task, we aim to create a system that benefits from a more holistic understanding of the text – one that recognizes not only *what* is being said, but *how* and *why* it is being said. The experimental results demonstrate that this joint learning approach yields substantial and statistically significant performance gains across a range of rhetorical analysis tasks, validating the crucial role of argumentation in understanding the rhetoric of scientific publications. Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has rapidly emerged as the dominant paradigm for machine translation, demonstrating substantial improvements over traditional statistical machine translation (SMT) systems (Cho et al., 2014; Sutskever et al., 2014). Early NMT models employed an encoder-decoder framework, where an encoder compresses the source sentence into a fixed-length vector representation, and a decoder generates the target sentence from this vector. While successful, these initial models often struggled with long sentences, as the fixed-length vector became a bottleneck, failing to capture all the necessary information from the input. To address this limitation, the concept of attention mechanisms was introduced to NMT (Bahdanau et al., 2015; Luong et al., 2015). Attention allows the decoder to selectively focus on different parts of the source sentence during the generation of each target word, effectively alleviating the bottleneck issue. By dynamically weighting the importance of each source word, the model can prioritize the most relevant information for the current translation step. This, in turn, leads to improved translation quality, especially for longer and more complex sentences. Despite the clear benefits of attention, a surprisingly limited amount of research has focused on systematically exploring different architectural choices for attentional mechanisms within NMT systems. The original attention proposal (Bahdanau et al., 2015) introduced a global attention mechanism, where the decoder considers all source hidden states to compute the context vector. Subsequent work proposed variations on this theme, modifying the attention scoring function or incorporating different weighting schemes (Luong et al., 2015). However, these investigations largely focused on refining existing approaches rather than challenging the fundamental architecture of global attention. This paper addresses this gap in the literature by presenting a comprehensive investigation into two distinct classes of attentional mechanisms: global attention and local attention. While global attention provides a complete view of the source sentence, it can be computationally expensive, especially for long sequences. Local attention, in contrast, aims to mitigate this cost by selectively focusing on a smaller, contextually relevant subset of source words at each decoding step. This allows for more efficient computation and potentially better performance by reducing the noise introduced by irrelevant source words. We hypothesize that both global and local attention mechanisms offer unique advantages and can significantly improve NMT performance. Through rigorous experimentation on the widely-used WMT English-German translation tasks, we demonstrate the effectiveness of both approaches. Importantly, our local attention model achieves a substantial gain of 5.0 BLEU points over a strong non-attentional baseline incorporating established techniques like dropout. Furthermore, an ensemble of models utilizing both attention architectures achieves a new state-of-the-art result on the WMT’15 English-to-German translation task, surpassing previous best results by a significant margin. This work not only demonstrates the practical benefits of carefully considering attention architectures but also provides a strong foundation for future research exploring the design of even more effective attentional mechanisms for NMT.

The burgeoning field of opinion mining, also known as sentiment analysis, has witnessed remarkable progress in recent years. Driven by advancements in machine learning and natural language processing, systems are now capable of automatically identifying and extracting subjective expressions from text with increasing accuracy. These technologies find application in a diverse range of domains, from market research and brand monitoring to political analysis and social media analytics. However, despite these impressive strides, we argue that a fundamental limitation underlies much of the current work: a restricted understanding of what constitutes an “opinion” in the first place. Current opinion detection methods largely focus on identifying explicitly subjective words and phrases – positive or negative descriptors, expressions of belief, and evaluative language. While valuable, this approach neglects the inherently pragmatic and contextual nature of opinion, and crucially, overlooks the multifaceted ways in which individuals *conceptualize* what an opinion fundamentally *is*. This conceptualization, which we term “metasubjectivity,” is itself subjective – a belief *about* beliefs – and profoundly influences how users interact with and interpret the results of opinion mining systems. Consider a scenario where a user seeks to understand public opinion regarding a controversial policy. One individual might define “opinion” narrowly as direct statements of support or opposition. Another might consider nuanced evaluations of the policy’s potential consequences, or even expressions of uncertainty as relevant opinions. A third might prioritize the credibility or expertise of the opinion source. These differing perspectives on what constitutes a meaningful expression of opinion directly impact the user’s expectations and evaluation of the system’s output. A system that fails to account for these disparate definitions risks providing results that, while technically accurate, are nonetheless irrelevant or misleading from the user’s standpoint. This paper proposes that recognizing and addressing metasubjectivity is crucial for unlocking the full potential of opinion mining. We argue for a more flexible and user-centric approach, one that acknowledges the inherent ambiguity surrounding the very definition of “opinion.” We will outline a framework for defining and characterizing different perspectives on metasubjectivity, and discuss the significant challenges this presents for both corpus development – how do we annotate data when the ground truth is itself subjective? – and for building robust sentence-level detection technologies. Finally, we contend that while explicitly modeling metasubjectivity will undoubtedly introduce complexity and associated costs, the long-term benefits – namely, more relevant, trustworthy, and truly useful opinion mining systems – will far outweigh these initial investments. This work is not a criticism of existing techniques, but rather a call for a broader, more nuanced perspective on the task of understanding and aggregating human opinion.
