Web search has become an indispensable tool for information access, but effective search relies heavily on the quality of user queries. Often, users formulate queries that are suboptimal – containing typos, grammatical errors, or simply lacking the clarity needed to retrieve relevant results. Query alteration, the process of automatically suggesting alternative query formulations, has emerged as a crucial component of modern search engines, aiming to improve search recall and user satisfaction. While substantial progress has been made in query alteration for English (Jones et al., 2006;Brocklebank et al., 2007;Cucerzan & Gaussier, 2007), the task presents unique challenges for languages with vastly different characteristics, such as Japanese. Japanese presents complexities not found in English. Its writing system combines three scripts – hiragana, katakana, and kanji – leading to significant orthographic variation for a single word or concept. Furthermore, the agglutinative nature of Japanese morphology means that slight changes in a query can drastically alter its meaning. Early approaches to Japanese query alteration largely focused on orthographic similarity, leveraging edit distance or keyboard layout proximity to generate candidate alterations (Kit et al., 2006;Suzuki et al., 2008). These methods, however, often struggle with the inherent ambiguity of Japanese orthography and can generate numerous irrelevant suggestions. More recently, researchers have explored incorporating semantic similarity into the query alteration process (Goto et al., 2009;Sakaguchi et al., 2010), but these approaches have generally been limited by data sparseness and their reliance on specific lexical resources. This paper introduces a novel and unified approach to Japanese query alteration that overcomes the limitations of previous methods. Rather than focusing solely on orthographic similarity, or relying on predefined linguistic rules, our model leverages semantic similarity to identify appropriate query alterations, even when orthographic differences are substantial. We build upon the successful framework for query correction developed for English by Jones et al. (2006), but with several key improvements tailored for the Japanese language. First, we significantly augment the training data by incorporating orthographically dissimilar but semantically similar query-candidate pairs. This addresses the inherent orthographic ambiguity of Japanese and expands the range of potential alterations. Second, we employ a kernel-based approach to lexical semantic similarity, which mitigates the challenges of data sparseness frequently encountered when computing similarity between Japanese words. Moreover, we present an efficient methodology for generating the necessary query-candidate pairs for both training and evaluating our model. Through experiments conducted on a real-world query log dataset, we demonstrate that our proposed method achieves approximately 80% accuracy on the query alteration task, demonstrating a significant improvement over existing methods that rely on semantic similarity. This work represents a crucial step towards building more robust and user-friendly Japanese web search systems. Data-to-text generation (DTG) is a crucial task in natural language generation, bridging the gap between structured data and human-readable text. It finds applications in diverse areas, including report generation, weather forecasting, and product description writing. Recent advancements in neural network architectures, particularly encoder-decoder models with attention mechanisms, have significantly improved the quality of generated texts (See, Vinyals & Bengio, 2014; Sutskever et al., 2014; Bahdanau et al., 2015). Within the DTG paradigm, the copy mechanism (Gu et al., 2016; Wiseman & Rush, 2016) has emerged as a powerful technique, enabling models to directly copy tokens from the input data into the generated text – a vital capability when dealing with numerical values, entity names, and other factual information present in the databases. Despite these successes, current DTG systems still struggle with maintaining the precision of data records within the generated text. While models may produce fluent and grammatically correct sentences, they can often introduce errors by including incorrect numerical values, substituting wrong entities, or misrepresenting the original data (Novikova et al., 2017). This is particularly problematic when dealing with complex datasets containing a large number of data points and intricate relationships, such as the ROTOWIRE dataset (Clarke et al., 2010). ROTOWIRE, a benchmark for DTG, presents a significant challenge due to its relatively short texts and the density of factual information they need to convey. Errors in this context can drastically alter the meaning and usefulness of the generated reports. Existing approaches have focused on improving the attention mechanism and the copy gate to mitigate these issues. However, these methods often operate within the confines of a single-stage generation process, where decoding and data copying occur simultaneously. This integrated approach may limit the model’s ability to fully consider the interplay between the overall text structure and the precise selection of data records. We hypothesize that a more deliberate, staged approach, decoupling the text planning and data realization phases, could lead to enhanced precision. To address this limitation, we propose a novel two-stage approach for data-to-text generation incorporating a *delayed copy mechanism*. Our framework first generates a template text with designated slots for data insertion. These slots represent placeholders for specific data records from the input database. Subsequently, our delayed copy mechanism selectively fills these slots with the most relevant and accurate data records. This separation of concerns allows the model to initially focus on structuring the text coherently, and then dedicate its resources to accurately populating the template with data. The core innovation lies in our delayed copying mechanism, which leverages a sophisticated attention framework. This framework employs *double attention* (attending to both the input data records and the generated template), *position-aware attention* (considering the position of slots within the template), and a *pairwise ranking loss* (encouraging the model to select the correct data record over incorrect alternatives). Crucially, the two stages – template generation and data copying – are trained independently, allowing each model to specialize in its respective task. Our experiments on the ROTOWIRE dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, showcasing substantial improvements in the precision of data records within the generated texts.

Aspect-level sentiment classification (ALSC) aims to identify the sentiment expressed towards specific aspects of an entity. Unlike traditional sentence-level sentiment analysis, ALSC provides a more granular understanding of opinions, enabling businesses to pinpoint areas of strength and weakness in their products or services. For example, in a restaurant review, a user might express positive sentiment towards the “food” but negative sentiment towards the “service.” Identifying these nuanced opinions is crucial for targeted improvements and enhanced customer satisfaction. Existing approaches to ALSC often rely on attention mechanisms to focus on the parts of a sentence that are most relevant to a particular aspect. These methods typically employ coarse-grained attention, where attention weights are assigned to entire words or phrases. While effective to a degree, coarse-grained attention can suffer from information loss, particularly when dealing with multi-word aspects or contexts requiring detailed contextual understanding. The inherent granularity of these methods may fail to capture subtle, word-level interactions crucial for accurate sentiment prediction. For example, consider the aspect “battery life” in a laptop review. The sentiment towards this aspect might be heavily influenced by the modifier describing the battery life ("long-lasting," "short,” “reliable”), which could be missed by a coarse-grained attention mechanism. To address this limitation, we propose a novel Multi-grained Attention Network (MGAN) for ALSC. MGAN incorporates a fine-grained attention mechanism that operates at the word level, capturing nuanced interactions between the aspect and its surrounding context. By attending to individual words, our model can better understand the specific words contributing to the sentiment towards the aspect, even in the presence of complex linguistic structures or subtle sentiment cues. Crucially, we don’t simply *replace* coarse-grained attention, but rather *combine* it with the fine-grained mechanism, creating a framework leveraging the strengths of both. This synergistic approach allows the model to capture both broad contextual information and specific word-level interactions. Furthermore, current ALSC models often treat each aspect independently during training, ignoring potential relationships between aspects that share the same context. We hypothesize that aspect-level interactions can provide valuable information for improving sentiment prediction. For instance, if a review expresses negative sentiment towards the “food” in a restaurant, it’s more likely that the sentiment towards other aspects, such as “atmosphere” or “service,” will also be negative. To exploit these relationships, we introduce an aspect alignment loss that encourages the model to learn consistent representations for related aspects within the same context. We evaluate MGAN on three benchmark datasets: the SemEval 2014 laptop and restaurant datasets, and a Twitter dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that MGAN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across all three datasets. Ablation studies further confirm the effectiveness of our proposed aspect alignment loss, highlighting the benefits of incorporating aspect-level interactions into the learning process. Our contributions, therefore, lie in the novel combination of multi-grained attention and the innovative aspect alignment loss, leading to a significant performance improvement in aspect-level sentiment classification.

Natural language instructions are a powerful and intuitive way to communicate complex tasks to both humans and machines. As robots and virtual assistants become increasingly integrated into our daily lives, the ability to seamlessly understand and execute instructions is paramount. However, natural language is inherently ambiguous and context-dependent. A simple directive like “Put the red block on the blue one” relies heavily on shared understanding, common sense, and the ability to infer the speaker’s intentions. These aspects fall under the domain of *pragmatics* – the study of how context contributes to meaning. While recent advances in deep learning have led to significant progress in natural language understanding and generation, these models often struggle with pragmatic reasoning, particularly when dealing with complex, sequential tasks involving multiple steps and potential ambiguities. Traditional approaches to instruction following often focus on syntactic parsing and semantic representation, neglecting the crucial role of pragmatic inference (Allen & Perrault, 1980). A significant gap remains in developing systems that can not only parse the literal meaning of an instruction but also reason about *why* the speaker chose to phrase it that way and *how* a listener is likely to interpret it. For example, consider the instruction “Grab the large cube.” A listener must infer whether “large” is relative to other cubes in the scene, or an absolute size threshold. A pragmatic model should be able to account for these subtleties. Inspired by theories of communication in linguistics and game theory (Grice, 1975; Shannon, 1948), recent work has begun to incorporate pragmatic reasoning into neural models (Andreas et al., 2017; Jia & Liang, 2016; Fried et al., 2018). These models typically employ a “speaker-listener” framework, where a speaker attempts to generate instructions that a listener can reliably interpret. Crucially, these models often incorporate a learned *base listener*, which provides a simulation of how a typical listener would understand different utterances. The speaker uses this simulation to evaluate candidate instructions and select the one most likely to be correctly understood. Similarly, a *pragmatic listener* can reason about alternative instructions the speaker might have chosen, and use this information to disambiguate the intended meaning. However, most existing pragmatic models have been evaluated on relatively simple tasks or restricted domains. They often fall short when applied to more complex scenarios involving sequential actions and intricate environmental interactions. In this paper, we extend these pragmatic models to the realm of complex, sequential instruction following. We demonstrate that explicit pragmatic inference significantly improves both the generation and interpretation of natural language instructions for such tasks. Our contributions are twofold: First, we adapt the speaker-listener framework to handle sequential instructions, allowing the model to reason about the entire task plan rather than individual actions in isolation. Second, we present empirical results demonstrating that our pragmatics-enabled models outperform state-of-the-art listener and speaker models in diverse settings, achieving improved accuracy in both human instruction interpretation and human-evaluable instruction generation. We believe this work represents a crucial step towards building truly intelligent agents that can seamlessly collaborate with humans through natural language.

The proliferation of online forums has created a vast repository of knowledge, frequently taking the form of questions posed by users and answered by community members. Extracting this question-answer (QA) knowledge automatically presents a valuable opportunity for building intelligent systems capable of providing succinct and relevant responses to user queries, or for directly mining insights from public discourse. However, automatically identifying the context surrounding a question, and pinpointing the corresponding answer within a potentially lengthy and complex forum thread, remains a significant challenge. Traditional information retrieval (IR) approaches often struggle with the nuances of informal language, the conversational nature of forum discussions, and the lack of clearly delineated question-answer boundaries. Existing methods for QA typically focus on structured knowledge bases or are designed for single-document scenarios. Applying these approaches directly to the structure of online forums proves difficult due to the inherent thread-like topology and the distributed nature of information. Forum discussions unfold as a series of posts, often with nested replies, creating a complex relationship between questions and potential answers. A successful system must therefore effectively model this structure to identify relevant contextual information and accurately locate the answer. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to extracting contexts and answers from online forum discussions. Our method leverages the strengths of Structural Support Vector Machines (SSVMs), adapting them to specifically address the unique characteristics of forum data. SSVMs are powerful machine learning models designed for structured prediction tasks, offering the ability to learn complex relationships between input features and output structures. We customize the standard SSVM framework in several key ways. First, we represent forum threads as comprehensive graphical models, capturing the hierarchical relationships between posts and the connections formed through replies and quotes. This graphical representation allows the model to explicitly reason about the structure of the discussion. Second, we design specialized inference algorithms tailored to the forum context, moving beyond the generic inference procedures typically associated with SSVMs. These algorithms are optimized for efficiently searching the graphical model to identify the most likely context and answer spans. Finally, our framework offers flexibility in adapting to different task preferences through the use of varying loss functions. This allows users to prioritize, for example, answer precision or contextual relevance depending on the specific application requirements. We evaluate our approach on a real-world dataset of forum discussions, demonstrating promising results and highlighting the adaptability of our model. Our findings suggest that the structural SSVM approach provides a robust and flexible solution for extracting valuable knowledge from the rich tapestry of online forum data. Probabilistic Context-Free Grammars (PCFGs) have long been a cornerstone of natural language parsing, providing a principled probabilistic framework for syntactic analysis. However, traditional PCFGs often struggle to adequately model the complexities of natural language due to the notorious sparsity problem – the inability to accurately estimate probabilities for all possible grammar rules, especially those involving rare syntactic constructions. Latent-Variable PCFGs (LV-PCFGs) offer an elegant solution to this problem by introducing latent variables that capture unobserved syntactic categories, effectively smoothing the probability distribution over grammar rules and allowing for more robust parsing performance. Despite their theoretical advantages, learning LV-PCFGs has proven to be a substantial challenge. Existing approaches, such as those based on the Inside-Outside algorithm extended to handle latent variables (Johnson, 2007; Petrov & Croft, 2007), often lack provable guarantees of convergence or correctness, and can be sensitive to initialization and local optima. Furthermore, many practical implementations employ approximations or heuristics that compromise the theoretical foundations. The goal of developing a learning algorithm that is *both* provably correct *and* efficient remains a significant open problem in the field. In this paper, we present a novel learning algorithm for LV-PCFGs that addresses this challenge. Our approach leverages the power of matrix decomposition techniques combined with the well-understood framework of the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm. Crucially, we demonstrate that the proposed algorithm enjoys provable convergence properties and guarantees of correctness under mild assumptions. The core of our algorithm consists of two distinct phases. First, we employ a matrix decomposition algorithm on a co-occurrence matrix constructed from the parse trees in the training data. This decomposition step aims to identify the underlying latent syntactic structure and extract meaningful representations of the latent variables. Second, we utilize EM to refine the model parameters, optimizing a convex objective function that simultaneously considers the training data and the output of the matrix decomposition. The convexity of this objective guarantees convergence to a locally optimal solution, providing a solid theoretical foundation for the learning process. We empirically evaluate the effectiveness of our algorithm on both parsing tasks and a related language modeling problem. Our results demonstrate that the algorithm is not only computationally efficient but also achieves competitive performance compared to existing state-of-the-art LV-PCFGs. These findings solidify the potential of our approach as a practical and reliable solution for learning latent-variable PCFGs, paving the way for more robust and accurate natural language processing systems.

The automatic generation of natural language from structured data is a long-standing problem in artificial intelligence with applications ranging from data-to-text summarization (Reiter & Dale, 2000) to report generation (Kukich, 1987). Historically, rule-based systems and template-filling approaches dominated this field, offering precise control over output but struggling with scalability and naturalness (Angeli et al., 2010). Recent advances in neural networks, particularly recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and their variants such as LSTMs (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) and GRUs (Cho et al., 2014), have led to significant progress in neural text generation. These models learn to map input data to output text in a data-driven fashion, offering greater flexibility and fluency compared to traditional methods. Despite these improvements, significant challenges remain, particularly when scaling neural generation models to large and complex domains. One major bottleneck is the difficulty of handling large vocabularies. As the size of the vocabulary increases, the computational cost of training and inference grows substantially, and the model’s ability to generalize to rare words diminishes. Furthermore, effectively incorporating structured data into neural generation models requires careful consideration of how to represent and process relationships between different data elements. Simply concatenating data fields is often insufficient to capture the nuances of semantic relationships and contextual information. In this work, we address these challenges by presenting a novel neural model for concept-to-text generation that is designed to scale to large, rich domains. We focus on the biography domain, motivated by the abundance of structured biographical data available in resources like Wikipedia. To facilitate research in this area, we introduce a new, large-scale dataset of biographical sentences extracted from Wikipedia, containing over 700k examples and a vocabulary of 400k words – an order of magnitude larger than existing resources. Our model extends conditional neural language models (Bengio et al., 2003) with two key innovations. First, we employ a mixed-vocabulary approach that combines a fixed vocabulary with “copy actions” inspired by pointer networks (Vinyals et al., 2015). This allows the model to effectively handle rare and domain-specific words by directly transferring them from the input database to the generated output. Second, we introduce field-specific word embeddings, allowing the model to represent the same word differently depending on the data field in which it appears. This enables the model to capture the varying semantic roles of words across different data dimensions. We evaluate our model on the newly created biographical dataset and demonstrate significant improvements over a strong baseline, a Templated Kneser-Ney language model. Our neural model achieves nearly a 15 BLEU score improvement, highlighting the effectiveness of our proposed techniques for scaling neural text generation to complex domains. We believe that this work represents a significant step towards building more robust and versatile systems for generating natural language from structured data.

Morphology, the study of word formation, is a fundamental component of natural language processing, impacting tasks ranging from machine translation to information retrieval. A crucial aspect of morphological analysis is the ability to learn and generalize *morphological paradigms* – the structured sets of inflectional forms a word can take. Traditionally, morphological paradigms were painstakingly hand-crafted by linguists, a process that is both time-consuming and requires substantial expertise. In recent years, there has been growing interest in automatically learning these paradigms from data, offering a pathway to rapidly creating morphological resources for diverse languages and potentially uncovering previously undocumented patterns. Early approaches to morphological paradigm induction relied heavily on rule-based systems or unsupervised learning techniques (e.g., Steinhauser et al., 2000; Goldsmith, 2001). While these methods offered a degree of automation, they often struggled with complex or irregular morphologies, requiring significant manual intervention or suffering from limited accuracy. The advent of supervised learning provided a promising avenue for improving performance, framing the task as a classification problem where the goal is to predict the inflectional forms for unseen words given labeled examples of morphological patterns. Existing supervised approaches vary considerably in their representation of morphological information. Some methods utilize feature engineering and traditional machine learning algorithms (e.g., Daelemans et al., 2004; Spyropoulos et al., 2008), while others explore more sophisticated representations like neural networks (e.g., Kann et al., 2016; Adel and Wu, 2018). However, many supervised techniques operate at the level of individual morphemes or surface forms, neglecting the inherent *structural* relationships that define a paradigm. Recently, a novel approach leveraging the concept of longest common subsequences (LCS) to generalize from inflection tables has emerged as a competitive method for morphological paradigm learning (Durrett et al., 2013). This non-probabilistic technique identifies shared patterns within observed inflection tables, allowing for the straightforward induction of morphological rules. While initially demonstrating promising results, this LCS-based approach lacked a powerful mechanism for integrating contextual information or discriminating between potentially ambiguous paradigms. In this work, we build upon this foundation by combining the strengths of inflection table generalization via LCS with a discriminative classifier. Our system learns from labeled examples of complete inflection tables, and then utilizes this knowledge to reconstruct the full paradigm for unseen lemmas or base forms. By framing the paradigm learning task as a classification problem *over entire inflection tables*, we enable the model to capture complex morphological patterns and make more informed predictions. We present comprehensive evaluations across eleven diverse languages, demonstrating that our approach consistently outperforms existing methods on this task, confirming its viability for rapidly creating high-accuracy morphological resources. The ability to represent meaning in a computationally tractable form is a cornerstone of Natural Language Processing (NLP). Historically, distributional semantics (Harris, 1954) – the idea that words are defined by the company they keep – has provided a powerful framework for capturing semantic relationships. More recently, neural network models, particularly recurrent neural networks (RNNs), have dramatically advanced the state-of-the-art in semantic representation learning. Among these, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) have emerged as a dominant force, demonstrating a remarkable capacity to model long-range dependencies in sequential data and achieving strong results across a diverse range of NLP tasks, including machine translation (Sutskever et al., 2014), language modeling (Mikolov et al., 2010), and sentiment analysis (Socher et al., 2013). Despite their success, the vast majority of work employing LSTMs has focused on a single, linear network architecture. This approach treats sentences as strictly sequential, processing words one after another. However, natural language is rarely a simple linear progression. Rather, it exhibits a rich hierarchical structure, dictated by syntactic rules, where words combine to form phrases, phrases combine to form clauses, and so forth. This hierarchical structure is crucial to understanding meaning; the meaning of a phrase is generally not simply the sum of the meanings of its constituent words, and understanding these compositional relationships is paramount for accurate semantic representation. Existing approaches to incorporating syntactic information into neural networks often rely on external parsers (Socher et al., 2013) which introduces error propagation from the parsing stage, and a reliance on the quality of hand-engineered features. We argue that a more elegant and potentially more robust solution lies in *inherently* structuring the LSTM network itself to mirror the hierarchical structure of language. In this work, we introduce the Tree-LSTM, a novel generalization of the standard LSTM architecture to tree-structured network topologies. Instead of a linear chain, the Tree-LSTM processes sentences according to their parse tree, allowing each word to be represented not only by its preceding context, but also by its relationship to its siblings and parent nodes. This structure enables the model to capture compositional semantics more effectively. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the Tree-LSTM on two challenging semantic tasks: predicting semantic relatedness (using the SemEval 2014, Task 1 dataset) and sentiment classification (using the Stanford Sentiment Treebank). Our results demonstrate that the Tree-LSTM consistently outperforms strong LSTM baselines and existing state-of-the-art systems, establishing its superiority in learning semantic representations from natural language. This suggests that incorporating structural information directly into the network architecture is a critical step towards achieving more human-like understanding of language. References: Harris, Z. The ability to assess the difficulty or complexity of words is a cornerstone of many applications in computational linguistics, educational technology, and language assessment. From tailoring reading materials to a student’s reading level to automatically evaluating the lexical sophistication of writing, having a reliable method for gauging word knowledge is crucial. Traditional approaches to this problem typically focus on estimating word *difficulty*, often operationalized as a singular scalar value representing how challenging a word is for a typical language user. While these methods, frequently leveraging corpus statistics like word frequency or document frequency (e.g., Zipf’s law-based measures), have proven useful, they often fall short of capturing the nuanced and developmental nature of word knowledge. A word isn’t simply “hard” or “easy”; rather, our understanding of it *matures* over time, progressing from a rudimentary grasp of its basic denotation to a more sophisticated understanding of its connotations, collocations, and subtle semantic relationships. Existing corpus-based methods, while providing a useful signal, often treat words as static entities. They struggle to represent the dynamic process of language acquisition – how a child, or a second language learner, gradually builds their understanding of a word’s meaning through repeated exposure and contextualization. Moreover, these measures frequently conflate rarity with difficulty. A low-frequency word may be challenging not because its concept is inherently complex, but simply because it is encountered less frequently in typical language use. This limitation can lead to mischaracterizations of word knowledge and ineffective educational interventions. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a new paradigm – *word meaning maturity*. This concept shifts the focus from a single difficulty score to a profile of knowledge development across stages of learning. We posit that each word possesses a maturity trajectory, reflecting the evolving understanding of its meaning as an individual gains linguistic experience. This framework acknowledges that “knowing” a word is not a binary state, but rather a continuum that encompasses various levels of semantic proficiency. In this work, we present a computationally tractable algorithm for estimating word maturity. Our approach leverages Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA), a well-established technique for capturing semantic relationships between words and documents, to model the process of language acquisition. We hypothesize that a word's maturity can be inferred by analyzing its evolving semantic representation within a corpus representing different stages of language learning. Specifically, we track how a word’s semantic context changes as it appears in texts associated with increasing levels of linguistic sophistication. We demonstrate, through correlation with external indicators of word knowledge (such as age-of-acquisition norms and vocabulary lists graded by school level), that our maturity metric provides a robust and reliable measure of word understanding. Furthermore, we show that this metric goes beyond simple frequency-based measures, capturing subtle semantic effects that are indicative of deeper linguistic knowledge. Our findings suggest that modeling word meaning maturity offers a more nuanced and accurate approach to computational lexical assessment, with significant potential for applications in education, language learning, and cognitive science.

The prevalence of online platforms has fundamentally altered the landscape of public discourse, fostering both unprecedented connectivity and concerning polarization. A critical element contributing to this polarization is dogmatism – the tendency to adhere rigidly to beliefs, regardless of evidence to the contrary, and to dismiss opposing viewpoints with unwavering conviction. While extensively studied in psychology and political science, understanding the manifestation of dogmatism in the dynamic and often volatile environment of social media presents a unique challenge. Traditional assessments often rely on questionnaires and structured interviews, methods impractical for analyzing the scale and speed of online communication. This paper addresses this gap by exploring linguistic and behavioral signals indicative of dogmatism within social media posts, specifically focusing on the platform Reddit, and constructing statistical models capable of identifying dogmatic content. Dogmatism, as conceptualized by theorists like Adorno et al. (1950) and Altemeyer (1988), involves a constellation of traits including closed-mindedness, resistance to new information, and a strong belief in the absolute correctness of one’s own views. Core characteristics – such as a sense of certainty, intolerance towards ambiguity, and a rejection of opposing arguments – would logically manifest in discernible patterns of language use and interaction. This work operationalizes these established psychological constructs and investigates their predictive power in a large-scale social media dataset. We hypothesize that dogmatic comments will exhibit features like heightened certainty (e.g., through the use of absolute language), simplified reasoning, and dismissive attitudes towards alternative perspectives. However, beyond applying existing theory, we also seek to identify novel signals of dogmatism that might emerge specifically within the context of online communication. We posit that dogmatic individuals, driven by a desire to firmly establish their position, may exhibit a reluctance to explicitly signal cognitive processes, such as acknowledging uncertainty or considering alternative viewpoints. This idea stems from the observation that conveying thoughtful consideration can be perceived as weakness or compromise. To test these hypotheses, we constructed a novel corpus of Reddit posts annotated for dogmatism via a carefully designed crowdsourcing experiment. This corpus, spanning a diverse range of conversational topics, provides a robust foundation for training and evaluating our predictive models. We employ a range of statistical techniques, including feature engineering and machine learning classification, to identify the most predictive linguistic and behavioral signals. Our findings not only validate the importance of established dogmatism indicators but also reveal previously unobserved patterns. Moreover, deploying our model to analyze millions of additional Reddit posts unveils intriguing evidence suggesting that dogmatism may represent a stable personality trait, consistently expressed by individuals across diverse conversational domains. Furthermore, we observe a concerning dynamic: users engaging with dogmatic comments tend to exhibit increases in dogmatic posting behavior themselves, hinting at a potential reinforcement mechanism contributing to online polarization. Coherence is a fundamental aspect of human communication, allowing us to seamlessly interpret and understand sequences of sentences as unified, meaningful texts. While semantic relationships between sentences have traditionally been central to computational models of coherence (e.g., through Rhetorical Structure Theory – RST – Mann & Thompson, 1988), a growing body of research suggests that syntactic structure plays a crucial, and often overlooked, role. This paper explores the hypothesis that syntactic patterns serve as a reliable proxy for the *intentional* discourse structure – the communicative goals that drive the organization of a text – and that coherent discourse exhibits detectable, non-random patterns in its syntactic realization. Existing approaches to coherence modelling have largely focused on identifying explicit discourse relations using techniques like cue phrase detection (e.g., “because”, “however”) or implicit relation classification based on semantic similarity. While effective, these approaches often struggle with ambiguity and can be computationally expensive. Furthermore, they frequently require large, manually annotated corpora like the Penn Discourse Treebank, limiting their scalability and adaptability across diverse text genres. Our work proposes a shift in perspective: rather than *inferring* intentional structure from semantic content, we directly model coherence through observable syntactic features. We posit that the choice of syntactic structures is not arbitrary but is strategically driven by the author’s communicative intent. For instance, a sentence introducing a new topic might favor a broader, more declarative structure, while a sentence elaborating on a previously introduced concept could employ more restrictive or embedded clauses. By analyzing the distribution and transitions of these syntactic patterns, we aim to construct a coherence model that can distinguish between well-formed, logically connected texts and those lacking a clear organizational structure. Specifically, we present a probabilistic model that analyzes sequences of syntactic parse trees, capturing the likelihood of transitioning between different structural patterns. This model leverages readily available, automatically generated parse trees, circumventing the need for extensive manual annotation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on two distinct corpora: a collection of news articles, where we achieve high accuracy in discriminating between coherent and deliberately incoherent texts, and a corpus of academic conference papers, where our syntactic patterns correlate significantly with human judgments of intentional discourse structure in key sections like abstracts, introductions and related work. The results demonstrate that our model effectively captures patterns indicative of genuine textual coherence, offering a novel and scalable approach to understanding how humans construct meaning through the deliberate arrangement of syntactic structures. This work opens avenues for further research into the interplay between syntax, semantics, and intentionality in discourse, with potential applications in areas such as automated text summarization, machine translation, and text generation. The increasing prevalence of online communication platforms—ranging from instant messaging and social media to customer service chatbots—has led to a surge in *interleaved* text conversations. In these scenarios, multiple participants often engage in simultaneous dialogues, resulting in a complex stream of messages where utterances from different conversational threads are interwoven. Accurately processing these conversations requires the ability to *disentangle* them—that is, to automatically group overlapping sequences of messages into their respective, coherent conversational units. This task presents a significant challenge for computational systems, impacting applications such as dialogue summarization, sentiment analysis, topic modeling, and conversational search. Existing approaches to conversation disentanglement have explored various features derived from the conversational data itself. These include lexical similarity between messages (e.g., using word overlap or distributional semantics), non-lexical cues like user identities and timestamps (Papineni et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2018), and even learned representations from recurrent neural networks (Joshi et al., 2016). While these methods have achieved some success, they often fall short in capturing the nuanced relationship between a message’s meaning and the rich context in which it is embedded. Specifically, they struggle to fully account for the temporal dependencies—how a message relates to preceding and succeeding utterances—and social dynamics—the roles and relationships of the participants involved. We argue that a message’s interpretation, and therefore its proper assignment to a conversation, is heavily influenced by its context. Consider a short utterance like “Great!”. Without knowing the preceding exchange, its meaning is ambiguous. Is it a positive response to a proposal? Agreement with a plan? Or even sarcasm? The surrounding messages and the identities of the speakers are crucial for disambiguation. Traditional methods often treat each message as an isolated unit, or consider only a limited window of surrounding messages, failing to incorporate the broader contextual information necessary for accurate disentanglement. To address these limitations, we propose a novel approach centered around *context-based message expansion*. Our method leverages both explicit (e.g., preceding messages, user information) and *hidden* contextual properties – inferred relationships between entities, topics, and sentiments – to probabilistically expand each message into a richer, more informative representation. This expansion aims to encapsulate the relevant contextual cues that would allow a downstream model to better determine the message’s conversational affiliation. Specifically, we utilize a neural network architecture that incorporates contextual embeddings derived from a transformer-based language model, fine-tuned to specifically predict the appropriate conversational thread for a given message. This allows the model to learn how to integrate temporal and social context into the message representation, effectively disentangling interwoven conversations. We demonstrate, through extensive experimental evaluation on benchmark datasets, that our context-based message expansion approach significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art disentanglement techniques. Our results highlight the critical importance of considering the broader conversational context for this challenging task, and pave the way for more robust and accurate processing of interleaved text conversations.

Cross-lingual transfer learning has become increasingly important in natural language processing, particularly for resource-poor languages where labeled data is scarce. A core component of many cross-lingual applications is the ability to represent words from different languages in a shared vector space – bilingual word embeddings. These embeddings allow for the direct transfer of knowledge learned in one language to another, enabling tasks like cross-lingual information retrieval, machine translation, and, as explored in this work, cross-lingual semantic and syntactic analysis. Traditional approaches to creating bilingual word embeddings rely heavily on parallel corpora (e.g., Mikolov et al., 2013; Xing et al., 2015). These methods learn mappings between languages by aligning embedding spaces trained on parallel text. However, the creation of large, high-quality parallel corpora is a costly and time-consuming process, limiting the applicability of these techniques to a small number of well-resourced language pairs. More recent methods have attempted to alleviate this dependency, utilizing techniques like adversarial training (e.g., Conrad et al., 2017) or projection-based approaches (e.g., Lauly et al., 2014). Still, these methods often require significant computational resources or rely on complex training procedures. In this paper, we introduce a surprisingly simple and effective method for learning task-specific bilingual word embeddings. Our approach is a wrapper that leverages readily available, off-the-shelf word embedding algorithms – such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) or FastText (Bojanowski et al., 2017) – and requires only a small, task-specific bilingual dictionary. Crucially, we do *not* require parallel corpora. Instead, we construct mixed context-target pairs using equivalence classes defined within this dictionary, essentially informing the embedding model about cross-lingual word correspondences. The advantage of our method lies in its flexibility and ease of implementation. By defining appropriate equivalence classes, we can tailor the learned embeddings to specific tasks, focusing on the semantic or syntactic relationships relevant to that task. The method is also agnostic to the underlying embedding algorithm, allowing practitioners to utilize their preferred embedding technique without modification. Furthermore, updating or adapting the embeddings to a new task or language pair simply requires redefining the equivalence classes and retraining the embedding model – a far simpler process than retraining complex cross-lingual alignment models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on two challenging cross-lingual tasks: unsupervised cross-language part-of-speech (POS) tagging and semi-supervised cross-language super sense (SuS) tagging. Our results consistently outperform existing off-the-shelf bilingual embeddings, demonstrating that even a small task-specific bilingual dictionary can significantly improve the quality of cross-lingual representations. We believe this work provides a valuable and accessible tool for researchers and practitioners seeking to leverage cross-lingual transfer learning in a variety of NLP applications.

Dependency parsing is a fundamental task in natural language processing, providing a structured representation of sentence syntax crucial for downstream applications like machine translation, information extraction, and question answering. Traditional dependency parsing approaches often rely on finding the single, most probable dependency tree – Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) inference – typically achieved through algorithms like the Cocke-Younger-Kasami (CYK) algorithm for projective grammars or variations of the Earley algorithm. However, many crucial NLP tasks require more than just the single best parse. Conditional likelihood training, where the model learns to assign probability to observed sentences, demands marginal probabilities over all possible parses. Similarly, posterior decoding – finding the most probable parse given a noisy input – benefits from considering a distribution over parses rather than a single hypothesis. Furthermore, quantifying the confidence in a parse requires examining the marginal probability of the predicted dependencies. Existing approaches to marginal inference in dependency parsing are often computationally prohibitive. Exact inference typically involves summing over an exponential number of possible parse trees, rendering it intractable even for moderately sized sentences. Approximate inference techniques like belief propagation (BP) offer a more efficient alternative, but remain computationally demanding, particularly as the complexity of the model increases – for example, when incorporating higher-order features or non-projective dependencies. The computational bottleneck stems from the need to process the full factor graph representing the dependency structure and the model’s probabilistic components. Recently, relaxation techniques have emerged as a powerful tool for accelerating MAP inference in various NLP problems. These methods strategically relax constraints in the original inference problem, allowing for efficient computation while retaining a strong approximation to the optimal solution. For example, Martins et al. (2011) demonstrated the effectiveness of relaxation for MAP inference in conditional random fields (CRFs). This work extends the benefits of relaxation to the more challenging domain of *marginal* inference for dependency parsing. We introduce a novel approach, Relaxed Marginal Inference (RMI), which leverages relaxation to significantly speed up marginal probability calculation without sacrificing accuracy. Our key insight is that for many inference tasks, processing only a carefully selected subset of the full factor graph can provide a sufficiently accurate approximation of the marginal probabilities. We empirically demonstrate this on second-order dependency parsing, achieving a tenfold speedup in inference time while maintaining performance comparable to exact methods. Crucially, we also provide a theoretical bound on the error introduced by the relaxation, quantifying the difference between the marginal probabilities computed over the reduced factor graph and those computed over the full graph. Furthermore, while our experiments focus on belief propagation as the inner-loop inference method, the RMI framework is deliberately designed to be general and applicable with any marginal inference algorithm. This generality positions RMI as a versatile tool for accelerating a wide range of dependency parsing applications and provides a foundation for further research in efficient approximate inference for structured prediction. The ability to automatically discover and represent the underlying semantic structure of text is a fundamental goal in natural language processing. Two prominent approaches to this end are topic modeling and word embedding. Topic models, such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) (Blei et al., 2003), operate by uncovering latent “topics” – probability distributions over words – that characterize collections of documents. These models excel at capturing high-level themes and relationships between documents, but often function at a relatively coarse granularity, primarily focusing on word co-occurrences within entire documents or sentences. In contrast, word embedding models, like Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), learn dense vector representations of words based on their contextual usage, typically by examining co-occurrences within a small sliding window. This fine-grained approach effectively captures semantic similarities between individual words, but may lack the broader thematic coherence provided by topic models. Both paradigms possess inherent strengths and weaknesses. A critical observation is that these two levels of granularity – the document/sentence level captured by topic models and the local context level captured by word embeddings – are complementary aspects of latent semantics. We hypothesize that a model capable of seamlessly integrating both perspectives could yield richer and more robust representations of meaning. Existing attempts to combine these approaches typically involve post-processing techniques, such as using topic models to inform word embedding initialization (e.g., Topic-Embedded Word Vectors - TEW; Liu et al., 2015) or leveraging word embeddings as features within topic modeling frameworks (e.g., using pre-trained embeddings as input to an LDA model). However, these methods often treat topic modeling and embedding learning as separate, sequential steps, potentially hindering the flow of information and limiting the overall effectiveness. To address these limitations, we propose Latent Topic Embedding (LTE), a novel framework that simultaneously learns latent topics *and* word embeddings within a unified probabilistic model. LTE is designed to capture word co-occurrence information at multiple levels of granularity, allowing for a more nuanced and comprehensive understanding of text semantics. Unlike previous hybrid approaches, LTE integrates topic generation and embedding learning in a joint optimization process, effectively allowing the two components to inform and refine each other. Furthermore, we present an efficient Monte Carlo Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm for parameter estimation within the LTE framework. This algorithm addresses the computational challenges inherent in jointly modeling topics and embeddings, providing a practical and scalable solution for real-world applications. We demonstrate through extensive experimentation on benchmark datasets that LTE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art topic modeling and word embedding techniques, achieving superior results in both topic coherence and word representation quality. Our results validate the hypothesis that integrating topic generation and embedding learning can unlock more powerful and insightful latent semantic representations. References: Blei, D. M., Ng, A. Chinese Word Segmentation (CWS), also known as Chinese lexical analysis, is a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing (NLP) for the Chinese language. Unlike languages like English where words are typically separated by spaces, Chinese text consists of a continuous stream of characters, necessitating the accurate identification of word boundaries. This task is critical as it directly impacts the performance of downstream NLP applications, including machine translation, information retrieval, and sentiment analysis. The dominant paradigm for CWS currently relies on supervised machine learning approaches, achieving state-of-the-art performance when trained on large, manually annotated corpora, such as the PKU corpus (LDC, 1998) and the ASBC corpus (Lin & Huang, 2009). However, a significant limitation of these supervised methods lies in their dependence on substantial, high-quality labeled data. Constructing such corpora is a laborious, time-consuming, and expensive process, particularly when dealing with specialized domains – such as biomedical texts, legal documents, or financial reports – where linguistic characteristics can differ significantly from general-purpose corpora. Applying a segmenter trained on a news corpus to a legal document, for instance, often results in substantial performance degradation due to domain mismatch. This phenomenon underscores the need for methods that can effectively adapt to new domains with limited or no labeled data. Traditional approaches to address this domain adaptation problem have focused on developing sophisticated algorithms, designing more representative features, or employing techniques like transfer learning. While these strategies can yield improvements, they often require significant expertise and careful tuning. Furthermore, they may not fully bridge the gap when faced with radically different domain-specific vocabularies or linguistic structures. In this paper, we present a novel and pragmatic approach to enhance CWS performance in out-of-domain scenarios: automatic corpus expansion leveraging the vast and readily available information on the Web. Our core idea stems from the observation that the Web contains a substantial amount of redundant information. Specifically, searching for phrases or sentences containing potentially ambiguous word segmentation candidates often returns numerous instances where those phrases appear in contexts that naturally suggest a clear and unambiguous segmentation. We hypothesize that by identifying and extracting these reliably segmented sentences from the Web, we can effectively augment the training corpus for CWS, improving segmenter performance without requiring manual annotation or complex algorithmic modifications. We propose an iterative methodology where we first identify complex or uncertain segmentation candidates within a target domain text. We then query the Web for sentences containing these candidates, filter for high-confidence segmented instances, and incorporate these into the original training corpus. Finally, we retrain the CWS segmenter using the expanded corpus. This process can be repeated, progressively refining the segmenter’s ability to handle domain-specific complexities. Our experiments, conducted on multiple datasets and domains, demonstrate that our approach consistently improves CWS performance and provides a stable and effective alternative to purely algorithm-focused solutions. We believe this work offers a valuable perspective on tackling the challenge of CWS, shifting the focus towards a data-driven approach of automatically expanding existing resources rather than solely relying on intricate model design.

Spontaneous speech is replete with disfluencies, including repetitions, hesitations, and, crucially, repairs – instances where a speaker interrupts their own utterance to revise or correct a prior segment. These disfluencies pose significant challenges for automatic speech recognition (ASR) and subsequent natural language processing (NLP) tasks, particularly syntactic parsing. While robust ASR systems are increasingly capable of transcribing disfluent speech, parsing such utterances remains a difficult problem, often requiring specialized methods to handle disruptions to syntactic structure. Existing approaches to parsing disfluent speech range from discarding disfluencies post-ASR (e.g., Shriberg, 1994) to augmenting grammars with rules to explicitly model disfluency phenomena (e.g., Stolcke & Shriberg, 1996; Kim et al., 2000). However, these approaches often operate under the assumption that repairs are inherently ‘marked’ – easily identifiable as such by the parser – or require substantial modifications to existing parsing frameworks. This paper stems from a different intuition concerning the cognitive processes underlying speech production and repair. We propose that the erroneous portions of a repair, termed *reparanda*, are not initially perceived as errors by the speaker during utterance planning or production. Rather, the erroneous nature of the reparandum emerges *after* the correction has been articulated. In other words, the brain doesn’t initially ‘know’ something is wrong until it has already formulated a viable alternative. Consequently, the syntactic analysis of a fluent utterance and a disfluent utterance with a similar underlying structure—were the reparandum not explicitly marked as an error—should be largely consistent. Minimizing the syntactic divergence between fluent and disfluent speech, therefore, provides a principled way to model the cognitive reality of repair. To test this hypothesis, we introduce three novel syntactic models specifically designed for parsing speech with repairs. These models are built around the premise of minimizing structural differences between fluent and disfluent segments while still acknowledging the presence of repair phenomena. Critically, our design is systematic, allowing us to isolate the impact of specific variables related to repair modeling. We systematically explore how different representations of reparanda – from minimal marking to more explicit annotation – affect parsing accuracy and the degree of structural divergence. By carefully controlling these variables, we aim to identify the simplest and most effective approach to parsing spontaneous speech, one that aligns with the proposed cognitive model of repair. The remainder of this paper details the design of the three syntactic models, describes the experimental setup and corpus used for evaluation, and presents a comparative analysis of the results. We demonstrate that these new models offer improvements over existing approaches while adhering to the central principle of minimizing the representation of reparanda as intrinsically erroneous components of the syntactic structure. This work contributes not only to improved parsing performance but also to a more nuanced understanding of the cognitive underpinnings of disfluent speech production and perception. Shriberg, E. Language modeling (LM) is a fundamental component in numerous natural language processing (NLP) applications, including speech recognition, machine translation, and text generation. The core task of a language model is to estimate the probability of a sequence of words, enabling systems to predict the likelihood of future words given the preceding context. Traditional n-gram language models, while simple and effective, suffer from data sparsity issues, particularly when encountering unseen word sequences. This limitation becomes particularly pronounced when the test data originates from a domain different from the training data – a scenario known as out-of-domain (OOD) generalization. To overcome the limitations of n-gram models, various techniques have been developed. Smoothing methods, such as Kneser-Ney smoothing (Kneser et al., 1995) and Witten-Bell smoothing (Witten and Bell, 1991), redistribute probability mass from observed events to unseen ones. However, these methods primarily address the data sparsity problem within the same vocabulary and may not fully handle OOD scenarios where the vocabulary itself differs, or where the underlying language patterns are substantially different. Latent Word Language Models (LWLMs) offer a promising approach to address these challenges. Introduced by Griffiths et al. (2004), LWLMs introduce a latent variable space, effectively clustering words into latent categories. This allows the model to generalize to unseen word sequences by considering the underlying linguistic properties captured by the latent variables, rather than relying solely on surface form co-occurrences. Subsequent works have explored various extensions to LWLMs, improving their performance and scalability. These include hierarchical LWLMs (HlLWLMs) (Blei et al., 2005), which introduce a hierarchical structure to the latent variable space, and factored LWLMs (Chen and Goodman, 2000), which decompose the probability into multiple factors. Despite these advances, existing LWLMs often struggle with modeling complex linguistic phenomena and achieving robust performance on truly OOD tasks. The latent variable space in standard LWLMs, while addressing data sparsity, may still be insufficient to capture the nuanced relationships between words, particularly when the test domain presents substantially different linguistic characteristics compared to the training domain. A single layer of latent variables might be inadequate to represent the hierarchy of abstractions present in language. In this paper, we propose a novel Hierarchical Latent Word Language Model (h-LWLM) designed to enhance robustness to out-of-domain tasks. The key innovation lies in introducing a *multiple* latent variable space with a *hierarchical* structure. This structure allows the model to flexibly incorporate linguistic knowledge and patterns not explicitly present in the training data – for example, representing both broad semantic categories (like “animals”) and more specific subcategories (like “mammals” or “birds”) within the latent hierarchy. This enhanced representation capability significantly improves the model’s ability to generalize to unseen domains. We detail the definition of h-LWLM, provide a layer-wise inference based training procedure, and outline a practical approximation technique for efficient usage in NLP applications. Finally, we present experimental results on the task of speech recognition, demonstrating the effectiveness of h-LWLM in out-of-domain scenarios compared to standard LWLMs and other baseline models. Our findings suggest that the hierarchical latent structure provides a substantial improvement in modeling robustness, highlighting the potential of h-LWLM

Surface realisation, the task of converting an abstract linguistic representation into a fluent and grammatical string, remains a core challenge in Natural Language Generation (NLG). While traditional approaches relied heavily on hand-crafted rules and linguistic constraints, recent years have seen a surge in data-driven methods, leveraging the power of machine learning to learn realisation patterns directly from corpora (Cochran et al., 2018; Gregor et al., 2018). A key aspect of this data-driven paradigm is the degree to which the input representation is *underspecified* – that is, how much information about the surface form is left open to the realisation model. The benefit of underspecification is that it allows for greater flexibility and potentially more natural-sounding output; the drawback is that it increases the complexity of the generation task, forcing the model to make more choices. This paper focuses on the interplay between underspecification and surface realisation performance within the context of German, a morphologically rich language exhibiting a high degree of syntactic freedom. German presents particular challenges for generation due to its relatively free word order and the pervasive phenomenon of voice alternation—the choice between active and passive constructions. While theoretically governed by grammatical rules relating to information structure and discourse pragmatics, the actual usage of voice is heavily influenced by stylistic preferences and corpus-specific patterns. We build upon a syntactic surface realisation system originally designed for word order variation (Lochbihler et al., 2017), extending it to encompass voice selection, thereby allowing us to model active and passive variants within the same framework. Crucially, our system operates within a reversible grammar, enabling us to train it to *regenerate* surface strings from their underlying semantic representations. This regeneration task provides a strong signal for learning the intricate relationships between semantic input, syntactic structure, and surface form. Our central research question is: how does the degree of underspecification in the input representation affect the model’s ability to accurately predict and generate the original voice of a sentence? We hypothesize that a carefully calibrated level of underspecification—leaving the voice information implicit in the input rather than explicitly specifying it—can unlock the model's ability to learn the complex interplay between voice, word order, and other subtle linguistic factors present in German corpus data. We present experimental results demonstrating that with an appropriately underspecified input, our linguistically informed realisation model achieves a significant improvement in voice prediction accuracy, reaching 91.5% compared to a baseline of 82.5%. This suggests that the model is indeed learning to leverage the subtle cues present in the input to infer the intended voice, offering a promising avenue towards more robust and naturalistic German surface realisation. We further analyze the model’s behavior to identify the linguistic features that are most indicative of voice selection. These results contribute to the broader understanding of data-driven surface realisation, highlighting the importance of strategically managing underspecification to optimize performance and capture the nuances of complex grammatical phenomena like voice.

Chinese Word Segmentation (CWS) is a fundamental task in Chinese Natural Language Processing (NLP), serving as a crucial pre-processing step for many downstream applications such as machine translation, information retrieval, and sentiment analysis. Unlike English, where words are naturally separated by spaces, Chinese text typically consists of a continuous sequence of characters, requiring explicit segmentation to identify meaningful word units. Traditionally, CWS has been approached as a sequence labeling problem, often utilizing Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) or Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) (Xue & Chen, 2003; Lafferty et al., 2001). However, the ever-evolving nature of the Chinese language introduces a significant challenge: the emergence of new words. These new words, frequently appearing in online media and social platforms, are often absent from standard dictionaries and pose a considerable obstacle to traditional CWS systems. Consequently, Joint models that simultaneously perform CWS and New Word Detection (NWD) have gained prominence (Zhou & Li, 2013; Liu et al., 2015). These models aim to leverage the interplay between known and unknown words to improve segmentation accuracy and effectively identify emerging lexical items. Recent advances have focused on incorporating richer feature representations, often involving both word-based features (character compositions, prefixes, suffixes) and contextual features derived from the surrounding text (edge features capturing label transitions). However, this pursuit of improved accuracy frequently comes at the cost of increased computational complexity. Specifically, the integration of high-dimensional feature spaces – necessary to capture the nuanced characteristics of both known words and potential new words – dramatically increases the training time required for these joint models. Training on large-scale datasets, which are essential for achieving robust performance, becomes prohibitively expensive and slow. Traditional batch learning methods, while capable of achieving high accuracy, are often impractical in scenarios demanding rapid model adaptation or frequent updates. Online learning, which updates model parameters incrementally with each new data instance, offers a viable alternative for large-scale datasets. However, even online gradient descent can be slow when dealing with high-dimensional features and vast amounts of training data. In this paper, we address the challenge of fast online training for joint CWS and NWD models equipped with high-dimensional features. We present a novel training method, an adaptive online gradient descent algorithm that leverages feature frequency information to dynamically adjust learning rates. The core idea is to accelerate training by prioritizing updates for features that appear more frequently in the training data, while diminishing the updates for less frequent, potentially noisy, features. This frequency-adaptive approach significantly reduces the computational burden without compromising model accuracy. Our experimental results demonstrate that this adaptive online gradient descent method achieves training speeds an order of magnitude faster than existing training techniques, while simultaneously achieving comparable, or even superior, accuracy on standard Chinese word segmentation and new word detection benchmarks. Crucially, the proposed optimization method is not limited to the specific task of joint CWS and NWD; it is a general-purpose technique applicable to a wide range of machine learning problems involving high-dimensional features and large-scale datasets. We believe this contribution provides a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners seeking to efficiently train complex models in resource-constrained environments.

Text classification remains a cornerstone of natural language processing, powering applications from sentiment analysis and spam detection to topic categorization and document routing. While supervised learning approaches have historically dominated this field, the requirement for large, labeled datasets presents a significant bottleneck in many real-world scenarios. Obtaining such labels can be expensive, time-consuming, and require specialized expertise, particularly for nuanced or domain-specific tasks. This limitation has fueled substantial research into semi-supervised learning (SSL) techniques, which leverage readily available unlabeled data to augment limited labeled resources and improve classification performance. Existing semi-supervised methods for text classification encompass a wide spectrum of approaches, including self-training, co-training, transductive SVMs, and graph-based methods (Chapelle et al., 2006). More recently, deep learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for SSL, with techniques like autoencoders, variational autoencoders, and generative adversarial networks being adapted to learn useful representations from both labeled and unlabeled data (Hinton & Salakhutdinov, 2006; Goodfellow et al., 2014). These deep SSL models often rely on pre-training followed by fine-tuning, or on complex architectural designs to jointly model data distribution and classification boundaries. However, effectively coordinating the learning process – particularly in exploiting the complementary information available from labeled and unlabeled sources – remains a key challenge. In this work, we introduce a novel approach to semi-supervised text classification based on a deep hybrid architecture and a distinctive fine-tuning algorithm. Our model blends the strengths of generative and discriminative learning, utilizing a bottom-up generative pass to establish robust data representations, followed by a top-down fine-tuning mechanism that optimizes classification performance. This process is iterative and incremental, forming what we term the Bottom-Up-Top-Down (BUTD) learning algorithm. Unlike traditional pre-training and fine-tuning paradigms, our algorithm pseudo-jointly modifies model parameters during each learning increment, allowing for a more integrated and adaptive learning process. The core innovation lies in the iterative interaction between generative representation learning and discriminative classification. The bottom-up phase learns a latent representation of the data, capturing underlying semantic structures from both labeled and unlabeled examples. Subsequently, the top-down phase refines these representations specifically for the classification task, guided by the labeled data. This cycle is repeated, progressively improving both the quality of the representations and the accuracy of the classifier. We demonstrate through extensive experiments that this BUTD learning algorithm consistently outperforms a variety of competitive models and baselines across a range of semi-supervised settings, exhibiting robust performance even with highly imbalanced labeled/unlabeled data splits. Topic modeling has emerged as a cornerstone technique in the field of natural language processing, offering powerful tools for discovering latent semantic structures within large collections of text. Traditional batch topic modeling approaches, such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) (Blei et al., 2003), are computationally expensive and often impractical for handling the scale of modern datasets. Consequently, online topic modeling, which employs stochastic variational inference (SVI) to update topic models incrementally with each new document, has gained significant traction (Hoffman et al., 2010). SVI allows for efficient and scalable analysis of massive corpora, making it well-suited for dynamic data streams characteristic of many real-world applications. A crucial component of successful online learning is the optimization algorithm used to update model parameters. Gradient descent, and its variants, are commonly employed in this setting. However, selecting an appropriate learning rate—the step size taken during each parameter update—is paramount for efficient convergence. Adaptive Gradient Algorithm (ADAGRAD) (Duchi et al., 2011) has become a popular choice for tuning learning rates in online settings. ADAGRAD adapts the learning rate for each parameter individually, based on the historical sum of squared gradients. Parameters associated with frequently occurring features receive smaller updates, while those associated with infrequent features receive larger updates. This strategy is intended to accelerate learning and improve convergence. Despite the theoretical advantages of ADAGRAD, empirical observations have shown that its combination with online topic modeling often leads to suboptimal performance, and even outright failure to converge. While ADAGRAD performs well in many other online learning tasks, applying it directly to stochastic variational inference for topic modeling frequently results in vanishing learning rates and a reluctance to fully explore the parameter space. This phenomenon has been reported by practitioners in the field, yet a rigorous explanation for this incompatibility has remained elusive. This paper aims to elucidate the underlying reasons why ADAGRAD fails when applied to online topic modeling. We demonstrate that the core issue stems from the large magnitude of gradients encountered during SVI for topic models. Specifically, the accumulation of these substantial gradients in ADAGRAD’s learning rate denominator causes the learning rates to shrink at an exceedingly rapid pace. Consequently, the model parameters become effectively frozen before they have a chance to fully converge, hindering the learning process and ultimately limiting the quality of the discovered topic structure.
