Relation classification – the task of identifying the semantic relationship between entities mentioned in text – is a core component of many information extraction (IE) systems and natural language processing (NLP) pipelines. Traditionally, feature engineering played a dominant role in achieving strong performance on this task, with researchers meticulously crafting linguistic features reflecting syntactic and semantic patterns indicative of specific relations (Zeng et al., 2008; Miwa & Suzuki, 2009). However, recent advances in deep learning have led to the widespread adoption of neural network architectures for relation classification, demonstrating the potential to learn relevant features automatically from raw text. Despite these advancements, a significant limitation remains in the current state of research: a lack of comprehensive and comparative evaluation across diverse datasets. Many studies focus on improving performance on a single dataset or a limited subset of benchmarks, making it difficult to assess the generalizability and adaptability of proposed models (Socher et al., 2012; Nguyen & Grishman, 2015). This narrow evaluation strategy raises concerns about the extent to which performance gains are specific to the characteristics of a particular dataset or intrinsically attributable to the architectural innovations themselves. Furthermore, it hampers meaningful comparisons between different approaches, hindering progress toward a unified understanding of effective relation classification techniques. To address this gap, we present a large-scale, systematic evaluation of several prominent neural relation classification architectures. We cast a wide net, evaluating these models across six benchmark datasets representing a broad spectrum of relational characteristics, complexities, and sizes. These datasets vary considerably in terms of the number of relation types, the sentence structure, the degree of ambiguity, and the overall size of the training data. Our exploration culminates in the proposal of a novel “Man for All Seasons” model – a multi-channel LSTM architecture integrated with a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). This model strategically combines the strengths of both recurrent and convolutional neural networks, leveraging a variety of linguistic features and architectural designs prevalent in current literature. Notably, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on two of the evaluated datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness. However, beyond achieving competitive results, our primary goal is to provide valuable insights into the persistent challenges faced by neural language models in relation classification. Through thorough analysis, we identify patterns in model performance across different datasets, shedding light on the types of relations and textual contexts that remain particularly difficult for current approaches. The code and data used in our study are publicly available to facilitate reproducibility and further research. We believe that this large-scale exploration serves as a crucial step toward a more comprehensive understanding of neural relation classification and will guide future development of more robust and generalizable models. Knowledge-based question answering (KBQA) has garnered significant attention in recent years, fueled by the increasing availability of large-scale knowledge graphs (KGs) like Freebase, Wikidata, and DBpedia. The core challenge in KBQA lies in bridging the semantic gap between natural language questions and the structured representation of facts within KGs. Early work focused on relatively simple questions, often requiring a single relation lookup to derive the answer (Popescu et al., 2013; Yates et al., 2007). Consequently, datasets like WebQuestions (Berant et al., 2013) and SimpleQuestions (Bordes et al., 2015) became benchmarks for evaluating KBQA systems. While these datasets have been instrumental in driving progress, they predominantly contain “simple” questions, answerable through a single relation path in the KG. This inherent limitation restricts the ability to adequately evaluate the capacity of KBQA systems to handle more complex, real-world queries that necessitate reasoning over multiple relations and constraints. Consider, for instance, the question "What novels were written by authors born in France who also won the Nobel Prize in Literature?". Answering this requires traversing multiple relation types (e.g., *author_of*, *born_in*, *award_received*) and imposing constraints on multiple entities – a task demonstrably more challenging than simply identifying the author of a particular work. Existing benchmark datasets lack sufficient instances of such “multi-constraint” questions, hindering a thorough assessment of KBQA system capabilities. To address this gap, we introduce ComplexQuestions, a new dataset specifically designed to evaluate KBQA systems on questions requiring multiple KG relations and constraints. ComplexQuestions deliberately focuses on queries that cannot be resolved using single relation lookup and necessitate complex graph traversals. The construction of this dataset involved a meticulous process of question generation and KG grounding, ensuring both semantic clarity and factual correctness. Beyond the release of the ComplexQuestions dataset, we also propose a novel constraint-based approach to KBQA intended to tackle these more complicated queries. Our method systematically decomposes the natural language question into a set of constraints derived from the question’s linguistic structure and KG schema. These constraints are then used to guide a graph traversal process, identifying entities that satisfy all imposed conditions. This contrasts with many existing approaches reliant on semantic parsing or embedding-based matching, which often struggle with the intricacies of multi-constraint questions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through comprehensive experiments across WebQuestions, SimpleQuestions, and, crucially, ComplexQuestions. Results show that our method achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art techniques on the existing datasets. Yet, our approach significantly outperforms existing methods on ComplexQuestions, highlighting its ability to effectively handle multi-constraint reasoning. The release of ComplexQuestions and the proposed approach together provide valuable resources for the KBQA community to advance the state-of-the-art in tackling real-world, complex information needs.

The notion of semantic primitives – fundamental, irreducible components of meaning – has long been central to linguistic theory (Lyons, 1977; Wierzbicka, 1996). The goal of identifying these primitives is to provide a concise and universal basis for describing the meaning of words, ultimately facilitating a deeper understanding of language and cognition. Within computational linguistics, lexicons like WordNet (Miller, 1995) and VerbNet (Schubert & Vanderwende, 2001) represent significant attempts to structure lexical semantics, often implicitly relying on the decompositional principle. VerbNet, in particular, stands out as a richly annotated lexicon of English verbs, grouping verbs into synsets based on their argument structure and semantic similarities. Crucially, each VerbNet class is associated with a set of semantic predicates – conceptually akin to the aforementioned primitives – which ostensibly represent the core components of the verb’s meaning. For instance, the verb “spray,” categorized under the ‘Spray’ class in VerbNet, is decomposed into predicates such as MOTION, NOT, and LOCATION. This decomposition suggests that the action of spraying can be understood as an agent causing a theme to move to a location, and specifically, that the theme was *not* previously in that location. Such decompositions are fundamental for various NLP tasks, including semantic role labeling, text summarization, and machine translation, as they provide a more fine-grained representation of verbal meaning than a simple lemma. However, despite the theoretical elegance and practical utility of VerbNet’s predicate-based approach, a critical limitation has persisted: a relative lack of robust empirical validation. While the predicates themselves are often grounded in linguistic theory and intuitive understanding, systematic evidence supporting their validity and completeness is scarce. Are these truly the ‘atomic’ components of meaning, or do they themselves benefit from further decomposition? Are there systematic biases in how predicates are assigned to verbs? These questions remain largely unanswered, hindering our confidence in the lexicon’s underlying semantic framework. Existing work on evaluating semantic representations often focuses on downstream task performance (e.g., using VerbNet for semantic role labeling and assessing the accuracy of the resulting labels). However, this indirect approach conflates the quality of the semantic representation with the effectiveness of the downstream model. A direct assessment of the semantic predicates themselves requires eliciting judgements *directly* from human subjects regarding the relationships between verbs and their proposed semantic components. This paper describes the “VerbCorner Project,” a recently launched initiative aimed at directly addressing this gap in empirical evidence. We detail a novel approach leveraging crowdsourcing, framing the evaluation of VerbNet’s predicates as a series of carefully designed “games” presented to online participants. Our goal is to systematically gather human judgements on the appropriateness and completeness of the current predicate sets, providing valuable insights into the validity of VerbNet’s semantic decomposition and guiding future improvements to the lexicon. We believe this project represents a crucial step towards a more empirically grounded understanding of verb semantics, with implications extending beyond the immediate scope of VerbNet itself.

The automatic detection of grammatical errors has long been a central goal in Natural Language Processing (NLP), driven by the potential to aid language learners, improve writing quality, and enhance machine translation systems. Recent years have witnessed significant progress in Grammatical Error Detection (GED) systems, fueled by the rise of neural network architectures and increasingly large corpora of written text (Lee & Schuler, 2012; Zhao et al., 2019). However, despite these advances, a critical and often under-addressed aspect of the field remains: the evaluation of these systems. While numerous GED systems have been proposed and benchmarked on standard datasets (e.g., CoNLL-2014 shared task (Nelken & Schuller, 2014)), drawing meaningful comparisons between different approaches has proven remarkably difficult. Performance numbers frequently vary across publications, even when evaluated on the *same* test set, obscuring true advancements and hindering progress. This discrepancy arises not from fundamental differences in system capability alone, but from a complex web of overlooked evaluation issues. Traditional evaluation paradigms in NLP, often borrowed from tasks like machine translation or text classification, are frequently ill-suited to the unique challenges presented by GED. Unlike many such tasks, GED involves a three-way contingency: the original writer’s sentence, the gold-standard correction provided by an annotator, and the output of the detection system. This intricate relationship introduces subtleties absent in simpler classification problems where a clear-cut “correct” or “incorrect” label suffices. Consider, for example, a system that flags a potentially incorrect article; the annotation might involve a full phrase rewrite, making a simple token-level comparison inadequate. Furthermore, the inherent skew in the data distribution exacerbates these problems. Grammatical errors are, by definition, relatively rare occurrences compared to correctly written text (Kilgarriff, 2007). This imbalance dramatically impacts commonly used evaluation metrics such as precision, recall, and F1-score, potentially inflating scores for systems that primarily identify correct sentences while missing a substantial proportion of actual errors. The pursuit of high aggregate scores can, therefore, mask significant deficiencies in error detection capability. This paper aims to address these critical evaluation issues head-on. We begin by presenting an intuitive evaluation scheme that explicitly accounts for the three-way contingency inherent in GED. We then emphasize the importance of reporting raw measurements – true positives, false negatives, false positives, and true negatives – to provide a more transparent and interpretable picture of system performance. Crucially, we delve into the challenges of *defining* those raw measurements, exploring complexities such as determining the scope of an error (e.g., a single word, a phrase, or an entire clause) and grappling with the graded nature of grammaticality. Finally, we propose recommendations for best practices in reporting GED results, emphasizing the need for clarity regarding underlying assumptions and the intended application of the error detection system. Our goal is not to prescribe a single, universally applicable evaluation metric. Rather, we aim to lay bare the inherent complexities of evaluating GED systems, fostering a more nuanced and informed discourse within the research community and, ultimately, facilitating genuine progress in the field. By highlighting these problems, we hope to pave the way for more robust and reliable evaluation methodologies that accurately reflect the capabilities of GED systems and their potential impact.

Large vocabulary continuous speech recognition (LVCSR) has achieved remarkable progress in recent decades, largely due to advancements in acoustic modeling (e.g., deep neural networks) and language modeling (e.g., n-grams, recurrent neural networks). However, a fundamental limitation of these systems remains: their inability to recognize words not present in their predefined vocabulary. This is particularly problematic in real-world applications, such as broadcast news transcription or lecture recordings, where spontaneous speech frequently contains named entities, foreign words, technical jargon, and newly coined terms – all likely to be out-of-vocabulary (OOV). Traditional approaches to handling OOV words often involve techniques like phonetic transcription or guessing based on acoustic similarity. However, these methods are often unreliable and prone to errors, especially for longer or complex OOV terms. A growing body of research has focused on hybrid word/sub-word systems as a more robust solution. These systems augment a standard word-based lexicon with a set of sub-word units (e.g., phonemes, morphemes, byte-pair encodings), enabling the recognition of novel words as sequences of these constituent units. Existing hybrid systems typically construct the sub-word lexicon using heuristic methods. These often involve identifying frequent phone sequences directly from phonetic transcriptions of text corpora (e.g., Gao et al., 2008). While effective to a degree, these approaches rely on simple statistical measures and lack the ability to explicitly optimize the sub-word units for a specific recognition task. The resulting lexicon may include sub-word units that are rarely helpful for discriminating between potential word candidates, or conversely, may miss crucial sub-word units vital for recognizing a significant portion of OOV terms. In this paper, we present a novel probabilistic model for learning a sub-word lexicon optimized for OOV word detection in speech recognition. Our approach frames the sub-word lexicon learning problem as a task-driven optimization, directly aiming to improve the performance of a hybrid word/sub-word model on the task of identifying OOV words. Instead of relying on frequency counts of phonetic sequences, our model learns sub-word units based on their ability to contribute to accurate OOV detection, leveraging the expected output distributions from a hybrid recognition system. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our learned sub-word lexicon on challenging English broadcast news and MIT Lectures datasets. Experimental results show that a hybrid model incorporating our lexicon significantly reduces OOV errors, achieving a 6.3% and 7.6% (absolute) reduction in error rate at a 5% false alarm rate respectively, compared to systems utilizing a traditionally constructed sub-word lexicon. This improvement underscores the benefits of learning sub-word units specifically tailored to the demands of the recognition task, and provides a promising direction for addressing the persistent challenge of OOV words in speech recognition. <!-- **References (to be included in the final version)** * Gao, Y., et al. (2008). A subword lexicon for large vocabulary speech recognition. *Interspeech*. -->

Morphological analysis – the decomposition of words into their meaningful components, or morphemes – is a fundamental task in natural language processing, crucial for applications ranging from machine translation and information retrieval to speech recognition and language learning. Despite its importance, obtaining manually annotated morphological data is a laborious and expensive undertaking, particularly for the vast majority of the world’s languages, which remain significantly under-resourced. This scarcity of labeled data motivates the development of unsupervised morphological analysis techniques that can automatically induce morphological structures from raw text. Traditional approaches to unsupervised morphology have largely focused on designing learning algorithms that embody inductive biases specific to the task. These biases, often based on principles of Minimum Description Length (MDL) (De Marcken, 1996; Goldsmith, 2001), aim to balance model complexity against the goodness of fit to the observed data, favoring analyses that offer a compact and elegant description of the language’s morphological patterns. While such MDL-based methods have proven reasonably successful, they often rely on hand-engineered features and thresholds, and may struggle to generalize across languages with diverse morphological typologies. In this paper, we propose a radically different paradigm for unsupervised morphological analysis. Rather than explicitly encoding linguistic knowledge into the learning algorithm, we treat morphology as a structured prediction problem, leveraging the wealth of morphological information available in well-resourced languages to bootstrap analysis in under-resourced ones. Our core idea is to define a *universal morphological feature space* where every language and its corresponding morphological analysis can be represented as a point. This space allows us to quantify the similarity between languages, and to transfer knowledge from languages with labeled data to those without. Crucially, we do *not* assume parallel corpora or cognate detection – our approach relies solely on the structural properties of the morphological analyses themselves. We develop a novel *structured nearest neighbor prediction method* that, for a given unlabeled language, seeks to find the morphological analysis of a training language which is closest in the universal feature space. This framework effectively casts morphological induction as a search for analogs in a high-dimensional space of language structures. The method’s performance is not predicated on resemblance to any single training language, but rather a composite of similarities across a range of structural characteristics. We apply our model to eight inflectionally rich languages and demonstrate substantial improvements in nominal morphology induction compared to a state-of-the-art MDL-based approach. Our results reveal a particularly promising trend: accuracy continues to improve significantly as the number of training languages increases, suggesting that our method benefits powerfully from increased cross-linguistic knowledge. This finding supports our central hypothesis that morphological analysis can be effectively treated as a structured prediction problem, and opens new avenues for cross-lingual transfer learning in morphology. References: De Marcken, P. H. (1996). MDL and morphological analysis. *Computational Linguistics*, *22*(1), 83–98. Goldsmith, J. A. (2001). *Unsupervised learning of morphology*. MIT press.

The ability to accurately determine the sentiment expressed in text – whether it’s positive, negative, or neutral – is a cornerstone of numerous Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications, ranging from customer feedback analysis and market research to social media monitoring and political polling. Sentiment classification, therefore, has become a vital area of study within the field. However, achieving robust performance in sentiment classification is heavily reliant on the availability of high-quality, labeled sentiment resources, such as sentiment lexicons and sentiment-annotated corpora. A significant challenge arises from the stark imbalance in the availability of such resources across different languages. While English benefits from a wealth of meticulously curated sentiment resources, many other languages, particularly those considered “low-resource,” suffer from a critical dearth of labeled data. This disparity presents a significant obstacle to building effective sentiment classification systems for a large portion of the world’s population. To address this issue, Cross-Language Sentiment Classification (CLSC) has emerged as a promising approach. CLSC aims to leverage the abundant sentiment resources available in a resource-rich language (often English, serving as the *source language*) to facilitate sentiment classification in a resource-scarce language (the *target language*). This transfer learning paradigm offers a viable pathway to building accurate sentiment classifiers even when limited labeled data exists in the target language. A key strategy in CLSC is the creation of bilingual word embeddings – vector representations of words that capture semantic relationships across languages. By mapping words from different languages into a shared vector space, these embeddings aim to bridge the semantic gap between the source and target languages, enabling cross-lingual transfer of knowledge. However, traditional bilingual embedding techniques primarily focus on semantic similarity, often neglecting the crucial aspect of *sentiment* information. A word's semantic meaning is distinct from its sentiment polarity; for example, “benefit” and “harm” are semantically dissimilar, but also carry opposing sentiment orientations. Ignoring sentiment can therefore severely limit the effectiveness of CLSC. In this paper, we present a novel approach to learning Bilingual Sentiment Word Embeddings (BSWE) specifically designed to enhance the performance of English-Chinese CLSC. Our B-SWE method explicitly incorporates sentiment information into the bilingual embedding learning process. Unlike existing approaches that require extensive parallel corpora – large collections of text and their translations – our method can effectively learn high-quality BSWE by leveraging readily available labeled corpora in both languages *and* their corresponding translations. This reduces the barrier to entry for developing CLSC systems, as acquiring large parallel corpora can be a costly and time-consuming endeavor. Through experiments on the NLP&CC 2013 CLSC dataset, we demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art CLSC systems, highlighting the importance of incorporating sentiment awareness into bilingual word embeddings. Named Entity Recognition (NER), the task of identifying and classifying named entities in text, is a core component of many Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications, including information extraction, question answering, and machine translation. While significant progress has been made in NER performance utilizing supervised learning techniques, a critical challenge remains: the generalization of models across different domains. NER classifiers, often trained on data from a specific domain (e.g., news articles), frequently exhibit a substantial drop in accuracy when applied to new, unseen domains (e.g., biomedical texts, social media posts). This performance degradation stems from the inherent differences in data distribution between the source (training) and target (application) domains – a phenomenon known as domain shift. The primary cause of this domain shift in NER lies in the domain-specific vocabulary and language usage associated with each domain. An entity type, such as “Organization,” may be represented by drastically different terms across domains. For instance, in the news domain, “Apple” refers to the technology company, whereas in the culinary domain, “Apple” denotes a fruit. Existing NER systems often struggle to disambiguate these contexts, leading to errors when applied to a new domain. Traditional approaches to domain adaptation in NER typically rely on acquiring labeled data from the target domain and fine-tuning the model trained on the source domain. However, this strategy is often impractical and costly. Creating high-quality annotated datasets demands significant human effort and expertise, making it a labor-intensive and time-consuming undertaking, especially when dealing with a large number of potentially diverse target domains. Zero-shot or few-shot domain adaptation methods aim to address this limitation, but often struggle to achieve performance comparable to fully supervised approaches. To alleviate the need for labeled target domain data, we introduce a novel domain adaptation method leveraging Latent Semantic Association (LaSA) for NER. Our approach is founded on the principle that underlying semantic concepts remain relatively consistent across domains, even if the surface-level term representations differ. LaSA models the relationships between words by grouping them into concepts based on shared contextual snippets found in unlabeled corpora. This allows us to bridge the gap between source and target domains by projecting their term spaces into a common, semantically-rich concept space. Specifically, LaSA constructs a model that captures latent semantic associations among words extracted from an unlabeled corpus representative of the target domain. By analyzing the contexts in which words appear, LaSA identifies underlying concepts and establishes relationships between terms that share similar meanings. In the domain transfer process, both the source and target domain term spaces are projected onto this concept space using the learned LaSA model. Subsequently, the original NER model is refined using features derived from these semantic associations. Our experiments, conducted on both English and Chinese corpora, demonstrate that LaSA-based domain adaptation significantly enhances the performance of NER systems without requiring any labeled data from the target domain. This makes our method a practical and effective solution for adapting NER models to new and unseen domains, offering a substantial improvement over existing domain adaptation techniques.

Automated essay scoring (AES) has seen significant advancement in recent years, propelled by the increasing availability of large text corpora and sophisticated machine learning techniques (Page, 1966; Landauer et al., 2003; Shermis & Burstein, 2013). Early AES systems focused largely on holistic scoring, assigning a single grade to an essay based on overall quality. However, a growing consensus within the educational community emphasizes the importance of formative assessment – providing students with detailed feedback on specific aspects of their writing (Andrade & Valtcheva, 2009). Consequently, research efforts have shifted towards *dimensional* essay scoring, where essays are evaluated along multiple, well-defined criteria. Recent work has focused on modeling dimensions such as coherence (Hu et al., 2017), grammatical correctness (Chung et al., 2014), relevance to the prompt (Pilán et al., 2010), and argumentation quality (Felner et al., 2013). These efforts aim to move beyond simple grading to provide actionable insights that help students improve their writing skills. Despite this progress, one crucial dimension of essay quality – *thesis clarity* – has received comparatively little attention. A clear thesis statement is arguably the cornerstone of a strong essay, providing a concise summary of the main argument and guiding the reader through the subsequent development of ideas (Bean et al., 2001). A vague, ambiguous, or absent thesis can significantly detract from an essay’s overall effectiveness, hindering comprehension and diminishing the persuasiveness of the argument. Consequently, the ability to accurately assess thesis clarity is paramount for both instructors and students. However, manual assessment of thesis clarity is time-consuming and subject to inter-rater reliability issues. Automated methods offer a promising solution, but pose unique challenges. Identifying thesis clarity requires not simply detecting the presence of a thesis statement, but evaluating its *quality* – its specificity, focus, and argumentative strength. To address this gap, we introduce a novel approach to modeling thesis clarity in student essays. This paper presents two key contributions. First, we introduce a new, manually annotated corpus of student essays, specifically labeled for thesis clarity. This corpus serves as a valuable resource for the development and evaluation of automated scoring models. Second, we propose a learning-based approach to scoring essays along the thesis clarity dimension, leveraging features extracted from both the essay text and potential thesis statement locations. Furthermore, recognizing that a score alone may not provide sufficient guidance to students, we present a secondary learning-based approach designed to identify specific errors within an essay that contribute to a lower thesis clarity score. Our goal is not only to predict *how clear* a thesis is, but to explain *why* it might be unclear. References: Andrade, H. L., & Valtcheva, A. (2009). Neural machine translation (NMT) has rapidly become the dominant paradigm for machine translation, achieving state-of-the-art results on a variety of translation tasks (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Sutskever et al., 2014; Vaswani et al., 2017). A key advantage of NMT is its ability to learn complex, non-linear relationships between source and target languages directly from data. Recent work has focused on extending NMT to the multilingual setting, where a single model is trained to translate between multiple language pairs (Johnson et al., 2017; Eck et al., 2019). Multilingual NMT offers several potential benefits, including improved translation quality, particularly for low-resource languages, and the ability to perform zero-shot translation – translating between language pairs not explicitly seen during training. While parameter sharing is a defining characteristic of multilingual NMT, allowing for knowledge transfer between languages, it’s not without its challenges. A single set of parameters may struggle to adequately capture the nuances and complexities of all possible language pairs. Languages exhibit varying syntactic structures, semantic ambiguities, and translational divergences. Imposing a single, unified model across all language pairs can lead to suboptimal performance, especially when source and target languages are typologically distant. Previous approaches to address this issue have explored various forms of parameter specialization. Some work focuses on adding language-specific embeddings (Luong et al., 2015), while others explore language-specific transformations of the hidden states (Malaviya et al., 2017). More complex approaches involve dynamically routing information based on the input language (Libovický et al., 2018). However, these methods often introduce significant additional parameters, potentially diminishing the benefits of parameter sharing and increasing the risk of overfitting, especially for low-resource languages. In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective technique for improving multilingual NMT: task-specific attention. We argue that while sharing the majority of model parameters is crucial for generalization, the attention mechanism—responsible for aligning source and target words—benefits from language-specific specialization. Our approach maintains a significant degree of parameter sharing, while introducing a separate attention model for each target language. This allows the model to learn language-specific alignment patterns without drastically increasing the model size. This differs from previous approaches which often specialized entire layers or introduced complex gating mechanisms. We evaluate our approach on a dataset comprising four European languages from the Europarl corpus. Our experiments demonstrate that using target-specific attention consistently improves translation quality across all translation directions compared to a fully shared attention model. Notably, we observe significant improvements even in zero-shot translation scenarios, where the model has never been trained on direct parallel data for that language pair. These results highlight the effectiveness of our approach in leveraging parameter sharing while enabling language-specific adaptation within the attention mechanism, leading to more robust and accurate multilingual NMT systems.

Named Entity Recognition (NER) – the task of identifying and classifying named entities in text, such as person names, organizations, and locations – is a fundamental component of many natural language processing (NLP) pipelines. While significant progress has been made in NER performance on well-defined domains like newswire (e.g., Tomanek et al., 2010; Lample et al., 2016), adapting NER systems to new, unseen domains remains a substantial challenge. This is particularly true when dealing with domains that differ drastically in their linguistic characteristics and entity distributions, such as the shift from formal newswire text to the often-unconventional and noisy language of web queries (e.g., Khosla et al., 2017; Lin et al., 2018). Traditional approaches to cross-domain NER often involve retraining models on limited labeled data from the target domain, or employing more complex domain adaptation techniques like feature augmentation or adversarial training (e.g., Ben-David et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2019). However, acquiring labeled data for new domains is expensive and time-consuming, and these methods can be computationally intensive and may still suffer from performance degradation when the domain shift is large. Moreover, web queries present unique difficulties: they are typically short, often contain misspellings and grammatical errors, and exhibit a diverse range of topics and intentions. In this work, we explore a novel approach to cross-domain NER that leverages the vast resources of search engines to bridge the gap between source and target domains. Our core idea, termed “Piggyback,” is to utilize search engine results as a source of contextual information to enhance NER performance. Specifically, given a token in context, we submit the surrounding text as a query to a search engine. We then analyze the snippets returned by the search engine to identify similar contexts that can provide valuable clues for determining whether the token is a named entity and, if so, its correct classification. This method elegantly circumvents the need for extensive domain-specific training data. The key novelty of Piggyback lies in its ability to dynamically incorporate external knowledge from the web into the NER process. By examining real-world usage patterns reflected in search results, we can disambiguate entities, resolve coreferences, and improve the robustness of NER systems in challenging domains like web queries. We hypothesize that even limited, but relevant snippets from a search engine can significantly improve NER accuracy by providing a richer and more informative context than is typically available within the query or document itself. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of Piggyback on both in-domain and out-of-domain NER tasks, with substantial performance gains observed on web query data. These results highlight the potential of search engines as a valuable resource for adapting NLP models to new domains and for addressing the challenges posed by real-world, user-generated text. Through Piggyback, we demonstrate that it is possible to achieve a robust cross-domain NER performance without relying on extensive domain-specific adaptation.

The study of emergent communication has rapidly gained momentum in the field of artificial intelligence, offering a unique lens through which to examine the foundations of language and its relationship to perception. In these settings, artificial agents are tasked with developing communicative systems from scratch, often through repeated interactions grounded in a shared environment. This approach allows researchers to sidestep the complexities of analyzing naturally evolved language, focusing instead on the fundamental principles that might drive the emergence of meaningful signals. A significant body of work in emergent communication has investigated the symbols agents adopt – the vocabulary they develop, the consistency of their usage, and the efficiency of their signaling strategies (Lazaridou et al., 2017; Mordatch & Abbeel, 2018; Andreas et al., 2017). However, a crucial, and often overlooked, aspect of this communication process is *how* agents perceive and represent the visual information that underpins their interactions. Simply observing successful symbol usage does not illuminate the grounding of those symbols in the agents’ perceptual world. An agent might consistently use a particular signal to refer to a specific object, but what does that signal *mean* to the agent? What features of the visual input are actually encoded in the agent's internal representation? If we aim to build truly language-like communication systems, understanding this perceptual foundation is paramount. Without it, we risk developing superficially coherent communication protocols that lack genuine semantic grounding. In this paper, we delve into the visual representations developed by agents playing a referential game, specifically building upon the framework introduced by Lazaridou et al. (2017). This game requires two agents to collaboratively identify objects within images, with one agent acting as the “speaker” and the other as the “listener.” Through repeated interactions, agents learn to associate visual stimuli with communicative signals. Our investigation moves beyond analyzing the resulting communication patterns to explore the internal representations the agents induce during this learning process. Surprisingly, our findings reveal that successful communication can emerge even when the agents’ learned visual representations dramatically diverge from human-intuitive conceptual properties of the objects themselves. While agents achieve remarkable alignment in their internal representations – essentially “seeing” the world in a remarkably similar way *to each other* – this shared understanding is not rooted in features that correspond to the objects’ color, shape, or other readily identifiable characteristics. Instead, the agents appear to converge on representations driven by lower-level visual features that are sufficient for distinguishing objects within the specific game context, but lack broader semantic meaning. This result highlights a critical gap in our understanding of emergent language: the alignment of agents' perceptual representations alone is not sufficient for building communication systems that reflect the richness and flexibility of natural language. We argue that a more focused attention to the visual semantics agents associate with their symbols is essential for progressing toward truly language-like emergent communication. Named Entity Recognition (NER) – the task of identifying and classifying named entities in text – is a cornerstone of information extraction, playing a crucial role in applications ranging from news analysis and knowledge base construction to question answering and clinical text mining. While significant progress has been made in developing high-performing NER systems, a dominant reliance on language-specific resources and substantial annotated data remains a persistent limitation. State-of-the-art systems frequently leverage extensive, manually curated corpora, language-specific gazetteers, and meticulously engineered features to achieve competitive performance within a single language (Nadeau & Sekine, 2007; Lample et al., 2016). This creates a substantial bottleneck when deploying NER capabilities to new languages, particularly those with limited resources or where labeled data is scarce. The challenge of low-resource NER is particularly acute in a world increasingly demanding multilingual processing. Traditional approaches, such as machine translation followed by NER in a high-resource language, often introduce errors and fail to capture the nuances of the target language. Cross-lingual transfer learning offers a promising alternative, but its success hinges on effective representation schemes that can bridge the gap between languages with differing orthographies and morphological structures. Existing transfer learning strategies typically rely on shared word embeddings (Chandu et al., 2018) or multilingual contextualized embeddings like mBERT (Devlin et al., 2019), both of which can be limited by the availability of parallel corpora and the inherent ambiguity of word-level representations. We hypothesize that focusing on the *phonology* of words – their sound structure – offers a powerful, language-universal pathway for cross-lingual transfer in NER. Phonological representations are less susceptible to orthographic variations and can capture meaningful similarities across languages, even when written forms diverge significantly. Recognizing this potential, we introduce a novel attentional neural model for NER that leverages solely language-universal phonological character representations alongside word embeddings. Our approach eschews language-specific feature engineering, relying instead on the model’s ability to learn meaningful representations directly from the phonetic properties of words and their contextual surroundings. This paper demonstrates that incorporating phonological information substantially improves NER performance in both supervised monolingual settings and, critically, in zero-shot and low-data transfer scenarios. We present empirical results showcasing that our phonologically aware model outperforms models relying on orthographic character representations and achieves state-of-the-art results with minimal annotation effort. Furthermore, we demonstrate how combining attention mechanisms with phonological features enhances the statistical efficiency of the model, enabling rapid adaptation to new languages even with extremely limited training data. Our contribution lies in offering a robust and adaptable NER framework that breaks free from the constraints of language-specific resources and paves the way for truly multilingual information extraction systems. The quality of word representations has become a cornerstone of modern natural language processing, impacting performance across a wide range of tasks, from sentiment analysis and machine translation to question answering and textual entailment. Traditionally, these representations – such as word embeddings derived from Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013), GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), or fastText (Bojanowski et al., 2017) – are learned in an unsupervised manner from massive text corpora. While effective in capturing general semantic relationships, these pre-trained embeddings often fall short when applied to specialized domains or specific downstream tasks. This necessitates the development of task-specific word representations that are tailored to the nuances of the target application. A promising avenue for improving word representation learning is the notion of *curriculum learning* (Bengio et al., 2009). Inspired by the way humans learn – starting with simpler concepts and gradually progressing to more complex ones – curriculum learning proposes training models on instances ordered according to their difficulty. However, defining an effective curriculum is far from trivial. Often, curriculum strategies rely on heuristics, such as sorting instances by length, frequency, or loss value during initial training. While these heuristics can sometimes yield improvements, they often lack the adaptability needed to optimize for a specific task. Moreover, determining what constitutes “difficulty” is highly dependent on the task at hand and the characteristics of the data. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to curriculum learning for task-specific word representation learning, leveraging the power of *Bayesian Optimization* (Shahriari et al., 2016). Instead of relying on hand-crafted heuristics, we treat curriculum design as a continuous optimization problem. We learn a linear ranking function that assigns a “complexity score” to each instance in the training corpus based on a set of engineered features representing different facets of instance difficulty. Bayesian Optimization is then used to iteratively refine the weights of this ranking function, maximizing performance on a designated downstream task. Our key contribution is a method for automatically discovering curricula that are tailored to the specific requirements of a given task, without requiring extensive domain expertise or manual tuning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach across a variety of downstream tasks, comparing it to both random instance ordering and the natural order of the corpus. The results consistently show that learning the curriculum through Bayesian Optimization leads to significant performance gains, highlighting the potential of this technique for enhancing task-specific word representation learning. By framing curriculum design as an optimization problem, we open the door to more adaptive and effective strategies for training word embeddings and achieving state-of-the-art results on a wide range of NLP applications. The rapid growth of social media and online forums has led to an explosion of user-generated text in Arabic, particularly in its diverse dialectal forms. This content provides a rich source of data for a variety of natural language processing (NLP) applications, including sentiment analysis, information retrieval, and machine translation. However, user-generated text is notoriously noisy, characterized by a high degree of orthographic variations, spelling errors, and informal lexical choices. These inconsistencies pose significant challenges for traditional NLP systems, which are often trained on clean, standardized text. The difficulties are further amplified when dealing with dialectal Arabic, where the inherent linguistic variations – encompassing morpho-syntactic differences, phonetic shifts, and a lack of standardized orthography – contribute to increased data sparsity and diminished model accuracy. Dialectal Arabic presents a unique set of challenges distinct from those faced in processing Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). While MSA benefits from standardized grammar and orthography, dialectal varieties exhibit considerable variation across regions and even within communities. This linguistic diversity, coupled with the inherent noise in user-generated content, makes morphological disambiguation – the task of correctly identifying the morphological features of a word (e.g., root, stem, affix, part-of-speech) – a particularly difficult problem. Accurate morphological analysis is crucial for downstream NLP tasks, as it provides the foundational building blocks for understanding the meaning and structure of text. Existing approaches to morphological analysis of Arabic dialects frequently rely on rule-based systems or statistical models trained on limited, often manually annotated, datasets. While these methods can achieve reasonable performance on clean data, they struggle to generalize to the noisy and inconsistent nature of real-world user-generated content. Recent advances in neural network architectures, particularly recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and transformers, have demonstrated promising results in various NLP tasks, including morphological analysis. However, these models often require large amounts of high-quality training data to achieve optimal performance, a scarce resource for many Arabic dialects. In this paper, we address the challenge of noise-robust morphological disambiguation for Egyptian Arabic, a widely spoken dialect with a substantial online presence. We present a neural morphological tagging and disambiguation model designed specifically to handle noisy and inconsistent input. Our approach incorporates several key extensions to enhance its robustness, including character-level embeddings to capture sub-word information and mitigate the impact of spelling errors, and a novel loss function that explicitly encourages consistency in morphological predictions. We evaluate our models on a challenging dataset of Egyptian Arabic social media text, demonstrating significant improvements over a state-of-the-art baseline. Specifically, our models achieve approximately a 5% relative error reduction in full morphological analysis (equivalent to a 1.1% absolute improvement) and a remarkable 22% relative error reduction in part-of-speech tagging (corresponding to a 1.8% absolute improvement). These results highlight the effectiveness of our approach in tackling the unique challenges posed by noisy dialectal Arabic text, paving the way for more accurate and robust NLP applications.

Humans effortlessly connect words to the senses—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—drawing upon a wealth of commonsense knowledge to interpret the sensorial information embedded within language. This ability underpins our understanding of descriptive passages, evocative poetry, and even everyday conversations. A computational system capable of similar sensorial reasoning would represent a significant step towards true natural language understanding. Consequently, a lexicon explicitly associating words with the senses they evoke would be an invaluable resource for a wide range of tasks, including sentiment analysis, text visualization, and the development of more immersive human-computer interfaces. Despite the clear potential, and to the best of our knowledge, a comprehensive and systematically constructed lexicon of this type remains conspicuously absent from the existing landscape of linguistic resources. Existing lexicons, such as WordNet (Miller, 1995), provide semantic relationships between words, but largely lack explicit connections to sensory experience. While some affective lexicons, like SenticNet (Cambria et al., 2010), incorporate emotional connotations, they do not systematically categorize words based on the specific sense they appeal to. This gap in resources hinders the development of computational models capable of processing and reasoning about sensorial language. In this paper, we address this deficiency by presenting Sensicon, a novel sensorial lexicon that associates English words with the five core senses. Our approach departs from manual annotation, which is costly and time-consuming, and instead leverages the power of computational linguistics and corpus statistics. We employ a bootstrapping method, initiated with a small set of seed words, and iteratively expand the lexicon by identifying words frequently co-occurring with those seeds within a large corpus. This process allows us to automatically construct a resource encompassing a substantial number of English words and their corresponding sensorial associations. To ensure the quality and reliability of Sensicon, we create a gold standard dataset through crowdsourcing, wherein human annotators manually label words with the senses they evoke. We then evaluate Sensicon's performance against this gold standard, demonstrating a significant degree of accuracy. Furthermore, we showcase the utility of Sensicon by applying it to a sensory classification task—determining the dominant sense evoked by a given word or sentence—and comparing its performance against two baseline methods. The results demonstrate that a simple classifier relying on Sensicon consistently outperforms these baselines, both at the word and sentence level. This work therefore not only introduces a valuable linguistic resource, but also validates our computational approach for its construction and establishes the practical benefits of incorporating sensorial information into natural language processing systems. We believe Sensicon represents a crucial step forward in enabling machines to “experience” language in a manner more akin to human perception. Sentence compression – the task of shortening a sentence while preserving its key information – has numerous applications, ranging from automatic text summarization and headline generation to simplifying text for readability and adapting content for devices with limited display space. Recent advances in neural network architectures, particularly sequence-to-sequence models based on Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on this task (Li et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2017). However, a significant challenge remains: the performance of these models often degrades substantially when applied to new domains different from the one they were trained on. This lack of domain adaptability limits the practical utility of these systems, requiring expensive and time-consuming retraining for each new application area. Current LSTM-based sentence compression models typically learn to identify and delete unimportant words or phrases based solely on distributional semantics – the patterns of word co-occurrence observed in the training data. While effective within a specific domain, this approach often struggles to generalize to new domains where the semantic cues for importance may differ. We hypothesize that incorporating explicit syntactic information into the model can improve its ability to identify salient content and make more informed deletion decisions, thereby enhancing domain adaptability. Syntactic structure provides valuable cues about the grammatical relationships between words, such as subject-verb dependencies and modifier attachments, which are often consistent across different domains. In this work, we explore two primary methods for integrating syntactic information into a deletion-based LSTM sentence compression model. First, we augment the model with explicit syntactic features, representing properties like part-of-speech tags and dependency parse labels as additional input to the LSTM layers. This allows the model to directly access information about the grammatical structure of the input sentence. Second, we introduce syntactic constraints during the decoding process using Integer Linear Programming (ILP). This ensures that the generated compressed sentence adheres to well-formed grammatical rules, preventing the model from producing syntactically invalid outputs. We evaluate our proposed model on a cross-domain sentence compression task, comparing its performance against the original LSTM-based model and a traditional, non-neural-network-based approach. Our results demonstrate that incorporating syntactic information significantly improves the model’s ability to generalize to new domains, yielding better compression rates and higher quality compressed sentences, as measured by standard evaluation metrics like ROUGE. Furthermore, the ILP constraints contribute to the generation of more grammatically coherent outputs. These findings suggest that syntax indeed plays a crucial role in building robust and adaptable sentence compression systems. Li, V., Yih, W. t., Tarlow, C., Brockman, D., & Dimakis, A. (2015). Understanding the temporal ordering of events is crucial for natural language understanding. Humans effortlessly process narratives and discern the sequence in which events occurred, leveraging rich contextual and linguistic cues. However, this seemingly simple task presents a significant challenge for computational systems. Accurately classifying temporal relations – determining how events relate in time (e.g., before, after, overlap, simultaneous) – is fundamental to applications such as information extraction, question answering, and story understanding. The prominent TimeBank corpus [1] has served as a valuable resource for investigating temporal relation classification. The corpus annotates temporal relations between events and times expressed in text. However, existing automated approaches to this task often simplify the complexity of temporal reasoning. Many systems collapse the original 14 temporal relation types defined in TimeBank into a smaller set of six coarser-grained relations [2, 3], losing potentially valuable information. This simplification, while easing the classification problem, diminishes the granularity of temporal understanding. Furthermore, a common thread in current methods is a reliance on relatively shallow linguistic features. Approaches frequently focus on morpho-syntactic patterns – such as verb tense, adverbs of time, and prepositional phrases – while underutilizing deeper semantic and discourse-level knowledge. We argue that a comprehensive understanding of temporal relations requires a more holistic consideration of linguistic information, including event aspect, causality, and discourse connectives. For instance, recognizing a causal relationship ("because X happened, Y followed") can be a strong indicator of temporal precedence. In this paper, we present a novel approach to temporal relation classification that addresses these limitations. We move beyond simplified relation sets, aiming to classify event-event or event-time pairs into *all* 14 distinct temporal relations as defined by the TimeBank corpus. Crucially, we incorporate a rich set of linguistic knowledge derived from various semantic and discourse sources, moving beyond purely syntactic features. This knowledge encompasses event properties, lexical semantic relations, and discourse connectives. Our approach also departs from the often-exclusive reliance on either rule-based or learning-based methodologies. Instead, we propose a hybrid system that synergistically combines the strengths of both paradigms. Rule-based components capture explicit temporal cues and constraints, while learning-based components generalize from observed patterns and handle ambiguous cases. We demonstrate through rigorous experimentation on the TimeBank corpus that this knowledge-rich, hybrid approach yields a substantial and statistically significant improvement – a 15-16% relative reduction in error – over a state-of-the-art learning-based baseline. This suggests that incorporating deeper linguistic knowledge and a hybrid architecture are key to achieving higher accuracy in temporal relation classification. [1] O. Neural machine translation (NMT) has rapidly emerged as a dominant paradigm in machine translation, offering a compelling end-to-end learning framework that bypasses many of the complex feature engineering steps characteristic of traditional statistical machine translation (SMT) systems (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Sutskever et al., 2014; Cho et al., 2014). Despite its theoretical elegance and often superior translation quality, NMT necessitates models of considerable size and complexity to achieve state-of-the-art results. These large models, typically comprised of deep recurrent or transformer networks with millions of parameters, demand substantial computational resources for both training and inference, hindering their deployment in resource-constrained environments or real-time applications. The challenge of reducing model size without significant performance degradation has spurred interest in model compression techniques. Among these, knowledge distillation (KD) – originally proposed by Bucila et al. (2006) and popularized by Hinton et al. (2015) – has proven remarkably effective in transferring knowledge from a large, cumbersome “teacher” model to a smaller, more efficient “student” model. This transfer is achieved by training the student to mimic the softened probability distributions produced by the teacher, rather than simply matching the hard target labels. KD has found success across a variety of tasks, including image classification and speech recognition. Applying knowledge distillation to NMT presents unique opportunities and challenges. While standard KD, focused on predicting the correct next word, can offer some benefit, it overlooks the sequential nature of translation and the rich, long-range dependencies within a sentence. The teacher model’s knowledge isn’t solely encapsulated in its word-level predictions; it’s also reflected in the overall sequence it generates, its decisions regarding attention, and the final probability assigned to the complete translated sentence. In this paper, we investigate the application of knowledge distillation to NMT, going beyond the conventional word-level approach. We demonstrate the effectiveness of standard KD for model compression in NMT, and introduce two novel sequence-level distillation strategies designed to explicitly transfer the teacher's understanding of entire translation sequences. Intriguingly, we observe that these sequence-level techniques significantly reduce the reliance on beam search during decoding, even to the point of achieving competitive results with simple greedy decoding – a finding that challenges conventional wisdom in NMT. Our results show that a student model, distilled with our proposed methods, can achieve a 10x speedup over a state-of-the-art teacher model with minimal performance loss. Furthermore, combining knowledge distillation with weight pruning allows for the creation of exceptionally compact models, demonstrating a 13x reduction in parameter count with a negligible drop in translation quality. These advancements bring us closer to deploying high-quality NMT systems in practical, resource-limited environments. References: Bahdanau, D., Cho, K., & Bengio, Y. (2014). Question classification (QC) – the task of identifying the semantic category of a user’s question – is a fundamental component in many natural language processing (NLP) applications, including question answering (QA) systems, information retrieval, and dialogue management (Voorhees & Tice, 2000; Moldovan et al., 2003). Accurate question classification is critical, as it dictates the subsequent processing steps and ultimately impacts the quality of the system’s response. For instance, in a QA system, correctly identifying a question as a ‘location’ query allows the system to focus its search on geographically relevant information, while misclassifying it as ‘person’ would lead to irrelevant results. Traditionally, question classification has been approached using machine learning (ML) techniques (Kwok et al., 2001; Seo et al., 2002). These methods typically involve feature engineering, extracting linguistic cues from the question such as keywords, part-of-speech tags, and syntactic dependencies, then training a classifier (e.g., Support Vector Machines, Naive Bayes) to map these features to question categories. While ML-based methods have achieved considerable success, they often require large labeled datasets for training and can struggle with out-of-vocabulary words or variations in question phrasing. Furthermore, the “black box” nature of many ML models makes it difficult to understand *why* a particular question was classified in a certain way, hindering debugging and refinement. In contrast, rule-based systems offer transparency and explainability. By explicitly defining rules based on linguistic patterns, developers can control the classification process and easily modify the system based on observed errors. However, crafting comprehensive and accurate rules manually can be a laborious and time-consuming process, and maintaining these rules becomes difficult as the number of categories and complexity of questions increases. Existing rule-based approaches often rely on simple keyword matching or shallow syntactic analysis, leading to limited accuracy. This paper presents a purely rule-based system for question classification that seeks to bridge this gap. We introduce a method which leverages both the syntactic structure and semantic content of questions to extract relevant information, then utilizes a hierarchical set of rules to categorize the questions based on these identified elements. Our key innovation lies in a two-stage process: first, structurally-informed extraction of key words and phrases, ensuring that only the most relevant parts of the question are considered; and second, a sophisticated rule set that maps these extracted elements to predefined concepts representing question categories. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving an impressive accuracy of 97.2% on a benchmark dataset. This represents a significant improvement of nearly 6 percentage points over the previous state-of-the-art rule-based system (91.6%). We believe that this performance highlights the potential of combining structured analysis with carefully crafted rules for highly accurate question classification. Moreover, we argue that our rule-based system provides a strong foundation for further improvement through the application of machine learning techniques, creating a hybrid approach that could leverage the strengths of both paradigms.

The increasing prevalence of Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) and other forms of dementia represents a significant global health challenge. With an aging population worldwide, the number of individuals affected by these neurodegenerative conditions is projected to rise dramatically in the coming decades (Alzheimer’s Association, 2023). This underscores the critical need for early and accurate detection methods to facilitate timely intervention, improve patient care, and potentially slow disease progression. While definitive diagnosis often relies on pathological examination post-mortem, the development of reliable biomarkers and cognitive assessment tools for early identification is a major focus of current research. Traditional approaches to dementia assessment rely heavily on neuropsychological testing, neuroimaging, and clinical evaluations. However, these methods can be expensive, time-consuming, and prone to inter-rater variability. Moreover, datasets compiled for AD research are frequently limited in size, suffer from missing data, and exhibit inherent heterogeneity across different patient populations and assessment protocols. This sparsity presents a significant obstacle to building robust and generalizable predictive models. Recent advances in machine learning, particularly in the realm of representation learning, offer promising avenues for addressing these challenges. Embedding techniques, such as word embeddings (Mikolov et al., 2013) and graph embeddings (Hamilton et al., 2017), have demonstrated success in capturing semantic relationships and latent structures in various domains. The core idea is to map high-dimensional data into a lower-dimensional embedding space where similar instances are located closer together, and meaningful patterns can be more readily identified. In the context of dementia assessment, the available data often comprises diverse modalities – linguistic features extracted from spontaneous speech, cognitive scores obtained from standardized tests, information gleaned from patient history, and potentially neuroimaging data. This naturally lends itself to a *multiview learning* framework, where the goal is to integrate information from multiple sources to achieve a more comprehensive and informative representation of the patient’s cognitive status. Multiview learning is motivated by the idea that different views of the same phenomenon can provide complementary information, enhancing the accuracy and robustness of predictive models (Xu et al., 2013). In this work, we explore the application of multiview embeddings to a small, yet valuable, dataset specifically designed for dementia assessment: DementiaBank (Becker et al., 2018). DementiaBank contains transcripts of live, naturalistic conversations with individuals diagnosed with varying stages of AD, alongside corresponding clinical scores. We hypothesize that by leveraging the multiview nature of this dataset – specifically, the linguistic features of the speech and the clinical assessments – we can learn embeddings that effectively capture different facets of cognitive impairment and improve performance on both AD classification and clinical score prediction. We employ Generalized Canonical Correlation Analysis (GCCA) (Hotelling, 1936; Kettenring, 1971) as a method for obtaining these multiview embeddings. Our experiments demonstrate that incorporating these embeddings significantly boosts performance in downstream tasks, achieving a substantial improvement in both classification accuracy and regression performance. Furthermore, we investigate the generalizability of our approach by showing that useful multiview embeddings can be obtained from additional publicly available datasets.

Maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE) remains a cornerstone of training structured prediction models for sequence generation tasks in natural language processing. Its widespread adoption stems from its computational efficiency and theoretical grounding. However, despite its success, MLE training is increasingly recognized as suffering from fundamental limitations when applied to tasks evaluated using sequence-level metrics. The core issue lies in a discrepancy between the training objective – maximizing the likelihood of individual tokens – and the evaluation metric, which considers the overall sequence structure and similarity. A particularly problematic consequence of this misalignment is *exposure bias* (Li et al., 2016), where the model is trained on ground truth sequences but tested by generating sequences autoregressively, leading to error accumulation. Beyond exposure bias, the fundamental mismatch in optimization goals also contributes to suboptimal performance. Metrics like ROUGE (Lin, 2004) and BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002) evaluate the quality of generated text based on n-gram overlap with reference summaries or translations, effectively rewarding sequences that capture the essential content and structure of the target. Simply maximizing the probability of the next word, as done in MLE, does not guarantee optimization of these sequence-level properties. Recent efforts have explored reinforcement learning (RL) and policy gradient methods as alternatives to MLE, aiming to directly optimize for the desired evaluation metrics (Ranzato et al., 2015; Paulus et al., 2017). These approaches treat sequence generation as a sequential decision process, where the model (agent) generates a sequence of tokens and receives a reward based on the final sequence’s evaluation score. While demonstrating promising improvements over MLE in tasks like abstractive summarization (Narayan et al., 2018) and machine translation (Wu et al., 2018), policy gradient methods are notoriously challenging to train due to their high sample variance. This instability often requires careful hyperparameter tuning and sophisticated variance reduction techniques, hindering their practical applicability. The high variance stems from the delayed reward signal – the evaluation metric is only calculated at the end of the entire sequence generation process. This sparse feedback makes it difficult for the model to accurately attribute credit or blame to individual actions (token predictions) that contributed to the final score. Consequently, the training process becomes susceptible to noisy updates and oscillations. In this work, we introduce a novel objective function, Continuously Approximating Longest Common Subsequence (CALCS), designed to bridge the gap between word-level prediction and sequence-level optimization without the inherent instability of policy gradients. Our approach leverages the Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) measure as a differentiable surrogate for sequence similarity. By continuously approximating LCS during sequence generation, we provide a dense, informative reward signal that guides the model towards producing sequences that align well with the reference text. Unlike policy gradient methods, CALCS offers a stable and efficient training process, while effectively capturing sequence-level structure and content. We demonstrate the effectiveness of CALCS through experiments on abstractive summarization and machine translation, showing consistent improvements over MLE baselines and competitive performance compared to policy gradient approaches.

Knowledge bases (KBs) like Freebase, Wikidata, and DBpedia have become essential resources for a wide range of natural language processing (NLP) applications. These KBs store structured information about entities – real-world objects, concepts, and events – and their relationships, providing a valuable source of semantic knowledge. Leveraging this knowledge is crucial for tasks such as question answering (Bordes et al., 2015), information retrieval (Chen et al., 2017), and text understanding (Zhang et al., 2018). A key challenge, however, lies in effectively representing both entities and the textual descriptions associated with them in a continuous vector space, enabling machines to reason about and generalize from this knowledge. Traditional methods for entity representation often rely on manually crafted features or graph-based approaches (Bordes et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2017). While effective, these methods often struggle to capture the rich semantic information contained in natural language descriptions. More recently, distributional semantic models (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014) have shown promise in learning entity embeddings directly from text. However, many existing approaches either focus solely on utilizing text corpora unrelated to structured knowledge (e.g., news articles, web pages) or operate on the KB graph structure without fully exploiting the descriptive text associated with each entity. In this work, we address this gap by presenting TextEnt, a novel neural network model designed to learn distributed representations of entities and documents *directly* from the wealth of textual descriptions available within a knowledge base. TextEnt is specifically trained to predict the entity described by a given document and, critically, learns to map the document and its corresponding entity close to each other in a continuous vector space. This joint embedding allows for effective semantic similarity comparisons between entities and documents, and facilitates knowledge transfer. Our model leverages the rich textual content of Wikipedia – a widely used and constantly evolving collaborative knowledge base. By exploiting the numerous documents associated with each entity within Wikipedia, we are able to train TextEnt on a large-scale dataset, resulting in high-quality representations. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we evaluate TextEnt on two challenging tasks: fine-grained entity typing and multiclass text classification. The experimental results demonstrate that TextEnt achieves state-of-the-art performance on both tasks, surpassing existing embedding models. Furthermore, recognizing the importance of reproducibility and fostering further research, we are making the code and the pre-trained representations publicly available. We believe that TextEnt provides a valuable tool for researchers working on knowledge base reasoning, text understanding, and related areas, and encourages exploration of learned representations for various downstream applications. Natural Language Inference (NLI), also known as Recognizing Textual Entailment (RTE), is a fundamental task in natural language understanding. Given two sentences – a premise and a hypothesis – the goal of NLI is to determine the relationship between them: whether the hypothesis is entailed by the premise, contradicts the premise, or is neutral relative to it. This task requires a deep understanding of semantic relationships, logical reasoning, and world knowledge, making it a crucial benchmark for evaluating the capabilities of NLP models. Recent advances in NLI have been largely driven by neural network architectures, particularly those leveraging the attention mechanism. Models like the Attentive Reader (Rocktäschel et al., 2016) and Enhanced Sequential Inference Model (ESIM) (Chen et al., 2016) have demonstrated impressive performance by explicitly modeling the alignments between words and phrases in the premise and hypothesis. These attention-based models operate by computing a weighted sum of the premise representations, where the weights represent the relevance of each word in the premise to the hypothesis. While successful, attention mechanisms can be computationally expensive, especially with longer sentences, and may not always capture the complex, multi-faceted interactions between the two sentences. Specifically, standard attention typically focuses on pairwise interactions, potentially overlooking higher-order relationships or more nuanced dependencies. In this paper, we introduce the Convolutional Interaction Network (CIN), a novel architecture designed to capture rich interactions between premise and hypothesis sentences. Unlike attention-based models, CIN frames the interaction as a dynamic filtering process. Specifically, CIN encodes one sentence (typically the hypothesis) using filters that are dynamically generated based on the other sentence (the premise). This approach allows the model to selectively focus on specific aspects of the premise when encoding the hypothesis, and vice versa. Crucially, CIN leverages the flexibility of convolutional filters – allowing for variation in both the number and size of filters – to capture a diverse range of interaction patterns. The inspiration behind CIN stems from the observation that interactions between sentences are not uniformly distributed; certain phrases and words in one sentence are more relevant to specific parts of the other. By dynamically generating filters based on the premise, CIN effectively learns to ‘probe’ the hypothesis for information that is pertinent to the premise. This dynamic convolution can capture both local, word-level interactions and more global, phrase-level relationships, offering a compelling alternative to traditional attention mechanisms. We demonstrate the efficacy of CIN through extensive experiments on three large-scale NLI datasets – SNLI (Bowman et al., 2015), MultiNLI (Williams et al., 2017), and SciTail (Khullar et al., 2018) – revealing that CIN achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art NLI models, offering a more efficient and potentially more expressive approach to sentence interaction modeling.
