We demonstrate that through these enhancements, the LSTM can approach the performance of the state-of-the-art joint model for opinion entity and IS-FROM relation extraction, and even achieve comparable results for the IS-ABOUT relation - all without requiring the extensive feature engineering and external resources demanded by the traditional CRF+ILP approach. This work highlights both the challenges and the promise of applying deep learning techniques to the complex problem of joint opinion entity and relation extraction. Semantic relation classification, the task of identifying the semantic relationship between two entities mentioned in a sentence, is a core problem in natural language processing with broad applications in information extraction, knowledge base construction, and question answering (Zeng et al., 2008; Rosso et al., 2017). Traditional approaches to semantic relation classification heavily relied on hand-crafted features derived from linguistic resources such as WordNet (Hearst, 1998) and dependency parsing (Moschitti, 2004). While achieving reasonable performance, these methods require substantial expertise and are often brittle when applied to new domains or datasets. More recently, deep learning models, particularly those employing recurrent neural networks (RNNs), have emerged as a promising alternative for automatically learning representations of sentences and their constituent parts (Socher et al., 2013; Kalchbrenner et al., 2014). These models can capture long-range dependencies and contextual information without the need for extensive feature engineering. However, many existing deep learning approaches treat the entire sentence as a single input sequence, potentially diluting the important contextual information surrounding the two entities of interest. Furthermore, they may struggle to effectively integrate information from different parts of the sentence that contribute to the overall relational meaning. In this paper, we propose a novel hierarchical recurrent neural network (HRNN) with attention mechanisms for semantic relation classification. Our model is designed to address the limitations of existing approaches by selectively focusing on the most relevant contextual information and effectively composing representations from different parts of the sentence. The key features of our model include: (1) a context partitioning strategy that divides the sentence into three subsequences based on the positions of the two annotated nominals, allowing the model to encode each context independently; (2) a hierarchical structure consisting of two RNNs – one for learning context-specific representations and another for computing the semantic composition of these representations; and (3) the incorporation of attention mechanisms within both RNNs to prioritize important information during sentence representation learning. By partitioning the context and employing a hierarchical architecture, our model is able to selectively focus on the information surrounding the target entities. The attention mechanisms further refine this process by highlighting the most salient words and phrases within each context. We evaluate our model on the SemEval-2010 Task 8 dataset and demonstrate that it achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods without relying on any hand-crafted features, highlighting the effectiveness of our approach for automatic relation classification. This work demonstrates the potential of hierarchical, attention-based RNNs for effectively capturing and reasoning about relational semantics in natural language. Persuasion is a fundamental aspect of human communication, pervading scenarios from everyday negotiations to critical decision-making. While traditionally studied in fields like psychology and marketing, the increasing capabilities of dialogue systems present a compelling opportunity to automate and understand the mechanisms of effective persuasion. Recent advances in neural dialogue models have yielded systems capable of coherent conversation, but truly *persuasive* dialogue requires more than just fluency – it demands strategic communication, an understanding of user beliefs, and the ability to influence those beliefs toward a desired outcome. A key technique humans employ in persuasive dialogue is *framing* – the subtle art of presenting information to emphasize certain aspects and evoke specific emotional responses (Tversky & Kahneman, 1981). For instance, a medical treatment can be framed as having a “90% survival rate” versus a “10% mortality rate,” despite conveying the same objective information, drastically altering perception. However, formulating dialogue policies that effectively leverage framing is a challenging task. Manually crafting such policies is laborious and may not generalize well to novel situations. This paper explores the application of reinforcement learning (RL) to automatically learn cooperative persuasive dialogue policies that incorporate framing strategies. RL offers a promising avenue for optimizing dialogue behavior through trial and error, adapting to user responses and maximizing long-term rewards. While RL has demonstrated success in various dialogue settings (Li et al., 2016; Zhao & Eskenazi, 2018), its application to *persuasive* dialogue presents unique hurdles. Specifically, constructing realistic user simulators and designing appropriate reward functions for persuasion are non-trivial. Unlike task-oriented dialogues with clear success criteria, the goal of persuasion is often probabilistic and depends on subtle shifts in user attitudes. To address these challenges, we leverage a corpus of human-human persuasive dialogues to inform the design of both our user simulator and reward function. This corpus provides valuable insights into common persuasive tactics, typical user reactions, and the interplay between framing and dialogue context. Our contributions are threefold. First, we present a novel method for building user simulators specifically tailored to persuasive dialogues, capturing user response tendencies observed in our corpus. Second, we design a reward function that encourages cooperative persuasion – aiming for mutually beneficial outcomes rather than forceful manipulation. Finally, we demonstrate through both simulated and real-user experiments that our RL-based approach effectively learns persuasive dialogue policies that utilize framing strategies, achieving improved persuasion rates compared to baseline methods. The automatic evaluation of text generation systems—spanning machine translation, text summarization, image captioning, and dialogue response generation—remains a central challenge in Natural Language Processing. While significant progress has been made in developing increasingly sophisticated evaluation metrics, practical adoption remains largely dominated by a handful of n-gram overlap-based measures, most notably BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002) and ROUGE (Lin, 2004). These metrics, despite their known limitations (Papineni et al., 2002; Bojar, 2015), continue to serve as the *de facto* standard for system comparison in many research areas, largely due to their simplicity, computational efficiency, and established correlation with human judgments – though this correlation is often weak and context-dependent (Tomlin & Neubig, 2017). Over the past two decades, the research community has proposed a vast array of alternative evaluation metrics aiming to address the shortcomings of n-gram overlap. These include semantic similarity-based metrics (e.g., METEOR, Gillick & Mollick, 2014; BERTScore, Qi et al., 2020), learned metrics leveraging neural networks (e.g., BLEURT, Sellam et al., 2020), and metrics focusing on specific aspects of text quality like fluency and coherence. Despite demonstrating promising results and improved correlation with human judgments in specific settings, these more advanced metrics have failed to achieve widespread adoption, often relegated to supplementary analyses in research papers. This paper investigates the reasons for this discrepancy between research innovation and practical usage in text evaluation. We begin with a thorough analysis of the state-of-the-art, outlining the strengths and weaknesses of various automatic evaluation measures. More crucially, we move beyond simply comparing individual metrics and focus on how combining multiple measures can enhance the *reliability* of evaluation. We formalize a set of properties that any similarity-based text evaluation measure – intended to approximate human assessment – must ideally satisfy. These properties, grounded in concepts of consistency and representativeness, lead to the central empirical finding of this work: corroborating observed system improvements with multiple, independent evaluation measures always increases the confidence in those improvements. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the benefits of combining measures are not simply additive. The *heterogeneity* of the measures used – a quantifiable measure of their dissimilarity in terms of underlying methodologies – directly impacts the combined reliability of the evaluation. Greater heterogeneity leads to more robust and trustworthy conclusions. This finding has significant practical implications, providing a strong rationale for embracing a more holistic, multi-metric evaluation approach in text generation research, and advocating for the development of tools and best practices to facilitate its implementation. Our results suggest that moving towards heterogeneous evaluation isn't merely desirable, but fundamentally essential for ensuring the validity and reproducibility of research findings in the field.

Question answering (QA) has rapidly advanced with the rise of neural networks, yet answering complex, compositional questions remains a significant challenge. These questions necessitate multi-step reasoning and the ability to understand how the meanings of individual words and phrases combine to form the meaning of the whole sentence. Existing neural QA models, while achieving impressive results on certain benchmarks, often struggle with questions requiring intricate logical operations or generalization to unseen question structures (Bordes et al., 2015; Weston et al., 2011). Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), and their tree-based variants (Tai et al., 2015), represent sentences sequentially or hierarchically, but typically lack a principled mechanism for compositional semantics – the systematic combination of meanings. Similarly, semantic parsing approaches (Zelle & Mooney, 1996; Kwiatkowski et al., 2013) excel at translating natural language into formal logical representations, but often require extensive hand-engineering of grammars and are brittle in the face of linguistic variation. In this work, we introduce a novel end-to-end differentiable model motivated by formal approaches to denotational semantics (Montague, 1970; Kamp & Partee, 1995) to tackle compositional QA. The core idea is to represent each span of text with a *denotation* – a set of entities in a knowledge graph (KG) – and an associated *vector* capturing aspects of meaning not directly grounded in the KG. This allows the model to handle phenomena like negation, quantification, and abstract concepts. Crucially, the model learns to *compose* these denotations and vectors recursively, mirroring the way meaning is built up from smaller constituents in a formal semantic framework. For example, when processing “not green,” the model represents “green” as a set of KG entities and “not” as a trainable, ungrounded vector. This “not” vector is then used to parameterize a composition function performing a complement operation on the denotation of “green.” A key innovation lies in our use of a parse chart. Rather than relying on a fixed, pre-defined parse tree, we construct a chart subsuming *all possible* parse trees for a given sentence. This allows the model to jointly learn both the compositional operators (e.g., conjunction, disjunction, negation) and the optimal output structure through gradient descent, directly from end-task supervision. By exploring many parses concurrently, the model avoids the limitations of assuming a single correct syntactic structure and enables the discovery of latent syntactic relationships that may not be explicitly encoded in the data. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. The model learns to perform a diverse range of challenging semantic operations, generalizing well to longer questions and outperforming strong RNN, tree-based RNN, and semantic parsing baselines. This suggests that our denotational compositional approach provides a more robust and flexible framework for tackling the complexities of compositional question answering.

Statistical machine translation (SMT) has undergone significant evolution, progressing from initial word-based models (Brown et al., 1993) to more sophisticated phrase-based and, subsequently, hierarchical phrase-based approaches (Chiang, 2005). While phrase-based SMT improves fluency by translating sequences of words as single units, hierarchical phrase-based translation (Hiero) introduces a formal grammar capable of capturing non-local dependencies and long-range reordering phenomena, leading to substantial improvements in translation quality. A crucial component in the success of any SMT system is its ability to accurately model the relationship between source and target languages, and to select the most appropriate translation options given the input sentence. Recent work has explored the incorporation of topic models into SMT systems as a means of enriching the statistical modeling of language. Topic models, such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) (Blei et al., 2003), provide a compact representation of document semantics by identifying underlying topical themes. Initial approaches utilized topic information at the word level, assuming that words sharing similar topical distributions are more likely to be good translations of each other (Topic Mixture Models - TMM, (Papineni et al., 2002)). These approaches propose to bias source/target word probabilities by considering the topical similarity between the source and target sides of the translation. Further work explored the use of topic models to improve word alignment (Goldwater and Griffiths, 2007) and to enhance fluency (Liang et al., 2009). However, existing topic-based SMT approaches largely operate at the word level. They fail to explicitly leverage the synchronous rule level structure inherent in modern SMT systems, particularly Hierarchical Phrase-Based Translation (Hiero). Hiero translation utilizes a set of synchronous Context-Free Grammar (CFG) rules that directly specify the mapping between source and target phrases. These rules represent meaningful translation patterns and capture important structural information related to the source and target languages. We argue that modeling topic information at the *rule* level is crucial for effectively capturing the semantic consistency between source and target phrases, and for guiding the search process towards more accurate and fluent translations. In this paper, we propose a novel topic similarity model (TSM) tailored for Hierarchical Phrase-based Translation. Our approach associates each synchronous rule with a topic distribution, enabling us to quantify the semantic affinity between rules. During decoding, we select desirable rules based on the similarity of their topical distributions to the topic distribution of the input sentence. This allows the decoder to prioritize rules that are semantically relevant to the context of the translation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our model through extensive experiments on the NIST Chinese-to-English translation task. Our results show that TSM consistently outperforms a strong baseline Hiero system, achieving significant improvements in BLEU score. Furthermore, we compare our rule-level approach to previous word-level topic modeling techniques, demonstrating its superior performance and computational efficiency. We also analyze several aspects of the approach showing how our model effectively captures nuanced semantic similarities amongst synchronous rules leading to improved translation performance.

The digitization of historical documents offers unprecedented opportunities for research across numerous disciplines, from history and literature to linguistics and social science. However, effectively leveraging this wealth of information is hampered by the significant challenges posed by the orthographic landscape of these documents. Unlike modern text, historical documents frequently display substantial orthographic variation, encompassing archaic spellings, inconsistent abbreviations, and even bespoke shorthand systems employed by individual authors or scribes. Optical Character Recognition (OCR) tools, while increasingly sophisticated, typically focus on generating *diplomatic* transcriptions—outputs that faithfully reproduce the original orthography, including all its idiosyncrasies. This approach, while valuable for certain applications like diplomatic editing, presents a significant obstacle for many downstream tasks, such as full-text search, text mining, and quantitative analysis, which often require transcriptions conforming to modern orthographic conventions. Existing approaches to normalizing historical orthography often involve manually curated dictionaries or rule-based transformations. These methods are labor-intensive to create and maintain, require substantial domain expertise, and struggle to generalize across diverse document collections and historical periods. More recent attempts have explored sequence-to-sequence models trained on parallel corpora of historical and modern orthography, but the scarcity of such annotated data severely limits their applicability. Moreover, these supervised approaches inherently rely on pre-defined mappings between historical and modern forms, potentially overlooking nuanced or context-dependent variations. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to historical document transcription that addresses these limitations by learning a probabilistic mapping between historical and modern orthography in a fully *unsupervised* manner. Our system eschews the need for parallel data, instead jointly modeling the diplomatic and normalized transcriptions of a document based on observed character sequences and linguistic constraints. The core innovation lies in a joint probabilistic model that captures the relationship between orthographic variants without explicit supervision, effectively learning to “translate” between the historical and modern forms directly from the document itself. Crucially, our model doesn’t simply perform a post-hoc normalization of a diplomatic transcription; rather, it produces both transcriptions *simultaneously*. This joint modeling allows the system to leverage the dependencies between the two representations, leading to improved accuracy for both diplomatic and normalized outputs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on a challenging dataset of historical documents. Our results show a substantial performance gain—a 35% relative error reduction on diplomatic transcription and a remarkable 46% reduction on normalized transcription—compared to a state-of-the-art OCR model. These findings highlight the potential of unsupervised learning to unlock the information embedded within historical documents and facilitate broader access to our collective cultural heritage. The ability to query large, openly available knowledge bases like OpenStreetMap (OSM) using natural language represents a significant step towards democratizing access to geographic information. While OSM provides a wealth of detailed world data, its utility is often limited by the need for specialized GIS tools and query languages, posing a barrier for many potential users. Recent advances in semantic parsing, coupled with the increasing availability of large-scale datasets, offer a promising path towards natural language interfaces (NLIs) for such databases. However, building robust NLIs requires addressing several key challenges, including the inherent ambiguity of natural language, the need to map vague concepts (e.g., “nearby”, “walking distance”) to precise spatial representations, and the desire to support multiple languages for global accessibility. Existing work in semantic parsing has demonstrated success on various domains, including question answering and database querying (Zettlemoyer and Collins, 2005; Berant et al., 2013; Dong and Lapata, 2016). However, many of these datasets focus on relatively constrained domains and lack the geospatial complexity inherent in querying OSM. Furthermore, multilingual extensions of semantic parsing are often hampered by a lack of parallel corpora covering diverse linguistic structures and geographic terminology. Building such resources is both expensive and time-consuming, limiting progress in cross-lingual information access. In this paper, we address these challenges by introducing a novel corpus and semantic parser specifically designed for multilingual natural language querying of OSM. Our corpus comprises 2,380 natural language queries paired with executable logical forms representing the underlying spatial queries. A key characteristic of this dataset is its emphasis on capturing the nuances of geographic language, including fuzzy spatial relationships and a reasonable level of lexical variability in how users express their information needs. The dataset supports complex compositional queries, challenging semantic parsers to accurately decompose and combine individual query components. We leverage this corpus to train a semantic parser that accurately translates natural language queries into formal queries executable against the OSM database. The resulting parser forms the core of an NLI to OSM, enabling users to retrieve geographic information simply by asking questions in natural language. Moreover, recognizing the importance of multilingual access, we employ a response-based learning approach to adapt a statistical machine translation (SMT) system for cross-lingual database access. This allows users to pose queries in multiple languages, expanding the potential user base for OSM-based applications. Critically, the feedback loop of successful or unsuccessful queries improves the translation system over time, focusing on the nuances required for accurate OSM querying. The contributions of this work are threefold: (1) the introduction of a new, publicly available corpus for semantic parsing of geographic queries; (2) the development of an accurate semantic parser for querying OSM; and (3) a demonstration of multilingual database access through response-based adaptation of SMT. We believe this work represents a significant step towards enabling more intuitive and accessible interaction with the vast amount of geographic information contained within OpenStreetMap.

Spatial information is fundamental to a wide range of applications, from geological surveys and urban planning to robotics and geographic information systems (GIS). Automatically extracting this information – specifically, spatial entities and the relationships between them – from natural language text is a crucial step towards enabling effective reasoning and knowledge discovery within these domains. While significant progress has been made in the field of spatial information extraction (SIE) for English text, notably demonstrated through initiatives like the SpaceEval competition (Pustejovsky et al., 2004), adapting these techniques to other languages, particularly those with significantly different linguistic structures, presents unique challenges. Korean, possessing a Subject-Object-Verb (SOV) sentence structure, extensive use of postpositions rather than prepositions, and a rich system of honorifics, diverges considerably from English. Direct transfer of English-centric SIE models and resources often yields suboptimal performance. Moreover, the scarcity of publicly available, annotated Korean corpora specifically tailored for spatial information extraction hinders the development of robust and accurate systems. Existing work often relies on manually curated gazetteers and rule-based approaches, which are labor-intensive and lack the generalization capacity required for handling the diversity of expressions found in natural language. This paper addresses the challenge of spatial information extraction from Korean text by proposing both a novel spatial entity extraction model and a corresponding spatial relation extraction model. Our approach recognizes the importance of incorporating linguistic knowledge specific to Korean. Specifically, the spatial entity extraction model leverages pre-trained word vectors to address the issue of over-generation, a common problem when identifying potential spatial entities based solely on lexicon matching. The use of distributed representations allows for a more nuanced understanding of word meaning and context, facilitating the identification of likely entity boundaries. For spatial relation extraction, we exploit the rich structural information provided by dependency parsing. Korean dependency parses, while complex, offer valuable cues for identifying the appropriate arguments in a spatial relation. Our model utilizes dependency parse labels to determine the semantic roles of words within a sentence, enabling it to accurately pinpoint the entities participating in a spatial relation and the nature of that relationship. We hypothesize that this dependency-aware approach will significantly improve the precision and recall of spatial relation extraction compared to methods that rely solely on surface-level patterns. We present experimental results using a Korean text corpus annotated with spatial entities and relations. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed models, achieving promising performance in both spatial entity and relation extraction tasks. By addressing the linguistic nuances of Korean and leveraging readily available resources like word embeddings and dependency parsers, our work constitutes a significant step towards building a robust and scalable spatial information extraction system for the Korean language. Deep learning has revolutionized numerous fields, and its impact on Natural Language Processing (NLP) is particularly profound. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), originally designed for image processing, have become a foundational architecture for a wide range of text-based tasks, including sentiment analysis, text classification, and machine translation (Kim, 2014; Kalchbrenner et al., 2014). The initial success of CNNs in NLP often relies on the premise that local, sequential patterns in text are indicative of underlying meaning. However, traditional CNN implementations for text largely inherit the operational limitations of their image-processing counterparts, specifically, reliance on linear convolutions over consecutive word embeddings. While effective, this approach can be suboptimal for capturing the complexities of natural language. Compositionality in language is often not strictly consecutive; the meaning of a phrase can depend on relationships between words that are not immediately adjacent. Furthermore, the assumption of linearity may hinder the model's ability to learn more abstract and non-linear interactions between words – interactions crucial for nuanced understanding. Existing adaptations such as dilated convolutions (Yu & Koltun, 2016) address the non-consecutive aspects but still largely rely on the linearity of the convolution operation. In this work, we revisit the core convolution operation in CNNs, aiming to better align its characteristics with the unique demands of text processing. We propose a novel approach that moves beyond simple concatenation of word embeddings and instead leverages the principles of tensor algebra. Specifically, we employ low-rank n-gram tensors to directly model the interactions between words *at the convolution stage*. This allows the model to efficiently capture relationships between groups of words, essentially encoding n-gram information directly into the convolutional filters. Crucially, we extend this n-gram convolution to operate over *non-consecutive* words. This enables the model to recognize patterns that span longer distances within a sentence, incorporating intervening words that might contribute to the overall meaning. To address the computational challenges introduced by these extensions, we present a dynamic programming-based method to efficiently evaluate the resulting convolution operation. This allows us to effectively handle higher-order n-gram interactions without incurring excessive computational costs. We evaluate the performance of our proposed architecture on standard sentiment classification and news categorization tasks. Our results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming existing CNN-based approaches in both accuracy and training speed. For instance, we achieve 51.2% accuracy on a challenging fine-grained sentiment classification benchmark. This suggests that our method successfully captures richer linguistic patterns and demonstrates the benefits of incorporating non-linear, non-consecutive convolutions into CNNs for text processing. The demand for large, labeled datasets has fueled the rapid growth of non-expert annotation services such as Amazon’s Mechanical Turk (AMT) (Kazai et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2012). These platforms offer a cost-effective and scalable solution for tasks ranging from image classification (Russakovsky et al., 2015) to sentiment analysis (Snow et al., 2008), and are frequently employed to evaluate the performance of machine learning systems (Homan et al., 2015; Sorokin & Forsyth, 2015). However, a significant challenge arises from the inherent variability in annotator quality. Unlike expert annotators, workers on AMT are often motivated by monetary reward rather than a dedication to accuracy, leading to instances of careless labeling, spam submissions, and deliberate attempts to game the system (Callison-Burch & Dredze, 2011; Little et al., 2015). Identifying unreliable annotators is crucial for ensuring the integrity of datasets and building robust models. Manual inspection of annotations is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming, especially for large-scale datasets. Existing approaches often involve simple heuristics such as qualification tests (AMT’s built-in system) or filtering based on agreement rates (Snow et al., 2008). While useful, these methods can be easily circumvented by malicious annotators and may inadvertently disqualify competent workers. More sophisticated techniques, such as those based on Dawid-Skene (Dawid & Skene, 1979), attempt to estimate annotator error rates, but typically rely on strong assumptions about error independence and can be sensitive to outliers. Recent work has explored more complex probabilistic models, often utilizing Expectation-Maximization (EM) for parameter estimation (Whitehill et al., 2009; Kamat et al., 2013), but these can become computationally expensive and may suffer from local optima. In this paper, we introduce MACE (Multi-Annotator Competence Estimation), a novel system for learning whom to trust in the context of multi-annotator tasks. MACE leverages an item-response modeling (IRM) framework to simultaneously estimate annotator trustworthiness *and* predict the correct underlying labels for each instance, all in an unsupervised manner. Our approach circumvents the need for pre-defined ground truth or explicit error modeling by framing the annotation process as a latent variable problem. Unlike traditional IRT models, MACE is designed to handle categorical annotations and allows for flexible specification of prior knowledge through Bayesian inference. Our experimental results demonstrate that MACE achieves performance comparable to, and in many cases superior to, state-of-the-art systems for identifying unreliable annotators and predicting correct labels. Notably, MACE performs well even under adversarial conditions, where a substantial fraction of annotations are intentionally corrupted. We further show how incorporating control instances (instances with known correct labels) and a prior on model parameters, coupled with Variational Bayes inference, can significantly improve both the accuracy of label predictions and the reliability of trustworthiness estimates. Finally, we illustrate the benefits of selectively focusing on instances where the model exhibits high confidence, enabling a trade-off between precision and recall. MACE is available for download to facilitate reproducibility and further research.

The ability to engage in natural, coherent, and contextually relevant dialogue is a hallmark of human intelligence and a longstanding goal of Artificial Intelligence. Recent advancements in neural network architectures, particularly sequence-to-sequence models with attention mechanisms (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Rush et al., 2015), have led to significant progress in dialog generation, enabling systems to produce increasingly human-like responses. However, most existing approaches treat each turn of a conversation as an isolated event, often failing to fully leverage the rich contextual information embedded within the entire dialog history. This limitation frequently results in generic, repetitive, or inconsistent responses that lack the depth and nuance of human conversation (Li et al., 2016; Serban et al., 2017). A critical aspect of human dialogue is the ability to reason about the conversation’s progression—to understand the underlying intent, track the evolving topic, and remember previous statements. This requires maintaining a coherent representation of the dialog history and utilizing it to inform the generation of appropriate responses. Inspired by recent breakthroughs in document comprehension, specifically multi-turn reasoning networks (Hill et al., 2016; Seo et al., 2017), we propose a novel approach to dialog generation that explicitly incorporates this reasoning process. Our framework reformulates the dialog generation task as a question-answering problem. The entire conversation session up to the current turn is treated as a “document,” and the current user query is treated as a “question.” By leveraging multi-turn reasoning, our model iteratively reads and processes the “document” (conversation history) to extract relevant information and generate an informed response or “answer.” This attention-based memory reading mechanism allows the model to extend the user's query with crucial contextual clues and generate optimal responses in a step-by-step fashion. Crucially, we recognize that human conversation involves multiple speakers, each potentially holding distinct perspectives and contributing to different topical threads. To address this, we extend the standard document comprehension memory structure by separating it into speaker-specific groups. We utilize separate memories for user queries, system responses, and a unified memory to capture the overall conversation flow, explicitly encoding the temporal sequence of interactions. This allows the model to better distinguish between the contributions of different speakers and maintain topic consistency. We evaluate our approach on a challenging Japanese 10-sentence (5-round) conversation modeling dataset. Our experimental results demonstrate that incorporating multi-turn reasoning significantly improves dialog generation performance, yielding more diverse and acceptable responses compared to state-of-the-art single-turn and non-reasoning baseline models. This work represents a significant step towards building more intelligent and engaging dialog systems capable of truly understanding and responding to the complexities of human conversation. Distributional semantics, the idea that the meaning of a word is encoded in its context of use (Harris, 1954), has become a dominant paradigm in computational linguistics over the last two decades. Fueled by the availability of large text corpora and advances in vector space modeling, numerous algorithms have been developed to successfully capture semantic relationships between words (Turney & Pantel, 2010; Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014). These techniques generally represent words as vectors in a high-dimensional space, where semantic similarity is reflected in the proximity of these vectors. However, a significant challenge remains: extending these successful methods beyond the single-word level. While distributional models excel at representing the semantics of individual lexical items, constructing meaningful representations of larger linguistic units – phrases, clauses, or even entire sentences – is considerably more difficult. The core problem lies in *compositionality*: how the meanings of individual words combine to form the meaning of the whole expression. Simply averaging word vectors, for instance, often fails to capture subtle semantic nuances and can lead to nonsensical representations (Mitchell & Lapata, 2010). Numerous approaches have been proposed to tackle this compositional challenge within the distributional framework. These range from simple linear combinations and matrix operations (Mitchell & Lapata, 2008) to more sophisticated tensor-based models (Smolensky et al., 1990) and neural network architectures (Socher et al., 2013). Baroni and Zamparelli (2010) introduced a particularly influential approach leveraging lexical functions to guide the combination of word vectors, demonstrating marked improvements over basic averaging techniques. Their method relies on identifying relational predicates and applying specific linear transformations based on the observed relationships in the corpus. Despite the proliferation of these methods, a comprehensive, large-scale evaluation of their performance remains lacking. Furthermore, many existing approaches are tailored to specific types of composition, or rely on hand-engineered features, limiting their generalizability. This motivates the need for methods that can systematically handle a wider range of compositional phenomena, and for robust evaluations that can reliably compare different approaches. This paper addresses these gaps. Our contribution is twofold. First, we present a large-scale evaluation of several prominent composition methods within the distributional semantics framework, focusing on two common compositional constructions: adjective-noun (e.g., “red car”) and noun-noun (e.g., “coffee table”). This evaluation leverages a newly developed dataset specifically designed to assess the quality of compositional representations. Second, we propose a novel method for composition that builds upon, and generalizes, the framework introduced by Baroni and Zamparelli (2010). Our approach aims to improve upon existing methods by enhancing the learning of compositional relationships from data. We evaluate the performance of our method on the aforementioned dataset, demonstrating its competitiveness with state-of-the-art techniques. The aim is not only a performance increase, but also to offer a more general approach to compositional semantics in distributional models.

Knowledge bases (KBs) represent structured knowledge as entities and relations, offering a powerful means of capturing factual information. Recent years have witnessed a surge in research focused on embedding KBs into continuous vector spaces, aiming to facilitate tasks such as knowledge base completion (KBC) – the prediction of missing facts. A dominant paradigm in KBC involves leveraging relation paths, which represent sequences of relations connecting two entities within the KB graph. These paths offer valuable contextual information, enabling models to infer plausible relationships beyond those explicitly stated. However, effectively utilizing relation paths poses a significant computational challenge. The number of possible paths between two entities grows exponentially with the path length. Consequently, existing approaches typically resort to sampling a limited subset of paths, introducing a trade-off between accuracy and efficiency. While effective to some extent, this approximation can lead to the omission of crucial relational evidence, particularly in complex scenarios where long or nuanced paths are indicative of underlying facts. The problem is further exacerbated when jointly modeling KBs with unstructured text. Natural language often provides direct evidence for KB facts, and incorporating this textual information alongside relational paths can significantly enhance KBC performance. However, accurately linking textual mentions to KB entities and relations requires a comprehensive understanding of the relationship landscape, necessitating the consideration of a broader range of relation paths than is typically feasible with sampling-based methods. Access to all relevant paths becomes paramount to accurately resolve ambiguities and contextualize textual evidence within the KB structure. In this paper, we address this critical bottleneck by proposing a novel approach for compositional learning of embeddings for relation paths. Our key contribution lies in the development of the first *exact* dynamic programming algorithm that enables the efficient incorporation of *all* relation paths of bounded length. Unlike prior methods that rely on approximations, our algorithm guarantees complete coverage of the relational landscape within the specified path length limit. Moreover, our approach extends beyond simply considering relation types; it explicitly models both relation types *and* intermediate nodes encountered along the paths, allowing for a richer and more nuanced representation of relational information. We provide a rigorous theoretical analysis demonstrating the efficiency gains afforded by our dynamic programming formulation, showcasing its scalability and computational advantages over naive enumeration. Empirical evaluation on two benchmark datasets reveals that our approach overcomes representational limitations inherent in existing methods and significantly improves accuracy in KBC tasks, particularly when textual context is integrated. Our results demonstrate the substantial benefits of considering the complete set of relation paths, and establish a new benchmark for comprehensive relational reasoning in knowledge base embedding models. Discourse relations, the semantic connections between segments of text, are fundamental to human comprehension. While some discourse relations are explicitly signaled by cue phrases (e.g., “because” indicating Cause), a substantial portion remains *implicit*, requiring deeper reasoning and contextual understanding to identify. Recognizing these implicit discourse relations is a long-standing challenge in Natural Language Processing (NLP), crucial for tasks ranging from machine reading comprehension and text summarization to dialogue systems and coherence modeling (Prasad et al., 2008; Stede, 2009). Existing approaches to implicit discourse relation classification often rely on feature engineering, employing hand-crafted features based on lexical overlap, syntactic structures, and rhetorical roles (e.g., Marcu et al., 1999; Soricută & Marcu, 2014). While achieving reasonable performance, these methods are limited by their reliance on expert knowledge and their inability to capture more subtle, contextual cues. More recently, neural network models, particularly those leveraging attention mechanisms (e.g., Lin et al., 2016; Li et al., 2018), have shown promising results by automatically learning relevant features directly from the data. These models typically attend to different parts of the argument sentences to identify crucial words and phrases indicative of the underlying relation. However, we argue that effectively capturing implicit discourse relations necessitates a more nuanced process than single-pass attention. Human readers rarely grasp relationships instantaneously; instead, they engage in a form of “repeated reading,” revisiting arguments from different perspectives, iteratively refining their understanding, and focusing on increasingly relevant details. This iterative process allows readers to dynamically adapt their focus, gleaning information across multiple levels of granularity—from broad contextual clues to specific lexical indicators. Inspired by this human reading strategy, we introduce Neural Networks with Multi-Level Attention (NNMA). Our model departs from traditional single-pass attention mechanisms by incorporating external memories and a hierarchical attention structure. This allows the model to repeatedly process the arguments, progressively refining its focus on the most informative words and phrases. Specifically, the external memory stores intermediate representations of the arguments, while the multi-level attention dynamically adjusts weights to emphasize different aspects of the text across multiple “reading” iterations. We evaluate NNMA on the widely-used Penn Discourse Treebank (PDTB) dataset (Prasad et al., 2008). The experimental results demonstrate that our proposed model achieves state-of-the-art performance in implicit discourse relation classification. Furthermore, visualization of the attention weights reveals the model's iterative refinement process—showing how it progressively focuses on salient words across different levels of abstraction, mirroring the cognitive process of human discourse comprehension. This paper contributes a novel neural architecture capable of mimicking the repeated reading behavior necessary for effectively recognizing implicit discourse relations. The explosive growth of social media platforms has created a vast repository of user-generated text data, offering unprecedented opportunities for social science research, market analysis, and public opinion monitoring. However, the inherent informal nature of this text – characterized by misspellings, abbreviations, slang, and grammatical errors – poses significant challenges for traditional Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques. These techniques, largely trained on formal written language, often struggle to accurately interpret and process social media content, hindering effective downstream applications such as sentiment analysis, topic modeling, and information retrieval. A crucial preprocessing step to overcome this challenge is *text normalization*, the process of transforming non-standard words and phrases into their canonical, standard forms. For instance, normalizing "u" to "you", "gr8" to "great", or correcting common misspellings like "teh" to "the" greatly improves the robustness and accuracy of subsequent NLP tasks. While seemingly straightforward, effective text normalization is a complex problem, particularly in the dynamic and ever-evolving landscape of social media language. Early approaches to text normalization largely relied on manually curated dictionaries mapping non-standard forms to their standard equivalents (Aw et al., 2007). However, the sheer volume and rapid evolution of social media slang and abbreviations quickly render such dictionaries obsolete and incomplete. More recent research has focused on automatic dictionary generation utilizing techniques like edit distance (Kernighan et al., 1999) and phonetic similarity (Soundex, Metaphone) (Wilbur, 2008). These methods, while effective, often operate in isolation, neglecting the crucial contextual information that frequently disambiguates the correct normalization. For example, “lol” can mean “laugh out loud” or be a proper noun depending on the surrounding words. In this paper, we introduce a novel, unsupervised text normalization approach that explicitly leverages both lexical *and* contextual information gleaned from a large, unlabeled corpus of social media text. Our method moves beyond simple dictionary lookups and surface-level similarity analysis by constructing a *word association graph* that encodes the grammatical relationships and co-occurrence patterns of words within the corpus. This graph allows us to consider the surrounding context of a non-standard word – its neighboring words, their parts-of-speech tags, and their relative positions – when determining the most appropriate normalization. Specifically, we combine lexical features based on longest common subsequence ratio, edit distance, and the Double Metaphone algorithm with graph-based contextual features derived from our constructed word association graph. This allows the system to not only assess surface similarity but also to understand the grammatical role and typical usage of potential normalization candidates. Unlike approaches focused on generating extensive normalization dictionaries, our method performs normalization *in-context*, leading to more accurate and robust results. We demonstrate through experimental evaluation on standard datasets that our approach achieves state-of-the-art F-score performance, and is readily tunable for high-precision applications without significant recall degradation.

Bilingual dictionary induction (BDI) – the task of automatically creating a dictionary between two languages without relying on parallel corpora – remains a core challenge in Natural Language Processing. The scarcity of high-quality parallel data for many language pairs necessitates exploring alternative approaches. Recent work has increasingly focused on leveraging zero-shot learning principles by projecting words from different languages into a shared vector space, thereby identifying translational equivalents (Lazaridou et al., 2015; Alodena et al., 2014; Vulić et al., 2020). This paradigm typically involves learning a mapping function that aligns the vector spaces of source and target languages, enabling the identification of nearest neighbors as potential translations. However, despite the elegance and theoretical appeal of this zero-shot approach, practical performance has often fallen short of expectations. Existing methods frequently struggle to achieve the accuracy levels necessary for real-world applications, particularly when dealing with low-resource language pairs. A key limitation lies in the difficulty of learning robust and accurate mapping functions with limited supervision. The alignment process, driven by distributional similarities, can be susceptible to noise and spurious correlations, especially when the available monolingual data is insufficient to capture the nuances of cross-lingual relationships. To address this challenge, we propose a novel bridging approach centered around *knowledge distillation*. Our core contribution is a training objective designed to transfer knowledge from rich-resource language pairs to low-resource pairs. In essence, we capitalize on translation paths available for well-resourced languages (e.g., English-Spanish) to guide the learning process for those with limited resources (e.g., English-Zulu). These rich-resource paths serve as “teachers,” providing strong signals for the alignment process, while the low-resource paths act as “learners”, striving to mimic the behavior of their teachers. A significant advantage of our framework lies in its modularity and scalability. The distillation objective allows for the seamless incorporation of additional teacher paths as they become available, enriching the learning process without requiring extensive retraining. This flexibility is crucial for adapting to the evolving landscape of language resources. Furthermore, recognizing that the quality of the underlying monolingual word embeddings fundamentally impacts the performance of zero-shot BDI, we propose enhancements to these vector representations by incorporating linguistic information. This strengthens the semantic encoding of words in both the source and target languages, improving the effectiveness of the alignment process. Through rigorous experimentation across diverse language pairs, we demonstrate substantial performance gains attributable to our knowledge distillation training objective. Specifically, we observe accuracy improvements of up to 17% compared to state-of-the-art zero-shot BDI methods. These results highlight the effectiveness of leveraging knowledge transfer and enhancing word embeddings in tackling the challenges of low-resource bilingual dictionary induction. Neural dialogue generation has witnessed substantial progress in recent years, largely driven by advancements in sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models and attention mechanisms (Vinyals & Le, 2015; Sutskever et al., 2014; Luong et al., 2015). These models, trained on large corpora of conversational data, demonstrate a remarkable ability to generate seemingly coherent responses to given prompts. However, a persistent challenge remains: generating responses that are not only grammatically correct and contextually relevant, but also engaging, diverse, and *human-like*. Traditional approaches relying on maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) often suffer from issues like generic responses (Li et al., 2016) – frequently outputting safe, predictable phrases like “I don’t know” or “That’s interesting” – and a lack of long-term coherence within a conversation. The core problem lies in the discrepancy between the training objective and the ultimate goal of dialogue generation. MLE optimizes for predicting the next word given the preceding words, effectively mimicking the statistical patterns of the training data. It doesn’t explicitly encourage the model to *reason* or to generate responses that would convincingly fool a human interlocutor. This realization draws a direct parallel to the Turing Test (Turing, 1950), a benchmark of artificial intelligence wherein a machine attempts to exhibit intelligent behavior equivalent to, or indistinguishable from, that of a human. Inspired by the Turing Test, we propose a novel approach to neural dialogue generation leveraging the principles of adversarial learning (Goodfellow et al., 2014). Our framework casts the dialogue generation task as a reinforcement learning (RL) problem, a paradigm well-suited to optimizing for non-differentiable rewards. Specifically, we train two models simultaneously: a *generator*, responsible for producing dialogue responses, and a *discriminator*, tasked with distinguishing between responses generated by the generator and those authored by humans. The discriminator effectively acts as an “evaluator,” mirroring the human judge in the Turing Test. The generator’s objective is to produce sequences that maximize the probability of fooling the discriminator, while the discriminator strives to accurately identify machine-generated utterances. The output of the discriminator – a probability indicating the likelihood of a response being human-generated – serves as a reward signal for the generator. This adversarial training process pushes the generator to produce responses that are increasingly indistinguishable from human dialogues, fostering greater fluency, relevance, and overall quality. Furthermore, we introduce a novel method for *adversarial evaluation* of dialogue systems. Rather than relying on traditional metrics like BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002) or perplexity which often correlate poorly with human judgments, we propose using the success rate in fooling an adversary (another discriminator) as a direct metric of dialogue quality. This approach avoids pitfalls common in automated evaluation, such as rewarding overly literal or cliché responses. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our adversarial learning framework on several established dialogue datasets, showing significant improvements over current state-of-the-art baselines across both traditional metrics and our proposed adversarial evaluation metric. This work represents a step towards building truly intelligent dialogue systems capable of engaging in natural, human-like conversations.

Query spelling correction is a crucial component of modern information retrieval systems. Users frequently mistype search queries, leading to zero or suboptimal search results. Correcting these misspellings is therefore essential for delivering a positive user experience and maximizing the effectiveness of search engines. Traditionally, query spelling correction has relied heavily on probabilistic models, particularly noisy channel models (Bilmeier & Mietz, 2011; Kukich, 1992). These models leverage statistical information about the likelihood of errors and the frequency of correct words to generate candidate corrections. However, a significant limitation of these early approaches is their inability to effectively incorporate contextual information or learn complex relationships between noisy and correct queries. More recently, discriminative machine learning techniques, particularly ranking models, have been applied to the task of query spelling correction (Jones & Lofton, 2012; Li et al., 2013). This typically involves a two-stage pipeline: first, a noisy channel model is used to generate a set of candidate corrections for a given query; second, a discriminatively trained ranker scores these candidates based on a variety of features, selecting the highest-scoring correction as the final output. This approach allows for the incorporation of richer feature sets beyond those readily available in traditional probabilistic models, capturing aspects like edit distance, language model probabilities, and query context. However, the performance of this two-stage pipeline is fundamentally limited by the recall of the first stage – the noisy channel model. If the correct spelling is not among the candidates retrieved by the noisy channel model, the subsequent ranking stage, no matter how accurate, will inevitably fail. This is a critical bottleneck, particularly for rare or unconventional misspellings that are not well-covered by the training data used to build the noisy channel model. Furthermore, existing discriminative rankers often treat each candidate correction as an independent instance, ignoring the inherent structural relationships that exist between the noisy query and its potential corrections. These relationships, such as the specific edits performed or the shared sub-sequences between the noisy and correct forms, contain valuable information for accurate spelling correction. In this paper, we propose a novel discriminative model for query spelling correction that addresses these limitations. Our approach utilizes a Latent Structural Support Vector Machine (SVM) (Joachims et al., 2003) to learn a ranking function that explicitly models the structural dependencies between the noisy query and its candidate corrections. By simultaneously learning the weights of the features *and* the latent structure, our model can better capture the complex relationships that govern spelling errors and improve correction accuracy, even in scenarios where the noisy channel model exhibits low recall. We demonstrate through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets that our latent structural SVM significantly outperforms existing discriminative ranking models for query spelling correction. Tree-to-tree transduction forms a powerful paradigm for modeling complex linguistic transformations, finding applications in areas such as machine translation, semantic parsing, and question answering. These transducers, often realized as synchronous context-free grammars (SCFGs) or more general formalisms, aim to map syntactic structures from a source language to corresponding structures in a target language. A conventional approach to building such transducers relies heavily on initial word alignments, typically derived from parallel corpora, followed by a rule extraction phase that attempts to generalize from these alignments to create a functional grammar (Chiang, 2000; Knight and Graehl, 1997). This strategy, however, suffers from a critical vulnerability: its reliance on reliable word alignments. When dealing with limited parallel data—a common scenario in specialized domains or for low-resource languages—word alignments quickly become sparse and noisy. Such unreliable alignments can lead to the extraction of spurious or overly-specific rules that fail to generalize effectively, resulting in poor coverage and ultimately, limited transduction performance. Moreover, the inherent ambiguity in natural language can exacerbate the alignment problem, leading to multiple potential alignments and difficulties in selecting the most appropriate one. Traditional rule extraction heuristics (e.g., those based on frequency thresholds or constituent matching) struggle to mitigate this issue when source data is limited. This paper proposes a novel rule extraction algorithm for tree-to-tree transducers that is specifically designed to address the limitations of alignment-based approaches in low-resource settings. Our method eschews a direct reliance on word alignments, instead framing rule extraction as a cost minimization problem over tree fragments. By defining carefully crafted cost functions that evaluate the “desirability” of potential rules, we can iteratively induce a grammar that minimizes an overall cost, effectively seeking the most consistent and generalizable set of transduction rules. A key innovation of our approach lies in the introduction of “back-off states.” These states allow the transducer to dynamically generate rules for previously unseen left-hand sides, effectively extending the grammar’s coverage “on-the-fly.” This capability is crucial for handling the open-ended nature of language and for mitigating the effects of limited training data. By generating rules as needed, we avoid the pitfalls of over-fitting to the observed training set and improve the transducer’s ability to generalize to novel inputs. We evaluate our approach on a question answering (QA) task over a large knowledge base, a domain where sophisticated syntactic processing is essential for accurate query interpretation. Our experiments demonstrate that the induced tree transducers achieve reasonable syntactic accuracy and, importantly, significantly improve coverage compared to traditional methods, particularly when trained on limited data. This work represents a significant step towards building robust and adaptable tree-to-tree transducers that can operate effectively in challenging, low-resource conditions. Chiang, D. (2000). The ability to understand and reason about everyday events is a hallmark of human intelligence, yet remains a significant challenge for natural language processing (NLP) systems. At its core, this challenge lies in the necessity for *commonsense knowledge* – the vast, largely implicit understanding of how the world works that humans acquire through experience (Davis & Marcus, 2015; Fellbaum, 2000). A crucial aspect of this commonsense understanding is grasping the causal and correlational relationships between events; knowing, for example, that turning on a stove typically *causes* heat, or that rain is *often associated with* cloudy skies. Without this foundational knowledge, even sophisticated language models struggle to move beyond pattern matching and achieve true semantic comprehension. Despite increasing interest within the NLP community, progress in representing and learning commonsense knowledge, particularly in a manner suitable for story understanding, has been hampered by a critical bottleneck: the lack of robust and targeted evaluation frameworks. Existing benchmarks often focus on narrow aspects of commonsense reasoning, or rely on datasets that are either too small to provide statistically significant results, or lack the narrative context necessary to truly assess understanding (Forbus, 2019; Davis & Marcus, 2015). Evaluating a system's ability to not only *recall* factual knowledge but to *apply* it within the dynamic context of a story requires a different approach. This paper directly addresses this need by introducing a novel evaluation framework – the ‘Story Cloze Test’ – specifically designed to probe deeper understanding of commonsense narratives. This test presents systems with a four-sentence story and requires them to select the most plausible fifth sentence from a set of options, effectively acting as a challenging completion task. Success in this task demands more than mere keyword matching; systems must infer unstated motivations, predict likely consequences, and leverage an understanding of typical event sequences. To facilitate this evaluation, we have created ROCStories, a new corpus consisting of 50,000 five-sentence commonsense stories. ROCStories distinguishes itself from existing story corpora in two key respects. First, it intentionally captures a rich spectrum of causal and temporal relations between everyday events, presenting scenarios that necessitate commonsense reasoning for comprehension. Secondly, ROCStories is a curated collection of high-quality, relatable stories about everyday life. This characteristic makes it not only suitable for the Story Cloze Test but also valuable for tasks such as story generation, offering a resource for both evaluating *understanding* and *producing* coherent narratives. Our experimental results demonstrate that current state-of-the-art models, often relying on relatively shallow language understanding techniques, struggle to perform well on the Story Cloze Test. This finding underscores the limitations of existing approaches and highlights the importance of developing systems that can effectively leverage and reason with commonsense knowledge. We discuss the implications of these results for advancements in both script learning and deep language understanding, and offer directions for future research aimed at bridging the gap between current NLP capabilities and true semantic comprehension.

Dialogue is the cornerstone of human communication, and its success fundamentally relies on cooperation between participants. In Gricean terms (Grice, 1975), effective dialogue hinges on adherence to conversational maxims – quantity, quality, relation, and manner – which implicitly guide participants toward informative, truthful, relevant, and clear contributions. However, real-world dialogues frequently exhibit deviations from these ideals, manifesting as instances of *non-cooperation*. Identifying and understanding non-cooperation is crucial for a comprehensive understanding of communicative dynamics, with implications spanning fields such as computational linguistics, human-computer interaction, and social psychology. Prior work on non-cooperation has generally taken two distinct paths. The first, often found in the realm of multi-agent systems and task-oriented dialogues, focuses on *task-related non-cooperation* – instances where a participant intentionally hinders the achievement of a shared goal (e.g., providing misleading information to an opponent in a negotiation; Sierra et al., 2008). Such approaches typically define non-cooperative behaviors based on pre-defined task success metrics. The second approach involves manually defining specific linguistic rules that delineate non-cooperative behaviors, such as deliberately vague responses, abrupt topic changes, or refusing to answer direct questions (e.g., Traister et al., 2016). While valuable, this second approach suffers from the limitations of relying on hand-crafted rules, which can be brittle, incomplete, and difficult to generalize across different dialogue contexts. This paper proposes a novel approach to measuring non-cooperation, shifting the focus from defining what *is* non-cooperative to quantifying the *degree of deviation* from expected cooperative behavior. Our central hypothesis is that linguistic non-cooperation can be operationalized as a function of how significantly dialogue participants diverge from established conventions governing the proper introduction and fulfillment of conversational obligations. Instead of explicitly encoding rules for undesirable behaviors, we leverage the inherent structure of cooperative dialogue itself. We achieve this by framing dialogue as a *dialogue game* - a formal system defining acceptable moves and state transitions based on principles of normative interaction. Specifically, we begin with rules specifying ‘normal’ or ‘correct’ dialogue behavior—those demonstrated in a corpus of genuinely cooperative dialogues—and subsequently assess the extent to which participants *comply* with these rules. By quantifying rule violations, we obtain a continuous measure of non-cooperation, offering a more nuanced picture than binary classifications of cooperative versus non-cooperative utterances. This method permits a quantitative evaluation of cooperation degrees, and does not rely on an artificially defined set of “non-cooperative” tactics. We evaluate our model on a corpus of political interviews, a domain characterized by potentially adversarial interactions and strategic communication. Our results demonstrate that the model accurately predicts the degree of cooperation exhibited by the interviewer role, and successfully identifies the relative levels of cooperation between interlocutors within each dialogue. This work contributes a new methodology for analyzing dialogue, opening doors to a variety of applications, including refined analysis of natural language interactions, more human-like virtual assistants, and sophisticated dialogue systems capable of understanding and responding to subtle cues of communicative intent.

Automated Essay Scoring (AES) has emerged as a valuable tool in educational settings, offering a scalable and cost-effective means of evaluating student writing. Traditionally, AES systems rely on machine learning models trained on datasets of essays paired with holistic scores assigned by human graders. These systems, while capable of achieving impressive accuracy, often exhibit a significant performance drop when applied to essays written in response to prompts different from those used during training – a phenomenon known as domain shift. This limitation presents a major challenge to the widespread adoption of AES, as educational institutions frequently introduce new writing prompts to align with curriculum changes or assessment objectives. The core issue lies in the inherent differences between prompts. Varying topics, required argumentation styles, and even subtle nuances in the prompt wording can all contribute to shifts in the distribution of essay features. An AES model trained on essays addressing one prompt may, therefore, struggle to generalize effectively to essays addressing a different prompt, leading to inaccurate and potentially unfair scoring. Addressing this challenge requires a method to transfer knowledge learned from essays scored on one prompt (the source domain) to essays scored on a new, unseen prompt (the target domain). The most straightforward solution – retraining the AES model on a substantial corpus of manually graded essays from the new prompt – is often impractical. Collecting and annotating such datasets is both expensive and time-consuming, making it infeasible for many educational contexts. Consequently, research in AES has increasingly focused on *domain adaptation* techniques, which aim to mitigate the effects of domain shift without requiring extensive relabeling of data. Existing approaches to domain adaptation in AES include feature engineering to reduce prompt-specific characteristics (Shermis & Burstein, 2005), instance weighting to prioritize essays that are more representative of the target domain (Taghipour & Ng, 2005), and transfer learning techniques leveraging pre-trained language models (Dong et al., 2015). In this paper, we explore domain adaptation for AES using a Bayesian framework built upon correlated linear regression. Unlike many existing methods that focus on transforming feature spaces or reweighting instances, our approach directly adapts the scoring function itself. We propose a novel method leveraging Bayesian linear ridge regression to model the relationship between essay features and scores, explicitly accounting for the correlation between source and target domains. This allows the model to effectively leverage the information contained in the source domain while simultaneously adapting to the nuances of the target domain, even with limited labeled data from the target prompt. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method using the publicly available Automated Student Assessment Prize (ASAP) dataset, showing that it achieves competitive performance compared to commonly used domain adaptation baselines. Our findings suggest that correlated linear regression provides a robust and effective approach to addressing the challenge of domain shift in automated essay scoring, paving the way for more reliable and adaptable AES systems in real-world educational settings.
