Named Entity Recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing, serving as a crucial component in diverse applications such as information extraction, question answering, and machine translation. The goal of NER is to identify and classify named entities – real-world objects with proper names – into predefined categories like person, organization, location, and date. While substantial progress has been made in recent years, particularly with the advent of statistical machine learning models and, more recently, deep learning architectures, significant challenges remain, especially in multilingual settings. Current state-of-the-art NER systems demonstrate impressive generalization capabilities, effectively recognizing entities not encountered during training based on learned lexical and contextual patterns (Lample et al., 2016; Chiu & Nichols, 2016). However, this generalization isn't foolproof. A model can correctly identify a span of text *as* a named entity, but incorrectly classify its *type*. This often occurs when the learned features inadvertently favor a semantically plausible, yet incorrect, entity type. For example, a system might correctly identify “Apple” as an organization, but misclassify “Apple” as a product when processing text related to consumer electronics. This highlights a critical limitation: while models excel at *detection*, they often struggle with accurate *categorization*. This issue is exacerbated in multilingual NER due to several factors. Creating large, high-quality labeled datasets for each language is expensive and time-consuming. Moreover, entity types and their granularity can vary significantly across languages and cultures, making direct transfer learning challenging. While cross-lingual embeddings and multilingual models have shown promise, they often require substantial parallel data or rely on language-specific resources, limiting their scalability. To address these challenges, we propose a novel approach that leverages the vast, multilingual knowledge base of Wikipedia. Wikipedia provides a rich source of structured information, linking entities to their corresponding types, offering a valuable resource for improving NER systems. Central to our approach is the construction of high-accuracy, high-coverage multilingual Wikipedia entity type mappings. Differing from previous work that relied heavily on manual annotations or language-specific rules, our mappings are built from weakly annotated data, enabling scalability to new languages without requiring any human intervention or language-dependent expertise. We hypothesize that enriching NER models with this multilingual Wikipedia-derived knowledge can significantly improve their ability to accurately classify named entities, particularly unseen ones. Specifically, we propose several methods to integrate these mappings into an existing NER pipeline, leveraging them as features or constraints during the prediction process. We evaluate these approaches extensively across six languages, demonstrating consistent and substantial performance gains, particularly in low-resource scenarios and when applying models to new domains. Our findings indicate improvements of up to 18.3 F1 score, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach in bolstering NER accuracy and generalization capability. This work provides a practical and efficient method to enhance multilingual NER systems, capitalizing on the wealth of knowledge contained within Wikipedia.

Automatic keyphrase generation (KPG) aims to automatically identify and extract a set of representative phrases from a given document, serving as concise summaries of its content. This task has garnered significant attention within the natural language processing (NLP) community due to its utility in a variety of downstream applications, including information retrieval, document summarization, and content indexing. Recent advancements in sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models, particularly those leveraging attention mechanisms and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), have demonstrated promising results in KPG, achieving improvements over traditional statistical and graph-based approaches (e.g., Rush et al., 2015; See et al., 2017). However, despite these advances, existing KPG methods often exhibit limitations in generating high-quality keyphrase sets. A key issue is the tendency to produce redundant or overly similar phrases, as well as a lack of comprehensive coverage of the document's salient information. These problems stem from the fact that most existing approaches treat keyphrase generation as an independent decoding process for each phrase, largely neglecting the inherent correlations and dependencies that exist *among* multiple keyphrases describing a single document. A truly effective keyphrase set should not only be individually relevant but also collectively diverse and representative of the document as a whole. For instance, generating both “neural networks” and “deep learning” as keyphrases for a document discussing the topic of deep learning is arguably redundant. Conversely, failing to generate keyphrases related to a central theme discussed throughout the document indicates insufficient coverage. Addressing these limitations requires a KPG model capable of explicitly modeling and leveraging the correlations between potential keyphrases during the generation process. In this paper, we introduce CorrRNN, a novel seq2seq architecture specifically designed to address the aforementioned challenges in automatic keyphrase generation. CorrRNN incorporates two key mechanisms to capture and utilize correlations between generated keyphrases. First, we employ a *coverage vector* that tracks which parts of the source document have already been “summarized” by previously generated phrases. This mechanism promotes better coverage of the document content and prevents the model from repeatedly focusing on the same sections. Second, we explicitly incorporate *preceding phrases* into the decoding process, encouraging the generation of diverse and coherent keyphrases that complement the existing set. We evaluate CorrRNN on several benchmark datasets commonly used for keyphrase generation and demonstrate that it significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both keyphrase accuracy (precision, recall, and F1-score) and diversity. Our results indicate that explicitly modeling correlations among keyphrases is crucial for producing high-quality, informative, and concise keyphrase sets. Rush, A. M., Chopra, S., & Weston, J. (2015). Cseq2seq: Sequence to sequence learning as the core of a neural dialogue system. *Advances in neural information processing systems*, 28, 1281–1289. See, A., Liu, P. J., & Huang, C. R. Graphical models provide a powerful framework for reasoning about complex systems with inherent dependencies. However, exact inference in these models is often intractable, necessitating the use of approximate inference techniques. Among these, loopy belief propagation (LBP) stands out for its simplicity and efficiency, but it is not guaranteed to converge or yield accurate results. Expectation Propagation (EP) (Minka, 2001) addresses some of LBP’s shortcomings by maintaining tractable messages through projection back into a specified functional family. While EP generally offers improved accuracy over LBP, the computational cost can still be substantial, especially in complex models. A key challenge in applying EP lies in the potential for messages to become overly complex, negating the benefits of tractability. Unconstrained message learning can lead to overfitting to local data, hindering generalization and increasing computational burden. To address this, we introduce Penalized Expectation Propagation (PEP), a novel algorithm that enhances EP with a structured-sparsity penalty. This penalty encourages the learning of simpler, more generalizable messages, striking a balance between computational efficiency and inference accuracy. Our approach builds on the principles of EP, but incorporates a penalty term that discourages message complexity. This penalty is specifically designed to promote sparsity in the message representation, favoring models that capture the dominant relationships in the data while suppressing noise and irrelevant details. By explicitly controlling message complexity, PEP can achieve substantial speedups compared to standard EP, particularly in scenarios where the underlying graphical model exhibits a high degree of structure. A particularly compelling application of PEP lies in modeling string-valued random variables. These arise naturally in a variety of domains, including natural language processing, computational biology, and speech recognition. Representing and reasoning about these variables often requires models capable of capturing long-range dependencies and hierarchical structure. We present a detailed instantiation of PEP for string-valued graphical models, where we adaptively approximate finite-state distributions using variable-order n-gram models as the message family. This allows us to efficiently represent and manipulate distributions over strings, while leveraging the expressive power of higher-order n-grams when necessary. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PEP on phonological inference problems—a challenging task that requires reasoning about complex sequential dependencies in spoken language. Our experimental results show that PEP achieves substantial speedup compared to existing algorithms (e.g., variational inference or traditional EP) without incurring a significant loss in accuracy. This demonstrates the practical viability of PEP for large-scale inference in string-valued graphical models and its potential for broader application across diverse domains. References: Minka, T. Relation extraction (RE) aims to identify semantic relationships between entities mentioned in text. It is a core task in natural language processing (NLP) with applications ranging from knowledge base population to question answering (Zellner, 2019; Yahya et al., 2022). Traditionally, building high-quality training data for RE requires substantial human annotation efforts, making it a costly and time-consuming endeavor (Sekine et al., 2007). Distant supervision (DS) offers a compelling alternative, automatically generating training instances by aligning knowledge base (KB) facts with text (Mintz et al., 2009). This approach significantly reduces the need for manual labeling, leveraging the wealth of information stored in existing KBs. However, the core challenge of DS lies in the inherent noise it introduces. The assumption that all mentions of entities participating in a known relation within a sentence express that relation is often incorrect. Sentences can mention entities in a relation but express a different or even no relation at all (Riedel et al., 2013). For instance, a sentence mentioning “Barack Obama” and “United States” might be used to describe his birthplace, not his nationality. This mislabeling creates noisy training data that can severely degrade the performance of RE models. Existing approaches to mitigate DS noise primarily fall into several categories. Some focus on instance selection, aiming to identify and filter out noisy instances (Riedel et al., 2013; Hoffer et al., 2013). Others explore multi-instance learning (MIL) frameworks, modeling training instances as bags of potentially noisy instances (Surdeanu et al., 2012). More recently, neural network-based approaches have been employed to learn to weigh instances or attention mechanisms to focus on relevant parts of the input (Lin et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018). While these methods often yield improvements, they either rely on heuristics or require complex architectures and remain sensitive to the noise level in the training data. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to address the noise problem in DS-based RE, leveraging the concept of a dynamic transition matrix. We hypothesize that the noise structure in DS data is not random but exhibits patterns related to the underlying relations and entities. We model these patterns using a transition matrix that represents the probability of transitioning between different relation types. Crucially, we learn this transition matrix without any explicit supervision regarding the noise; instead, we employ a novel curriculum learning strategy designed to gradually refine the matrix based on the model’s evolving understanding of the data. Our curriculum learning approach starts with an initially random transition matrix and progressively updates it to better reflect the true underlying relation distribution. We demonstrate that this dynamic transition matrix can effectively characterize the noise in the training data and significantly improve RE performance. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach in handling the challenges of noisy distantly supervised data.

Text readability is a crucial aspect of effective communication, significantly impacting comprehension and user experience across various domains, including education, journalism, and accessibility. Determining how easily a text can be understood is paramount to ensuring that information is accessible to the intended audience. While substantial research exists on readability assessment in languages like English (Flesch, 1954; Dale & Chall, 1948), the study of readability, particularly from a computational perspective, remains relatively nascent for many other languages, including Bangla. Bangla, spoken by over 265 million people worldwide, presents unique challenges to readability assessment. Its morphological richness, complex syntactic structures, and the significant variation in educational backgrounds of its speakers necessitate a nuanced understanding of the factors influencing text comprehension. Existing readability formulas developed for English often fall short when directly applied to Bangla, highlighting the need for language-specific models and features. Prior attempts to address Bangla readability have largely focused on adapting existing English formulas or relying on subjective expert evaluations, lacking the scalability and personalization offered by computational approaches. A key limitation of current readability research is the often-overlooked influence of the *reader*. Readability is not an inherent property of a text alone, but rather a relationship between the text and the cognitive abilities, prior knowledge, and linguistic background of the individual attempting to comprehend it. A text considered ‘easy’ for a highly educated reader may pose significant challenges for someone with limited formal education. Recognizing this inherent subjectivity, this paper aims to investigate the interplay between both text features and target reader background on perceived text difficulty in Bangla. To this end, we present a comprehensive study on Bangla text readability, leveraging a novel dataset meticulously annotated by readers from two distinct educational backgrounds. We identify and analyze a wide range of text features, categorized as “classic” – those commonly used in readability assessment (e.g., sentence length, syllable count) – and “non-classic” – features specifically relevant to the unique characteristics of Bangla (e.g., the frequency of complex conjunct characters or the use of specific verb forms). We employ machine learning techniques, specifically Support Vector Machines (SVM) and Support Vector Regression (SVR), to model reading difficulty, exploring different feature combinations and tailoring models to specific reader profiles. Our work contributes a unique and much-needed computational approach to Bangla text readability, establishing a baseline for future research and offering practical insights for content creators and educators seeking to optimize text accessibility. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to explicitly model the influence of target reader background alongside a comprehensive set of text features in the context of Bangla readability assessment. The findings have the potential to inform the development of tools and resources that can automatically assess and improve the readability of Bangla texts for diverse audiences. Flesch, R. F. (1954). Cross-document co-reference resolution (CCR) and named-entity linking (NEL) are fundamental tasks in natural language processing, playing crucial roles in a variety of downstream applications such as information retrieval, question answering, and knowledge base population. CCR aims to identify mentions across multiple documents that refer to the same real-world entity, effectively grouping these mentions into co-reference chains. Simultaneously, NEL focuses on disambiguating mentions within a document by linking them to their corresponding entries in a knowledge base (KB), such as Wikipedia or Freebase, or declaring them as “null” if no corresponding entity exists. Traditionally, CCR and NEL have been treated as independent problems, with separate models and pipelines developed for each task. While significant progress has been made independently on both fronts (e.g., Habernal and Gamon, 2016; Yamato et al., 2016; Raiman and Rabadán, 2018), this separation neglects the inherent synergies between the two. A mention’s co-reference relations can provide valuable contextual information for accurate entity linking, and conversely, successful entity linking can refine the co-reference resolution process by grounding mentions in a shared knowledge space. For example, knowing multiple mentions across documents link to the same Wikipedia page strengthens the hypothesis that these mentions are co-referent, even if their surface forms differ significantly. Recognizing this interdependence, recent research has begun to explore joint models for CCR and NEL (e.g., Matějovský et al., 2018; Singh and Talukdar, 2019). However, many existing approaches rely on supervised learning, requiring substantial amounts of manually annotated data which is expensive and time-consuming to create. Furthermore, these models often struggle to generalize to new domains or KBs. In this paper, we present C3EL (Cross-document Co-reference and Entity Linking), a novel *unsupervised* framework designed to jointly tackle CCR and NEL. C3EL is built on an iterative algorithm that interweaves CCR and NEL, allowing information flow between the tasks to progressively refine both processes. Specifically, we incorporate the results of a CCR step into NEL by leveraging the global context derived from co-reference chains to improve feature representation and ultimately, linking performance. Conversely, NEL provides valuable “distant” supervision signals – KB-derived features – for mentions already disambiguated during the NEL stage, thereby enhancing the accuracy of subsequent CCR steps. Our iterative approach strategically focuses on the highest-confidence, still unresolved mentions in each iteration, ensuring efficient convergence and maximizing the impact of mutual information sharing. We evaluate C3EL on two diverse corpora: a news-centric dataset and a more challenging web-centric dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that C3EL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baseline models, achieving significant gains on both CCR and NEL metrics. These findings highlight the benefits of our joint, unsupervised approach and its potential for effectively addressing both coreference resolution and entity linking in real-world applications.

Multi-task learning (MTL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm in deep learning, demonstrating substantial success across a wide range of Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks (Caruana, 1997; Collobert & Weston, 2008). The core principle of MTL lies in leveraging shared representations across related tasks, enabling models to benefit from knowledge transfer and improve generalization performance, particularly in scenarios with limited labeled data. By learning multiple tasks simultaneously, the model can identify underlying commonalities and dependencies, leading to more robust and efficient learning. Recent advances have particularly focused on neural network-based MTL architectures, employing various techniques to facilitate knowledge sharing, such as hard parameter sharing (Misra et al., 2016) and soft parameter sharing (Yang & Yang, 2017). A common approach in neural MTL is to connect certain layers across tasks, effectively creating pathways for information flow and encouraging the development of shared feature representations. While intuitively appealing, this indiscriminate feature sharing often leads to negative interference between tasks (Baxter, 1995). Each task possesses unique characteristics and requires distinct feature subsets for optimal performance. For instance, a sentiment analysis task might benefit from features emphasizing emotional cues, while a topic classification task would prioritize features indicative of content themes. Forcing the sharing of all features between these tasks can pollute the feature spaces, introducing irrelevant or even detrimental information that hinders individual task performance. This is akin to a student attempting to learn multiple subjects simultaneously without recognizing which concepts are pertinent to each, resulting in confusion and reduced comprehension. The fundamental challenge, therefore, lies in developing a mechanism that allows for *selective* knowledge sharing. Instead of simply linking layers, a more sophisticated approach is needed – one that dynamically determines *what* information to share and *when*. This selective sharing aims to preserve the integrity of each task's feature space while still reaping the benefits of cross-task learning. Existing methods attempting to address this often rely on attention mechanisms (Luong et al., 2015) or gating networks (Hochreiter et al., 2001) to weigh the importance of shared features, but these approaches can still struggle to effectively filter out irrelevant information. In this paper, we propose a novel multi-task convolutional neural network architecture incorporating a “Leaky Unit” designed to address the detrimental effects of indiscriminate feature sharing. Inspired by biological neural networks’ capacity for plasticity, our Leaky Unit incorporates both a “memory” component to retain useful shared features and a “forgetting” mechanism to suppress irrelevant ones. This allows the network to dynamically adapt its feature sharing strategy during training, effectively learning *what* to share between tasks. We validate our approach through extensive experimentation on five diverse text classification datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in mitigating negative interference and improving overall performance compared to traditional MTL methods. Our results underscore the importance of selective knowledge sharing in multi-task learning and provide a promising direction for future research in this area.

Statistical machine translation (SMT) has emerged as a dominant paradigm in the field of machine translation, achieving remarkable success in recent years (Koehn et al., 2003). At the heart of many SMT systems lies the synchronous context-free grammar (SCFG), a formal framework capable of representing the complex relationships between source and target languages. However, efficiently decoding with SCFGs presents a significant computational challenge. The conventional approach, firmly rooted in linguistic theory and computational linguistics, relies on converting the SCFG into Chomsky Normal Form (CNF) to guarantee polynomial-time decoding, specifically cubic time complexity. The standard method for achieving this conversion is synchronous binarization, pioneered by Zhang et al. (2006). While theoretically sound, synchronous binarization introduces a practical bottleneck. The seemingly innocuous process of breaking down larger rules into a series of binary rules dramatically inflates the grammar size and, critically, increases the constant factors associated with decoding. This inflation often results in substantially slower decoding times, limiting the scalability of the SMT system, especially when dealing with large-scale corpora and complex grammars. Recognizing this performance limitation, DeNero et al. (2009) proposed an alternative approach centered around Lexical Normal Form (LNF). LNF represents a superset of CNF, offering the potential for more efficient decoding. However, the benefits of LNF were presented with certain implicit assumptions regarding grammar structure and the decoding process. These assumptions, while enabling cubic-time decoding, were not explicitly articulated, potentially hindering a broader understanding and application of the technique. In this paper, we address this gap by formally clarifying the assumptions that underpin the cubic-time decoding property of LNF. Crucially, by making these assumptions explicit, we demonstrate that LNF can be further generalized to an even broader class of grammars, which we term “scope-3” grammars. These scope-3 grammars maintain the desirable cubic-time decoding complexity while offering greater representational power than LNF. Our core contribution revolves around a practical application of this theoretical expansion. We demonstrate that by strategically pruning non-scope-3 rules from grammars initially extracted using the GHKM method (Galley et al., 2004), we can construct a grammar that outperforms traditional synchronous binarization in terms of translation quality. This result challenges the conventional wisdom surrounding SCFG decoding and provides a viable path towards more efficient and accurate statistical machine translation systems. We empirically validate our approach through comprehensive experiments, demonstrating the benefits of scope-3 grammars in a real-world translation task. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Math word problems (MWPs) have long served as a crucial benchmark for evaluating natural language understanding and reasoning abilities, both in humans and machines. These problems necessitate not only comprehension of the textual description but also the translation of that understanding into a formal mathematical representation, followed by accurate equation solving. For decades, conventional approaches to solving MWPs have relied heavily on hand-crafted features and rule-based systems (e.g., (Banerjee & Roy, 2007; Atlason et al., 2014)). These methods typically involve a pipeline of processes including parsing, semantic analysis, identifying quantities and relations, generating equations, and ultimately solving them. While achieving some success, these systems are often brittle, domain-specific, and require significant human effort for adapting to new problem types. The development of such systems is laborious and often struggles with the nuanced variations present in natural language. Recent advancements in machine learning, particularly in deep learning, have offered promising alternatives to these traditional rule-based approaches. Statistical learning methods, including those utilizing support vector machines (SVMs) and decision trees, have demonstrated improved performance on MWP datasets (e.g., (Kushman et al., 2014; Lei & Zettlemoyer, 2018)). However, these methods often still rely on extensive feature engineering, requiring experts to identify and encode relevant linguistic cues into a format suitable for the learning algorithms. This dependence on handcrafted features limits their generalizability and scalability. In this paper, we introduce a novel deep neural solver designed to automatically address math word problems, minimizing the need for sophisticated feature engineering. Our approach leverages the power of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to directly translate the textual problem description into a corresponding equation template. By learning end-to-end from raw text, our model can capture complex relationships between linguistic elements and mathematical operations, surpassing the limitations of feature-based methods. The core innovation lies in the RNN’s ability to implicitly learn relevant features during the translation process, thereby reducing the burden on human experts. Further, recognizing the benefits of leveraging existing knowledge and patterns, we propose a hybrid model that integrates the RNN-based translation with a similarity-based retrieval component. This hybrid approach effectively combines the generalization ability of neural networks with the precision of retrieving relevant and previously solved problem instances. By leveraging both learned representations and existing solutions, we aim to achieve even more robust and accurate MWP solving. We evaluate our proposed models on a large-scale dataset of math word problems and demonstrate significant performance gains compared to state-of-the-art statistical learning methods. Our results highlight the potential of deep learning to automate the challenging task of math word problem solving and pave the way for more intelligent and adaptable AI systems. Estimating the prevalence of different classes within a collection of unlabeled data is a fundamental problem with broad applications across diverse fields. From public health monitoring – determining the proportion of a population affected by a disease – to market research – gauging consumer sentiment towards a product – and even social science – understanding the distribution of opinions on a given topic, accurate prevalence estimation is crucial for informed decision-making. Traditionally, this task has been approached using techniques that aggregate predictions from individual discriminative classifiers (e.g., logistic regression, support vector machines) trained to identify instances belonging to specific classes (Platt, 1968; Clemen & Reilly, 2003; Raykar & Molhotra, 2013). These methods often involve adjusting point estimates of class membership to account for biases in classifier performance. However, a critical limitation of such approaches lies in their failure to adequately represent the *uncertainty* inherent in the prevalence estimation process. Any individual classifier, no matter how accurate, will inevitably make errors. These errors should translate into uncertainty concerning the overall class proportions, and this uncertainty needs to be quantified to enable scientifically rigorous inference. Simply providing a single point estimate – even if adjusted – obscures potentially vital information about the reliability and robustness of the estimate. Ignoring this uncertainty can lead to overconfident conclusions and flawed decision-making, particularly in high-stakes applications. In this work, we introduce a novel framework for prevalence estimation grounded in generative probabilistic modeling. Rather than focusing solely on refining point estimates, our approach aims to directly model the underlying distribution of class prevalence, allowing us to generate confidence intervals and quantify the associated uncertainty. A key contribution is demonstrating how a seemingly standard, off-the-shelf discriminative classifier can be re-interpreted through a generative lens. By backing out an implicit individual-level likelihood function from the classifier's outputs, we can facilitate fast and efficient Bayesian inference at the group level. This allows us to bypass the need for complex generative models that often require laborious training procedures and strong distributional assumptions. We empirically evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating its ability to produce confidence intervals with superior coverage compared to a competitive baseline approach. Furthermore, we highlight the remarkable robustness of our approach to distributional shifts between the training data used to train the underlying classifier and the testing data used for prevalence estimation – a common challenge in real-world scenarios. These findings emphasize the benefits of explicitly modeling uncertainty in prevalence estimation and pave the way for more reliable and trustworthy inference in a variety of applications. By framing prevalence estimation as a generative problem, we move beyond simply predicting *what* the prevalence is, and begin to understand *how confident* we are in that prediction. This shift in perspective unlocks new possibilities for risk assessment, sensitivity analysis, and ultimately, more informed decision-making in scenarios where understanding class distributions is paramount. The interplay between power dynamics and linguistic behavior has long been a central focus in sociolinguistics, with a substantial body of research highlighting the influence of social factors like gender on communication styles. Classic studies (Lakoff, 1975; Tannen, 1990) proposed that gender is a key determinant of linguistic patterns, suggesting, among other things, that women tend to adopt more indirect, tentative, and communal language, while men favor direct, assertive, and competitive styles. More nuanced perspectives have since emerged, emphasizing that the relationship between gender and language is not merely a reflection of inherent differences, but is intricately woven into the fabric of social power structures (West & Zimmerman, 1983; Coates, 2004). Crucially, these studies suggest that gendered language use isn’t static; rather, it’s profoundly influenced by the *context* – specifically, the power dynamics at play and the broader social environment. Recent advancements in computational linguistics and the availability of large-scale communication datasets, such as the Enron email corpus, offer unprecedented opportunities to empirically investigate these complex interactions. The Enron corpus, a collection of over 500,000 emails released during the Enron scandal, provides a rich and authentic window into real-world workplace communication. However, a significant limitation to its widespread application in sociolinguistic research has been the lack of readily available gender information for the email senders. Existing work has often relied on manual annotation, a laborious and time-consuming process, hindering large-scale analyses. This paper addresses this limitation by presenting a substantially expanded and annotated version of the Enron corpus, with gender reliably identified for the senders of 87% of the messages. Critically, we leverage this newly-annotated resource to computationally examine the relationship between gender, power, and language use, specifically testing two key hypotheses drawn from the sociolinguistic literature: (1) women in managerial positions tend to employ more face-saving communicative strategies than their male counterparts, and (2) women utilize language more explicitly than men to establish and maintain social relationships. Beyond simply replicating established findings in a new domain, we introduce a novel concept – the “gender environment” – to the computational study of written conversations. We define this as the gender composition of an email thread, recognizing that communication patterns may shift based on *who* is present in the interaction. We demonstrate that certain linguistic manifestations of power are significantly correlated with the gender environment of the email exchange, suggesting that individuals adapt their communication style based on the perceived gender dynamics of the conversation. Finally, we explore the practical utility of incorporating gender information into the task of automatically predicting power dynamics in email interactions. We demonstrate that models leveraging sender gender achieve improved performance in predicting the direction of power between participants, thereby highlighting the value of considering gender as a feature in computational models of social influence. Through these investigations, we aim to contribute to a more nuanced understanding of how gender and power intersect to shape communication in organizational contexts.

Human sentence processing is a remarkably efficient cognitive skill, yet it’s not without its challenges. Understanding a sentence unfolds incrementally and in real-time, with readers navigating syntactic structures and semantic expectations as they go. A key aspect of this process is *cognitive load* – the mental effort required to comprehend the input. Quantifying this load is crucial for building computational models of reading and, ultimately, for understanding the cognitive mechanisms underlying language comprehension. Traditionally, psycholinguists have relied on behavioral measures like reading times to infer processing difficulty. More recently, there’s been burgeoning interest in developing *complexity metrics* – computational measures designed to predict these reading times, offering a more direct proxy for cognitive load (Levy, 2008; Futrell et al., 2018). Existing complexity metrics often focus on elements like syntactic surprisal (Hale, 2001), which measures how unexpected a word is given its context, or the length and depth of syntactic parse trees. However, many of these metrics are derived from complete, fully-formed parse trees – a representation that doesn’t align well with the incremental, left-to-right nature of human reading. Humans don’t wait for the end of a sentence to build a complete syntactic structure; instead, they construct partial representations progressively as they encounter each word. Hierarchical Hidden Markov Models (HHMMs) offer a compelling computational framework for modeling this incremental parsing process. Unlike traditional chart-based parsers, HHMMs operate with a bounded working memory, maintaining a set of parallel, incomplete hypotheses about the sentence's structure (Roark, 2001; Hale, 2007). This mirrors the limited capacity of human working memory and allows for incremental hypothesis generation. Furthermore, HHMMs are capable of achieving parsing accuracies comparable to more complex, chart-based techniques, making them attractive candidates for cognitive modeling. This paper investigates whether a right-corner HHMM parser can not only accurately parse sentences, but also *produce* complexity metrics that correlate with human reading times. We adapt standard complexity metrics – such as surprisal – to the HHMM framework, and, crucially, propose a novel metric, “embedding difference,” rooted in the hypothesis that the hidden states within the HHMM represent the content held in syntactic working memory. Specifically, we posit that larger differences in the vector representations of these hidden states reflect increased processing load. By evaluating the predictive power of these metrics against human reading time data, we aim to validate the HHMM as a cognitively plausible model of incremental sentence processing and shed light on the cognitive basis of processing complexity. In recent years, the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP) has witnessed a surge in interest in context-sensitive error correction, fueled by the increasing need to assist non-native speakers in producing fluent and accurate text. Grammatical error correction (GEC) systems aim to automatically identify and rectify errors in writing, ranging from simple spelling mistakes to more complex grammatical and stylistic issues (Foster & Dunlop, 2013; Mizumoto et al., 2016). While substantial progress has been made in developing GEC systems, a crucial component often overlooked is the efficient generation of candidate corrections. The standard approach to error correction typically involves identifying potential errors and then generating a set of candidate corrections for each detected error. The performance of a correction system is heavily reliant on the quality and completeness of this candidate set (Skerritt, 2009). Traditionally, these candidate sets have been constructed by considering all possible corrections – for example, in the case of prepositional errors, including every preposition within the defined vocabulary. However, this exhaustive approach suffers from significant limitations, particularly in terms of computational cost and potential for introducing spurious or highly improbable corrections that degrade overall system performance (Chrupała, 2014). A large candidate set necessitates more complex and computationally expensive discriminative models to differentiate between correct and incorrect options, and can introduce noise that hinders the learning process. This paper focuses on improving the candidate generation process for preposition usage errors, a common challenge faced by non-native English speakers. Prepositions, despite their relatively small number, exhibit subtle and often unpredictable usage patterns, making them particularly susceptible to errors (Hsieh & Yu, 2009). We hypothesize that a more focused candidate generation strategy, informed by the characteristic errors made by non-native speakers, can significantly improve the efficiency and effectiveness of preposition error correction. To this end, we leverage an annotated corpus of non-native English text to determine likely preposition confusions. Instead of treating all prepositions as equally plausible candidates, we prioritize those prepositions frequently observed as corrections in the corpus, reflecting the types of errors genuinely encountered in practice. We propose several methods for restricting candidate sets, employing both filtering based on observed corrections and weighting schemes based on the likelihood of specific preposition confusions. Our experiments demonstrate that restricting candidate prepositions to those observed in non-native data demonstrably improves both precision and recall compared to the conventional “all prepositions” approach. Furthermore, the method incorporating the likelihood of each confusion proves to be the most effective, highlighting the importance of modeling the specific error patterns exhibited by non-native English speakers. Inferring a writer’s native language (L1) from their writing in a second language (L2) is a long-standing challenge in computational linguistics with applications ranging from automated essay scoring and forensic linguistics to personalized language learning. The persistent influence of an author’s L1 on their L2 production manifests in subtle yet systematic linguistic patterns, creating a “textual fingerprint” potentially revealing of their linguistic background. Early work in Native Language Identification (NLI) relied heavily on error analysis, identifying characteristic errors made by speakers of specific L1s when using English as a second language (e.g., Koppel et al., 2005). More recent approaches have largely framed NLI as a classification problem, leveraging machine learning techniques to automatically learn patterns indicative of different L1s. A prevalent feature set in these classification-based approaches consists of character n-grams, part-of-speech (PoS) tag n-grams, and unigrams of function words (Tetreault et al., 2012; van Halteren et al., 2005). These features capture statistical regularities in the use of characters, grammatical structures, and common words, which often differ across languages. While effective, this approach is often limited by the fixed length of the n-grams used. Syntactic analyses suggest that longer-range dependencies and collocations – arrangements of words or PoS tags extending beyond short n-gram windows – can be particularly informative for NLI. For instance, a speaker of Spanish may consistently use a particular verb construction that is less common in English, and this dependency could span several words. To capture these arbitrarily long-range dependencies, we explore the use of adaptor grammars (AGs) – a formalism originally developed in computational linguistics for representing syntactic and semantic information (Pereira and Riley, 1997). Adaptor grammars offer a powerful mechanism for defining and extracting collocations of arbitrary length over a mix of PoS tags and words, effectively extending the capabilities of traditional n-gram-based approaches. The core idea is to define “adaptors” that represent recurring patterns, allowing the AG to efficiently identify instances of these patterns in text. This work investigates the application of AGs to NLI, focusing on the task of learning and utilizing collocations of arbitrary length as features for classifying author L1s. We explore two different approaches to classification: a maximum entropy (maxent) model, which leverages the learned collocations as features in a standard statistical classifier, and an induced syntactic language model, which attempts to integrate the AG-derived knowledge directly into the language modeling process. We also introduce a new, simple baseline method for comparison, and carefully analyze the performance of each approach, shedding light on the strengths and limitations of using adaptor grammars for NLI. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of learned collocations as features in a maxent model, while the performance of the induced syntactic language model is more nuanced.

Semantic understanding of natural language hinges on the ability to accurately identify the meanings of words in context (Word Sense Disambiguation, or WSD) and to determine the semantic relationships between words in a sentence (Semantic Role Labeling, or SRL). These two tasks – WSD and SRL – represent crucial steps towards building truly intelligent natural language processing (NLP) systems. Traditionally, however, these tasks have been treated as largely independent problems, tackled with separate models and pipelines. While significant progress has been made on both fronts individually (Koller et al., 2004; Palmer et al., 2005; Surdeanu et al., 2008), this isolation overlooks a fundamental truth: WSD and SRL are inherently interconnected. The semantic role of a word is often dependent on its specific sense, and conversely, identifying the appropriate sense of a word can be facilitated by understanding its role within the sentence's broader semantic structure. For example, the verb “bank” has multiple senses – a financial institution or the side of a river. Determining whether “bank” is an Agent in a sentence like “The teller deposited the check at the bank” versus a Location in “We sat on the bank of the river” immediately provides strong clues regarding its intended meaning. Similarly, knowing a word is a Patient in a SRL structure can help to narrow down the likely senses in ambiguous scenarios. Previous attempts to leverage these dependencies have largely relied on pipeline architectures, where the output of one task (e.g., WSD) is fed as input to the other (e.g., SRL). While better than treating the tasks in complete isolation, these pipeline approaches suffer from error propagation – errors made in the earlier stages cascade and negatively impact the performance of subsequent stages. They also lack the ability to directly model complex, logical constraints that exist *between* the two tasks. For instance, a specific SRL configuration (e.g., Agent-Verb-Patient) often implies a narrow set of plausible word senses for the verb and its arguments. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel approach that jointly models WSD and SRL within a probabilistic logic framework called Markov Logic (ML) (Richardson & Domingos, 2006). ML combines the expressive power of first-order logic with the probabilistic modeling capabilities of Markov networks, providing a natural and powerful way to represent and reason about the interdependencies between WSD and SRL. By encoding both task-specific knowledge and logical constraints in the ML model, we can perform inference to simultaneously determine the most likely word senses and semantic roles for all words in a sentence. In this work, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this joint ML model on the widely used OntoNotes 3.0 dataset. Our experimental results show that the proposed approach consistently outperforms pipeline-based systems, achieving higher F1-scores for both WSD and SRL. This improvement underscores the benefits of directly modeling the inherent connections between these two foundational NLP tasks. Furthermore, our analysis reveals valuable insights into the types of logical constraints that contribute most significantly to performance gains, paving the way for future research in joint semantic understanding.

Information Retrieval (IR) has long been a cornerstone of accessing and organizing the ever-growing volume of digital information. Traditionally, IR systems heavily relied on lexical matching – determining the relevance of documents to a user’s query based on the shared occurrence of keywords. However, this approach often falls short in capturing the nuanced meaning behind words, frequently leading to issues of synonymy, polysemy, and relatedness. A user searching for “car” may be interested in documents containing “automobile,” “vehicle,” or even specific brands like “Toyota,” none of which would be retrieved by a purely lexical match. Recognizing these limitations, the field has witnessed sustained interest in incorporating lexical semantic knowledge into IR systems. This has manifested in various forms, from query expansion techniques utilizing thesauri to more sophisticated methods leveraging ontologies and semantic networks. The goal remains consistent: to move beyond surface-level matching and understand the underlying *meaning* of both queries and documents. Recently, the landscape of lexical semantic resources has been dramatically altered by the emergence of large-scale, collaboratively constructed knowledge bases, most notably Wikipedia and Wiktionary. These resources, built and maintained by a community of editors, offer a wealth of lexical and semantic information, including definitions, relationships between concepts, and usage examples. Unlike more curated resources like WordNet, which requires expert linguistic annotation, Wikipedia and Wiktionary benefit from their openness and scale, reflecting a broader range of real-world language use. Despite their potential, the optimal manner in which to integrate these new resources into IR pipelines remains an open question. Simply injecting terms from related Wikipedia articles into a query, for instance, may introduce noise and dilute the original intent. A more principled approach requires a deeper understanding of the types of semantic relationships present between query and document terms, and how effectively these relationships can be quantified through measures of semantic relatedness. This paper undertakes a detailed investigation into the semantic relatedness of query and document terms. We analyze the diverse lexical semantic relations revealed within Wikipedia, Wiktionary, and the established resource WordNet, examining how these relations map onto scores derived from semantic relatedness measures. Furthermore, we explore the potential of leveraging these relatedness scores as indicators of document relevance, comparing the performance and characteristics of each knowledge base in a genuine IR context. Our findings aim to illuminate the most promising avenues for harnessing the power of collaborative knowledge bases to enhance the effectiveness of information retrieval systems. Coreference resolution, the task of identifying mentions in text that refer to the same entity, is a fundamental problem in natural language processing with applications ranging from information extraction and question answering to machine translation and summarization. Despite significant progress in recent years (Soon et al., 2001; Bengtson and Kübler, 2004; da Cunha et al., 2006), current coreference systems still struggle with achieving human-level performance, particularly on complex and lengthy documents. A common observation is that many mentions encountered during coreference resolution are *not* anaphoric – that is, they do not refer back to previously introduced entities but rather represent new entities or refer to entities not present in the context. These non-anaphoric mentions present a significant challenge to coreference systems. By incorrectly attempting to link such mentions to existing entities, the system introduces noise and can significantly degrade overall performance. Recent work (Ng and Cardie, 2002; Strubell et al., 2009) has demonstrated that explicitly identifying and filtering these non-anaphoric mentions *prior* to the coreference linking stage can lead to substantial improvements in coreference resolution accuracy. The task of distinguishing between anaphoric and non-anaphoric mentions, therefore, constitutes a crucial pre-processing step for building robust coreference resolution systems. Existing approaches to anaphoricity determination typically rely on machine learning techniques, utilizing features designed to capture syntactic, semantic, and contextual cues (Ng and Cardie, 2002; Strubell et al., 2009). While these approaches have shown promise, they often require careful feature engineering and can be sensitive to the specific training data used. Moreover, they treat anaphoricity determination as a classification problem for each individual mention in isolation, potentially overlooking important relationships between mentions in the surrounding context. In this paper, we present a novel approach to anaphoricity determination based on graph cuts (Boykov and Kolmogorov, 2004). We formulate the problem as a labeling task where each mention is assigned a label indicating whether it is anaphoric or non-anaphoric. The labels are then determined by finding a minimum cut in a graph constructed from the mentions, with edge weights representing the compatibility between assigning specific labels to pairs of mentions. This graph-based formulation allows us to model contextual dependencies between mentions and incorporate global information into the decision process. We demonstrate through experiments on the ACE 2004 data set that our graph-cut-based approach significantly outperforms competing anaphoricity determination methods when integrated into a learning-based coreference system, resulting in improved overall coreference resolution performance ( §3 & §4). We argue that the graph-cut approach's optimization of global coherence leads to more accurate anaphoricity judgements. (§5 concludes the paper with a discussion and outlines future work).

The proliferation of online social platforms has fostered unprecedented opportunities for communication and community building. However, this connectivity comes at a cost: a significant increase in antisocial behaviors, ranging from uncivil discourse to outright harassment and personal attacks (Papacharissi, 2004; Suler, 2004). Moderating these platforms and ensuring a safe and productive environment for users presents a formidable challenge, largely due to the sheer volume of interactions and the nuanced nature of harmful communication. Traditional approaches to detecting antisocial behavior often rely on identifying problematic content *after* it has been posted (e.g., flagging abusive language, identifying threats). While valuable, these reactive methods offer limited opportunities for intervention; once a conversation has descended into negativity, it’s often difficult, if not impossible, to repair the damage. This paper introduces a fundamentally different perspective: proactively predicting whether a conversation will ultimately become toxic, starting from its very inception. We posit that subtle cues present in the initial exchanges of a conversation – the opening lines, the framing of questions, the expression of sentiment – can serve as early warning signals of future conflict. By identifying these signals, we aim to enable timely interventions, potentially allowing moderators or even the participants themselves to steer the conversation toward a more constructive path. This preventative approach represents a significant departure from the post-hoc detection paradigm dominant in the field. Our work centers on the concept of *conversational failure*, defining it as a trajectory toward antisocial behavior characterized by increased negativity, aggression, or uncivil language. We tackle the challenge of predicting this failure by focusing on the pragmatic devices employed by users when initiating a conversation. These devices – including politeness strategies, rhetorical prompts, and framing choices – reveal underlying intentions and establish the initial conversational landscape. We hypothesize that certain combinations of these features predispose a conversation to later deterioration. To investigate this hypothesis, we present a framework for systematically capturing and analyzing these pragmatic features. This framework draws on insights from conversation analysis (Sacks et al., 1974) and pragmatics (Grice, 1975), allowing us to quantify aspects of conversational style that are often overlooked by traditional content-based analysis. We then apply this framework to a controlled experimental setting, demonstrating the feasibility of detecting early warning signs of antisocial behavior with statistically significant accuracy. Our results suggest that leveraging these initial conversational cues offers a promising pathway toward creating more resilient and harmonious online communities. Ultimately, our goal is to move beyond simply *reacting* to harmful behavior and begin *preventing* it by anticipating and addressing the factors that contribute to conversational breakdown. Machine translation (MT) systems have seen remarkable progress in recent years, propelled by advancements in neural network architectures and the availability of increasingly large parallel corpora (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Vaswani et al., 2017). However, the optimization of these systems remains a complex task. A dominant paradigm for system optimization is Minimum Error Rate Training (MERT) (Och, 2003), a technique which seeks to find the system parameters that maximize performance on a designated tuning set, typically as measured by an automatic metric like BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002). While computationally efficient and widely adopted, the inherent limitation of MERT lies in its reliance on automatic metrics as proxies for human judgment. The ultimate evaluation of MT quality, particularly in real-world applications, often incorporates a strong human component. Metrics like adequacy, fluency, and overall quality are frequently assessed by human evaluators, offering a more nuanced and comprehensive assessment than automatic metrics alone. This disconnect between the optimization objective (BLEU maximization) and the eventual evaluation criteria (human judgment) raises a fundamental question: can we directly optimize MT systems with respect to human evaluations? The seemingly obvious solution – performing MERT with human-based metrics – is impractical due to the substantial time and cost associated with obtaining reliable human judgments for each parameter configuration explored during the tuning process. The combinatorial explosion of possibilities in parameter space renders such an approach infeasible. This paper investigates a novel approach to bridge this gap, leveraging the benefits of human evaluation without the prohibitive expense of real-time human input during tuning. We introduce RYPT, a novel metric designed to incorporate human preferences without requiring human intervention during the MERT process itself. RYPT operates by constructing a reusable database of human judgments, gathered from a preliminary analysis of translation candidates. This database then allows for efficient estimation of human preference for candidates generated during MERT, effectively sidestepping the need for constant human feedback. The core idea is that human preferences, while subjective, exhibit underlying patterns that allow for generalization to unseen translations. Beyond the introduction of RYPT, we present an in-depth analysis of the behavior of MERT itself, specifically focusing on the diversity (or lack thereof) in the candidate translations it generates. We demonstrate that MERT often produces a surprisingly redundant set of candidates, a phenomenon we exploit to improve the efficiency and reliability of RYPT. Our experiments reveal that RYPT demonstrably outperforms BLEU in its correlation with human judgements of translation quality, suggesting that it provides a more accurate signal for system optimization. This work represents a significant step towards aligning MT system optimization with the ultimate goal of producing translations that are favorably received by human users. Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) has seen remarkable progress in recent years, largely driven by advances in modeling techniques and the availability of increasingly large parallel corpora. Log-linear models, a dominant paradigm in modern SMT, represent translation as a probabilistic function conditioned on a set of features, offering flexibility and expressiveness. However, the initial parameter estimation within these models – typically Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) – often optimizes for likelihood rather than directly for translation quality as measured by metrics like BLEU. This discrepancy motivates the use of discriminative training methods, which aim to directly optimize a desired evaluation metric. Early work in discriminative training for SMT focused on Minimum Error Rate Training (MERT) (Och and Ney, 2002), a widely adopted approach that searches for optimal feature weights by minimizing errors on a development set. While effective, MERT often suffers from computational expense and sensitivity to the quality of the development set. More recent advancements, such as the work by He and Deng (2012), have explored more efficient and scalable discriminative training algorithms based on stochastic gradient descent. These methods offer advantages in terms of speed and the ability to incorporate larger feature sets. Despite these advancements, a significant limitation has persisted: the scale of parameters that can be effectively trained discriminatively has remained relatively constrained. Previous efforts have typically focused on tuning the weights of a limited number of features – often in the hundreds or low thousands – or training features with a comparatively small number of parameters. This limitation stems from the computational complexity of discriminative training, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional parameter spaces and large datasets. In this paper, we address this limitation by proposing a method to substantially scale up discriminative training for log-linear SMT models. Specifically, we demonstrate the feasibility of training features with 150 million parameters – an order of magnitude larger than previously reported in the literature. This significant increase in model capacity opens up new possibilities for capturing complex relationships between source and target language features and potentially improving translation quality. Furthermore, we explore a novel application of discriminative training in the context of model pruning. Pruning, a technique used to reduce model size and computational cost, often involves removing parameters deemed less important, which can lead to a degradation in translation performance. Our experimental results, conducted on the NIST MT06 dataset over a strong baseline system, confirm the effectiveness of our proposed approach. Analyzing and Inferring the Intentions of Vulgar Expressions **Introduction** The use of vulgar language is a ubiquitous feature of human communication, yet its function remains surprisingly complex and poorly understood, particularly from a computational perspective. While often dismissed as simply “bad” language, vulgar expressions – commonly referred to as swear words, profanity, or obscenities – serve a diverse range of pragmatic functions extending far beyond mere aggression or offense. They can signal informality, establish in-group solidarity, express emotional intensity, provide comic relief, and even function as linguistic fillers (Jay, 2002; Pinker, 2007). This multifaceted nature presents a significant challenge for Natural Language Processing (NLP) systems. A system that encounters a swear word cannot simply categorize it as negative or offensive, but must instead grapple with the nuanced intention behind its use—an intention heavily dependent on context and social dynamics. Existing research in computational linguistics has largely treated vulgarity as a signal of toxicity, focusing primarily on its detection in contexts like hate speech, cyberbullying, and online abuse (Davidson et al., 2017; Nobata et al., 2016). While critical, this perspective overlooks the broader spectrum of pragmatic functions fulfilled by vulgar expressions. A failure to accurately discern these functions can lead to misinterpretations, biased downstream applications, and a limited understanding of the social forces at play in online discourse. For example, a seemingly offensive tweet might, in reality, be a sarcastic expression of solidarity amongst friends, or a playful jab devoid of malicious intent. Furthermore, the variability in perceived offensiveness, cultural context, and even individual sensitivity further complicates the matter. What might be considered innocuous in one setting could be deeply offensive in another. Understanding these nuances is crucial for building robust and socially aware NLP systems. This paper addresses the gap in understanding the pragmatic aspects of vulgarity by presenting the first quantitative analysis of vulgar word use, facilitated by a novel, carefully annotated dataset. We introduce a dataset of 7,800 tweets, constructed from users with known demographic traits, where instances of vulgar words are annotated with one of six distinct categories representing their intended function. Using this dataset, we provide a detailed exploratory analysis of how these functions relate to social factors. We then develop a machine learning model capable of predicting the category of a vulgar word based on its surrounding context, achieving a promising 67.4% macro F1-score across all six categories. Finally, we demonstrate the practical utility of modeling vulgarity’s intended use by integrating this information into a hate speech detection task, achieving state-of-the-art performance on a benchmark dataset. Our work contributes a novel dataset, a comprehensive analysis of vulgar pragmatics, and a practical demonstration of the benefits of incorporating this understanding into downstream NLP applications. Phrase-based statistical machine translation (PB-SMT) has, for over a decade, remained the dominant paradigm for high-quality machine translation. Despite substantial advances in modeling techniques – including sophisticated language models (Chelba & Jelinek, 1998) and distortion models (Tillmann et al., 2004) – a fundamental limitation persists: the reliance on discrete representations of words and phrases, and the associated challenges of data sparsity. Traditional PB-SMT systems estimate translation probabilities by counting occurrences of phrase pairs in parallel corpora. When phrase pairs are infrequently observed, or entirely absent, the resulting probability estimates are unreliable, leading to degraded translation quality. This problem is exacerbated when considering broader contextual information, as the number of possible contexts grows exponentially with the phrase length, further compounding the data sparsity issue. Existing approaches to address this sparsity often involve smoothing techniques (Koehn et al., 2003) or back-off models, which redistribute probability mass from observed phrases to unseen ones. While effective to a degree, these methods can only partially mitigate the underlying problem. Another direction has focused on leveraging monolingual data to augment the parallel training data (Popović, 2015), but this approach is computationally expensive and requires careful handling of noise and domain mismatch. In this paper, we explore an alternative approach rooted in continuous space representations of translation units. Instead of treating phrases as discrete entities, we map them to continuous vectors in a high-dimensional space, where similarity reflects semantic relatedness. By estimating translation probabilities in this continuous space, we can effectively generalize beyond observed phrase pairs, leveraging the underlying semantic structure of the languages involved. This allows us to utilize information from a much larger set of related phrases, effectively addressing the data sparsity problem. Previous work in continuous space translation modeling has explored various techniques, including centering word embeddings (Mihalcea et al., 2006) and distributional semantic models (Clark et al., 2011). However, scaling these techniques to the large vocabulary sizes and complex relationships inherent in natural language translation remains a challenge. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel framework employing a multi-layer neural network with a Simplified Orthogonal Unit Layer (SOUL) architecture (Glorot & Bengio, 2011). This architecture enables the efficient joint learning of continuous representations and translation probabilities, even for very large phrase sets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through comprehensive experiments in both small-scale and large-scale English-to-French translation tasks. By integrating our continuous space translation models on top of a strong n-gram translation system, we achieve significant improvements in translation performance, demonstrating the benefit of leveraging continuous representations for capturing nuanced semantic relationships and mitigating the limitations of traditional discrete phrase-based models. This work represents a step towards more robust and data-efficient machine translation systems, capable of handling the complexities of real-world language data.

Relation extraction (RE) aims to identify semantic relationships between entities mentioned in text. It is a core task in natural language processing (NLP) with applications in knowledge base construction, question answering, and information retrieval. Traditional RE approaches rely on manually annotated datasets, which are expensive and time-consuming to create. Distantly supervised relation extraction (DS-RE) offers a promising alternative by leveraging existing knowledge bases (KBs) to automatically generate training data. However, DS-RE suffers from a significant challenge: noisy labels. Due to the many-to-one mapping between entities and relations in KBs, distantly supervised instances often contain false positives, where sentences are incorrectly labeled with a relation. A crucial component of effective DS-RE systems is the ability to distinguish valid instances (sentences truly expressing the target relation) from noisy ones. Attention mechanisms have become a popular tool for this purpose. By selectively focusing on informative parts of the input sentence, attention models can learn to assign higher weights to valid instances and lower weights to noisy ones. Existing approaches largely employ 1-dimensional (1-D) vector-based attention mechanisms, which operate on word embeddings or hidden states to calculate attention weights. While effective to a degree, these traditional attention models often struggle to capture the complex contextual interactions necessary for accurately identifying valid instances. They treat the sentence as a linear sequence, potentially overlooking crucial relationships between different parts of the sentence relating to the two entities of interest. To address this limitation, we propose a novel multi-level structured self-attention mechanism for DS-RE. Our approach departs from the conventional 1-D attention framework by leveraging 2-dimensional (2-D) matrix-based self-attention. This allows us to capture a richer representation of contextual information by modeling relationships between all pairs of words within the sentence, enabling a more nuanced understanding of the arguments surrounding the entity pair. We integrate this mechanism within a multi-instance learning (MIL) framework, recognizing that each sentence can be considered a bag of instances, and the model must learn to identify the most relevant instances within each bag. Specifically, we introduce two levels of structured self-attention. The first, a word-level attention mechanism, learns a 2-D matrix where each row represents a weight distribution reflecting the importance of different aspects of the instance concerning the two target entities. This allows the model to attend to specific words or phrases that contribute most to expressing the relation. The second level, sentence-level attention, further addresses the MIL challenge by discerning which sentences (instances) are likely to be valid. It also learns a 2-D matrix where each row denotes a weight distribution over the selection of different valid instances. By modeling attention at both word and sentence levels, our framework provides a more comprehensive and effective approach to handling noisy labels in DS-RE. We evaluate our proposed framework on two publicly available datasets commonly used for DS-RE. Experimental results demonstrate that our multi-level structured self-attention mechanism significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving substantial improvements in PR curves, P@N, and F1 measures. These findings highlight the efficacy of our approach in discerning valid instances from noise and extracting accurate relations from distantly supervised data.

The demand for cross-lingual natural language processing (NLP) capabilities has grown exponentially with the increasing globalization of information. Tasks such as machine translation, cross-lingual information retrieval, and multilingual sentiment analysis all require robust methods for representing text in different languages within a shared vector space – effectively, creating high-quality bilingual (or multilingual) embeddings. Traditional approaches to learning such embeddings rely heavily on parallel corpora, where sentences in different languages are direct translations of one another. However, the scarcity of high-quality parallel data for many language pairs makes this a significant bottleneck. Recent work has explored leveraging weakly supervised signals to bridge the gap between languages, including dictionary-based methods and techniques utilizing comparable corpora. However, these approaches are often limited in their ability to capture the nuanced semantic relationships that exist across languages. A particularly promising avenue has emerged through the use of images as an interlingual bridge. Images provide a modality grounded in real-world perception, offering a shared semantic space accessible regardless of linguistic differences. The intuition is clear: if a concept is depicted in an image and described in multiple languages, that image can serve as a common anchor for aligning the corresponding text embeddings. However, simply concatenating image features with text embeddings often proves insufficient. The inherent differences in dimensionality and representational power between visual and textual data necessitate more sophisticated alignment strategies. Existing methods often employ linear transformations to project the different modalities into a common space, but these linear approaches may fail to capture the complex, non-linear relationships present in natural language and visual data. In this work, we introduce a novel deep learning approach, grounded in the principles of Partial Canonical Correlation Analysis (PCCA), to effectively align bilingual text embeddings using image information. PCCA seeks to find projections of two variables that maximize their correlation while controlling for the influence of a third, shared variable. While originally formulated for linear projections, we extend this framework to a non-linear setting with Deep PCCA (DPCCA), leveraging the representational power of deep neural networks. Crucially, we also develop a novel stochastic iterative algorithm for optimizing this DPCCA model, addressing the challenges associated with training such a complex architecture. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on both multilingual word similarity and cross-lingual image description retrieval tasks. Notably, our models consistently outperform a wide range of previous methods, even without access to any visual information during test-time inference – highlighting the quality of the learned cross-lingual representation. Our results demonstrate the power of DPCCA as a principled and effective method for bridging languages through the shared semantic space provided by images. That is the introduction!
