Machine translation (MT) evaluation remains a central challenge in natural language processing. While automatic metrics have become indispensable for rapid development and comparison of MT systems, their correlation with human judgments is often imperfect (Papineni et al., 2002; Lin & Och, 2004; Chiang, 2007). Traditional metrics, such as BLEU, METEOR, and TER, largely focus on n-gram overlap between the machine-generated translation and one or more human reference translations. These metrics, though computationally efficient and widely adopted, often fail to capture important aspects of translation quality, such as fluency, adequacy, and discourse coherence. A translation can achieve high n-gram overlap scores and still be disfluent or misrepresent the meaning of the source text, particularly in cases where the stylistic or rhetorical structure differs substantially. The limitations of n-gram-based metrics have motivated research into alternative evaluation approaches. Some studies have explored incorporating syntactic information (Owczarek et al., 2007; Popović & Ney, 2015), semantic similarity (Liu et al., 2014), or adequacy features (Conroy et al., 2018). However, a crucial aspect of text quality that remains largely underexplored in MT evaluation is *discourse structure*. Discourse structure refers to the way sentences in a text are organized to convey meaning, reflecting relationships such as cause-effect, contrast, and elaboration. A good translation should not only be accurate at the sentence level, but also preserve the discourse relations present in the source text. Failing to maintain discourse coherence can render a translation confusing or unnatural, even if individual sentences are grammatically correct. This paper investigates the use of discourse structure for improving machine translation evaluation. We hypothesize that leveraging discourse information can provide a more nuanced assessment of translation quality, capturing aspects of coherence that are missed by traditional metrics. The World Wide Web represents an unparalleled repository of human knowledge, interconnected through a vast network of hyperlinks. These hyperlinks, and crucially, the *anchor text* associated with them, serve as vital navigational cues for users and are fundamental to the Web’s organization and usability. While traditionally authored by humans, the sheer scale of the Web necessitates exploration into automated methods for hyperlink creation and, specifically, anchor text generation. Poorly chosen or generic anchor text (e.g., "click here") diminishes the information value of hyperlinks, hindering both user experience and search engine optimization. Existing approaches to automatic anchor text generation often rely on analyzing the content of the target document – the document being linked *to* – to identify salient keywords or phrases. However, these methods frequently overlook the crucial contextual relationship between the source document – the document *from* which the link originates – and the target document. A truly effective anchor text should not only describe the target document's content but also *why* that document is relevant to the reader within the context of the source document. This paper introduces a novel approach to automatic anchor text creation that addresses this limitation by leveraging the concept of *localized similarity*. Instead of solely focusing on the target document, our method explicitly measures the similarity between different parts (segments, phrases, or sentences) of the source document and the entirety of the target document. We hypothesize that the sections of the source document most similar to the target document represent the most appropriate context for a hyperlink, and thus, should inform the construction of the anchor text. Our approach departs from traditional information retrieval paradigms by focusing on identifying granular, localized relationships rather than assessing overall document similarity. We adapt and evaluate a range of established techniques from the fields of information retrieval and natural language processing – including vector space models, term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF), and semantic similarity measures – to rank segments within the source document based on their relevance to the target. These rankings are then used to automatically extract and formulate the anchor text. We contrasted automatically generated anchor texts against the original anchor texts present in a real-world web corpus. Crucially, we also leveraged crowdsourcing to obtain independent judgments of the quality of both the original and automatically generated anchors, providing a nuanced understanding of their respective strengths and weaknesses. Relation extraction (RE) – the task of identifying semantic relationships between entities mentioned in text – is a core component of many information extraction (IE) systems and a crucial step towards truly understanding natural language. Traditionally, RE systems have relied heavily on supervised learning techniques, training models on manually annotated corpora like ACE (Automatic Content Extraction) (Voorhees and Mitchell, 1999). While these supervised approaches have achieved impressive performance on benchmark datasets, they suffer from significant limitations. Constructing such labeled datasets is a costly, time-consuming, and domain-specific process. The domain dependence of these datasets restricts the generalization ability of learned models to new domains or relation types. Consequently, the need for methods capable of effectively extracting relations without relying on extensive hand-labeled data is paramount. This paper addresses this challenge by exploring a novel paradigm for relation extraction: distant supervision. Our approach leverages the vast amount of knowledge contained within large semantic databases, specifically Freebase (Bollacker et al., 2008), to automatically generate training data. Rather than requiring manual labeling, we exploit existing knowledge triples in Freebase – representing relationships between entities – as a source of weak supervision. For instance, if Freebase states that ‘Barack Obama’ *born_in* ‘Honolulu’, we automatically identify all sentences in a large, unlabeled corpus that mention both ‘Barack Obama’ and ‘Honolulu’ and consider those sentences as potential instances of the *born_in* relation. This line of work builds upon and contrasts with previous approaches to relation extraction. Supervised IE systems, while accurate when provided with sufficient labeled data, struggle with scalability and domain adaptation. Unsupervised IE methods (e.g., Hearst, 1998) can identify relations without labeled examples, but often suffer from low precision and difficulty in identifying nuanced relationships. Our distant supervision method aims to bridge the gap between these two paradigms, combining the strengths of both. We leverage the power of probabilistic classification, similar to supervised IE, but train our classifiers on automatically generated, noisy data derived from a large knowledge source. This allows us to extract a substantial number of relations from corpora of any size and domain, exceeding the scope of traditional, manually annotated datasets. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. Utilizing Freebase, and applying our distant supervision methodology to a large unlabeled corpus, we are able to extract over 10,000 instances of 102 distinct relations with a precision of 67.6%. Furthermore, we perform a detailed analysis of feature performance, revealing that syntactic parse features are particularly valuable for identifying relations that are either expressed ambiguously or involve considerable lexical distance between the participating entities. The key contribution of this work lies in demonstrating a viable path towards large-scale, domain-independent relation extraction, reducing the reliance on laborious manual annotation and unlocking the wealth of relational knowledge hidden within unstructured text. In the following sections, we will detail our distant supervision approach, describe the features utilized in our relation classifier, present experimental results and analysis, and discuss future research directions.

Statistical machine translation (SMT) has remained a dominant paradigm in machine translation for over two decades, achieving significant progress through increasingly sophisticated models of source and target language distributions and their alignment (Koehn et al., 2003; Och & Ney, 2003). Traditionally, phrase-based SMT models have been highly successful, decomposing sentences into segments, or “phrases”, and learning translation probabilities between them. However, these models often struggle with long-distance dependencies and non-contiguous phrase alignment, particularly in language pairs with significantly different syntactic structures. This limitation stems from the fundamental assumption that translations are built from contiguous segments of the source sentence. More recently, tree-based machine translation models have emerged as a promising alternative. These models leverage syntactic structure to improve translation quality by operating directly on parse trees, explicitly capturing hierarchical relationships within sentences (Knight & Graehl, 1997; Chiang, 2005). Tree sequence models, in particular, represent a sentence as a sequence of contiguous subtrees, allowing for more flexible alignment compared to phrase-based models. These models effectively permit the violation of syntactic boundaries, capturing aspects of meaning not directly represented by the syntactic parse. This allows the model to capture non-syntactic phrases or idioms that might be missed by strict syntactic alignment. Despite the improvements offered by tree sequence models, a core limitation persists: the requirement for contiguity. Many natural language phenomena involve non-contiguous phrase alignments, where elements of the source and target sentences are separated by intervening material. Handling such cases effectively necessitates allowing gaps within the tree sequence. For instance, consider a sentence where an adverbial phrase is moved from an immediate position after a verb to the beginning of the sentence for emphasis. Accurate translation requires recognizing the relationship between the verb and the moved adverb, despite their separation. This paper addresses this limitation by introducing a novel statistical machine translation model based on *non-contiguous* tree sequence alignment. Unlike contiguous tree sequence models, our approach explicitly models sequences of subtrees *and* gaps, providing a mechanism for capturing long-distance dependencies and accurately translating non-contiguous phrases, regardless of the size of the gaps between constituent elements. We propose a decoding algorithm targeted specifically for non-contiguous constituent decoding, enabling efficient search through the expanded space of possible translations. The key contribution is therefore the explicit representation and modeling of gaps within tree sequences, facilitating improved alignment and translation of non-contiguous phrases. We present experimental results on the NIST MT-05 Chinese-English translation task, demonstrating that our model statistically significantly outperforms strong baseline systems, showcasing the effectiveness of non-contiguous tree sequence alignment for statistical machine translation. Document-level sentiment classification – the task of determining the overall sentiment expressed within a longer piece of text, such as a review or article – remains a significant challenge in natural language processing. While traditional approaches relied heavily on hand-crafted features and lexicons (Turney & Pang, 2002; Wilson et al., 2005), recent advances in deep learning, particularly recurrent neural networks (RNNs), have demonstrated substantial improvements by automatically learning relevant features from data (Socher et al., 2013; Kim, 2014). Among RNN variants, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) have become particularly popular due to their ability to mitigate the vanishing gradient problem and effectively capture long-range dependencies in sequential data. However, despite the success of LSTMs, scaling them to handle long documents remains problematic. The core limitation lies in the LSTM’s memory cell, which, even with its gating mechanisms, struggles to retain crucial sentiment-bearing information across extended contexts. As the input sequence grows, early information can be “forgotten” or diluted, leading to a loss of overall semantic understanding and diminished classification performance. This is especially true for document-level sentiment, where nuanced expressions and contextual cues dispersed throughout the text can significantly influence the overall sentiment. Existing strategies to address this issue include techniques like hierarchical attention networks (Yang et al., 2016) which decompose the document into smaller units, and employing truncated backpropagation through time. While these methods offer improvements, they often introduce added complexity or fail to fully preserve the complete semantic flow within the entire document. Furthermore, simply increasing the hidden state size can lead to increased computational cost and overfitting. In this paper, we introduce a novel architecture – Cached Long Short-Term Memory networks (CLSTM) – designed specifically to improve the modeling of long-range dependencies in document-level sentiment classification. Inspired by the concept of caching in computer science, CLSTM incorporates a novel memory division strategy within each LSTM unit. We divide the memory cell into multiple groups, each assigned a distinct forgetting rate. This allows the network to selectively retain different types of sentiment information over varying timescales. Specifically, groups with slower forgetting rates can preserve broader contextual cues, while those with faster rates can focus on more immediate sentiment signals. Our experimental results on three publicly available document-level sentiment analysis datasets demonstrate that CLSTM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models, including standard LSTMs and other recent deep learning approaches. This performance gain highlights the effectiveness of our caching mechanism in capturing and leveraging the overall semantic information present in long documents, ultimately leading to more accurate sentiment predictions. Distributed representations, learned through neural networks, have proven remarkably effective in capturing semantic information about words and phrases, and increasingly, about relations between entities. This has spurred significant work in learning distributed representations for relation *instances* – specifically, representations of individual facts or relationships as they appear in text, rather than the relation type itself. However, a primary challenge in developing robust relational representations lies in effectively modeling the *patterns* that define those relationships. Relations aren't simply a connection between two entities; they manifest through diverse linguistic constructions. For example, the relationship “employed_by” can be expressed through a wide range of patterns such as "X works at Y", "Y is X's employer", or "X is an employee of Y". Capturing the nuances of these patterns and their influence on the overall relation instance representation is critical for performance. Existing approaches often treat relations as monolithic entities or rely on limited contextual information, failing to adequately capture the intricate semantics embedded within the relational patterns themselves. To address this gap, this paper focuses on building and utilizing distributed representations specifically designed to encode and compose information from these relational patterns. Through this work, we aim to contribute to a deeper understanding of how to effectively model and leverage relational patterns for enhanced semantic representation learning. Humans effortlessly interpret visual scenes by recognizing the actors, objects, and their relationships within a given situation. Replicating this capability in machines requires moving beyond object recognition towards a deeper semantic understanding, specifically identifying *who* did *what* to *whom*, a process formalized as Semantic Role Labeling (SRL). While SRL has been extensively studied in the realm of natural language, its application to visual data – visual Semantic Role Labeling (vSRL) – remains a significantly more difficult and largely unexplored problem. Existing approaches to vSRL have been hampered by the scarcity of directly annotated visual data. Obtaining precise, pixel-level annotations mapping semantic roles to image regions is a laborious and expensive undertaking. This has limited the development of robust and scalable vSRL models. Prior work often relies on weak supervision, or leverages specialized datasets focused on limited actions and scenes. These limitations motivate the search for alternative approaches that can learn effectively with less reliance on exhaustive manual annotation. The organization of knowledge into hierarchical taxonomies—structures representing “is-a” relationships between concepts—is fundamental to human cognition and crucial for a wide range of natural language processing applications. From information retrieval and knowledge base construction to question answering and machine reasoning, effective concept taxonomies enable machines to understand the world in a manner akin to humans. Traditionally, these taxonomies, such as WordNet (Miller, 1995), have been painstakingly constructed by lexicographers and domain experts, a process that is both time-consuming and expensive. Consequently, there has been burgeoning interest in the automatic induction of concept taxonomies from readily available data sources. Early approaches to taxonomy induction primarily focused on leveraging the rich relational information embedded within large text corpora (Lin, 1998; Hearst, 1998; Snow et al., 2005). These methods typically rely on distributional semantics – the principle that words appearing in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings – to identify hypernymy (is-a) relations. For example, Hearst’s patterns (Hearst, 1998) exploit syntactic clues like "X, such as Y and Z" to infer that X is a hypernym of Y and Z. More recently, research has explored utilizing structured knowledge resources like Wikipedia (Moldovan and Novischi, 2006; Navigli et al., 2011) and other ontologies for bootstrapping and refining taxonomy induction processes. However, a significant limitation of prior work is its reliance almost exclusively on textual data. In the real world, our understanding of concepts is rarely formed through text alone. Vision plays an equally, if not more, important role. The visual appearance of an object or entity provides crucial perceptual information that complements and often clarifies textual descriptions. Consider the concepts “canine” and “feline”; while textual definitions can distinguish them, visual features – shape, size, texture – often provide more immediate and intuitive understanding. The burgeoning availability of large-scale image datasets alongside textual descriptions creates a unique opportunity to leverage multi-modal data for improved taxonomy induction. This paper addresses this gap by proposing a novel probabilistic model for learning concept taxonomies from both text *and* images. Our approach explicitly incorporates visual semantics into the taxonomy induction process and, critically, avoids the need for laborious feature engineering. We utilize pre-trained distributed representations of both images and words – specifically, embeddings learned through deep neural networks – as end-to-end features, allowing the model to automatically capture relevant visual and textual characteristics. Further, our model is designed to be discriminatively trained, requiring only a small number of existing ontologies as supervision to build full taxonomies from scratch for collections of unseen conceptual label items, each associated with an image. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive evaluations on the widely-used WordNet hierarchies. Our results significantly outperform prior taxonomy induction methods, showcasing the benefit of jointly leveraging textual and visual information. This work represents a substantial step towards building more comprehensive and accurate concept taxonomies, paving the way for more robust and human-aligned NLP systems.

Semantic parsing – the task of mapping natural language sentences to formal meaning representations – has emerged as a critical component in a wide range of applications, including question answering, dialogue systems, and program synthesis (Zettlemoyer & Collins, 2005; Wong & Mooney, 2006; Popović et al., 2015). Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG) (Steedman, 2000) provides a powerful and mathematically elegant framework for semantic parsing, offering a compositional approach to building meaning representations from syntactic structure. However, a significant bottleneck in building practical CCG-based semantic parsers remains the creation of a comprehensive and accurate lexicon, which dictates how words and phrases combine with logical forms. Traditional CCG lexicons enumerate lexical items that map words to syntactic categories and associated semantic content. This approach, while conceptually straightforward, can become unwieldy and inefficient, especially when dealing with large vocabularies and polysemous words. A single word can appear with multiple senses and a range of syntactic behaviors, requiring a potentially exponential number of lexical entries. Furthermore, many words share systematic relationships in their semantic and syntactic behavior - for instance, verbs of buying and selling share a similar argument structure but differ in the roles assigned to their arguments. Representing these regularities requires explicit duplication of information within a traditional lexicon. To address these limitations, we introduce the concept of *factored lexicons* for CCG grammar induction. Unlike traditional lexicons, factored lexicons decompose lexical entries into two key components: *lexemes* and *templates*. Lexemes capture the core meaning of a word, representing its inherent semantic properties. Templates, on the other hand, model the systematic variations in word usage, capturing how a lexeme manifests in different syntactic contexts and associated semantic roles. This factorization allows for a more compact and generalizable lexicon, reducing redundancy and promoting knowledge sharing. In this paper, we present a novel algorithm for learning factored CCG lexicons directly from sentence-meaning pairs. This algorithm aims to automatically discover both the underlying lexemes and the appropriate templates for each word in the vocabulary. Alongside the lexicon induction method, we also introduce a probabilistic parse-selection model, which effectively combines the output of the CCG parser with the learned lexical probabilities and semantic representations. The key innovation lies in the synergistic effect between the factored lexicon and the parse-selection model – the reduced lexicon complexity facilitates more robust generalization, while the probabilistic model ensures accurate parsing in the face of ambiguity. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark semantic parsing datasets, demonstrating that the learned factored lexicons lead to highly accurate parsers. Notably, we observe significant improvements in generalization performance, particularly for unseen words and novel syntactic constructions. These results suggest that factoring the lexicon effectively captures the underlying regularities in language, enabling the parser to generalize more effectively to new input. This work marks a crucial step towards building more scalable and robust CCG-based semantic parsers with minimal manual effort.

The ability to generate coherent and contextually relevant text is a cornerstone of natural language processing, with applications ranging from machine translation to dialogue systems. However, many real-world generation tasks require conditioning on more than just prior textual input. This is particularly true when dealing with structured data – a common scenario in tasks like data-to-text generation, image captioning, and, as we address in this work, code generation. In these cases, effectively integrating both unstructured (e.g., natural language descriptions) and structured (e.g., database schemas, API definitions) inputs poses a significant challenge. Existing approaches to conditional generation often rely on concatenating structured and unstructured inputs, or employing separate encoders for each modality followed by a fusion mechanism. While these methods can be effective, they often struggle to scale to a large number of input features or complex structured representations. Furthermore, they frequently make strong assumptions about the relevance of each input feature, potentially hindering performance if irrelevant or noisy information is included. For example, in code generation, effectively utilizing a natural language description alongside a formal specification like a set of API calls requires carefully weighting the contribution of each. A key limitation of many current methods is the lack of a principled mechanism for determining *which* elements of the input context are most important at each step of the generation process, and at *what granularity* this context should be considered. Should we condition on the entire input specification at each token generation step, or focus only on a subset relevant to the current partial output? Should we operate at the character level, the token level, or some intermediate representation? Manually engineering these decisions is often brittle and task-specific. To address these challenges, we introduce Latent Predictor Networks (LPNs), a novel neural network architecture designed for generating sequences conditioned on an arbitrary number of input functions. Multi-document summarization (MDS) aims to condense information from a collection of texts into a concise and coherent summary. This task has gained significant attention due to the exponential growth of online information and the need for efficient information access. Traditional approaches to MDS often rely on generic features like term frequency, sentence position, and cue phrase identification to determine the importance of sentences for inclusion in the summary (Mani, 2001; Nenkova & McKeown, 2012). However, these methods often fail to capture the nuanced relationships between documents within a specific context or domain. Consider, for instance, a collection of news articles about “financial markets” versus a collection about “sports.” The salient information and the relative importance of different concepts will vary drastically between these two categories. This paper argues that leveraging category-specific information significantly enhances the quality of multi-document summaries. We introduce the concept of *category-specific importance (CSI)*, which refers to the degree to which a sentence contributes to the central theme or key aspects of a document set *given its category*. Our central hypothesis is that sentences intrinsically relevant to a category, as evidenced by their linguistic characteristics within that category, are more likely to be informative and therefore valuable for inclusion in a summary. A primary challenge in exploiting CSI is the need for labeled data—specifically, knowledge of which documents belong to which categories. While some datasets provide this information, many real-world scenarios do not. Therefore, we explore methods for computing CSI without relying on manually curated document-to-category mappings. We propose two novel features, computable solely from the document collection itself, that effectively capture CSI. These features enable the identification of sentences that are statistically representative of the category based on their word usage and contextual relationships. Furthermore, we demonstrate that even *automatically* assigning documents to categories—through the application of text categorization techniques—can yield performance improvements. This indicates that even approximate category awareness is beneficial for MDS, confirming the robustness of the CSI concept. To facilitate reproducibility and further research, we have integrated these features into SWING, a simple yet powerful, freely available, open-source extractive summarization system. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through rigorous evaluation on the challenging TAC-2011 guided summarization task. Remarkably, SWING, incorporating our CSI features, outperformed all other participant systems in the task, as measured by standard ROUGE evaluation metrics. This result underscores the practical impact of leveraging category-specific knowledge for improved multi-document summarization. This work contributes a novel perspective on MDS, emphasizing the importance of contextual understanding and category-specific information. We believe this approach represents a significant step towards building more intelligent and effective summarization systems capable of handling the complexities of real-world information landscapes. The demand for efficient natural language processing (NLP) tools continues to grow alongside the increasing availability of textual data and the complexity of NLP tasks. Parsing, a fundamental component of many NLP pipelines, remains a computational bottleneck, particularly for high-quality, broad-coverage grammars. Traditional parsing algorithms, often designed for sequential processing, struggle to leverage the massive parallelism offered by modern hardware. In recent years, graphics processing units (GPUs) have emerged as a promising platform for accelerating NLP tasks, due to their inherent architectural advantages for parallel computation. However, effectively harnessing the power of GPUs for NLP algorithms presents unique challenges. GPUs were originally designed for computer graphics, thriving on “dense” problems – those where the same operation is applied uniformly across large datasets. Many core NLP algorithms, though, are built upon principles of “sparsity.” This sparsity arises from the inherent structure of language; not all words relate to all other words, and grammatical rules are rarely universally applicable. Consequently, directly porting traditional NLP algorithms to GPUs can result in inefficiencies, as significant computational resources may be wasted on irrelevant operations. Canny et al. (2013) addressed this challenge with an innovative approach to GPU parsing that intentionally embraced density. Their system sacrificed traditional sparsity, effectively computing parses for all possible combinations, and then relied on the GPU’s raw computational power to achieve impressive throughput – approximately 164 sentences per second using a mid-range GPU and a high-quality probabilistic context-free grammar. While a significant accomplishment, this approach comes at a cost: increased memory usage and potentially wasted computation. In this work, we revisit the problem of GPU parsing, arguing that a thoughtful reintroduction of sparsity can yield substantial performance gains. We present a novel system that adapts a coarse-to-fine pruning strategy – a technique commonly employed in traditional parsers to reduce the search space – to the specific constraints and capabilities of GPU architecture. By strategically eliminating unlikely parse candidates early in the process, we significantly reduce the overall computational burden. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, achieving a throughput of over 404 Viterbi parses per second on the same hardware used by Canny et al. (2013) – more than a 2x speedup. Furthermore, our pruning strategy enables the efficient implementation of minimum Bayes risk (MBR) inference, a more accurate but computationally expensive parsing algorithm. We demonstrate a nearly 6x speedup for MBR parsing, increasing its throughput from 32 sentences per second (unpruned) to over 190 sentences per second with pruning. These results highlight the potential for combining the strengths of both sparsity and parallelism to create faster and more efficient GPU parsing systems, paving the way for more sophisticated and scalable NLP applications. The automatic identification and correction of spelling errors is a long-standing problem in Natural Language Processing with applications ranging from text editors and search engines to accessibility tools and machine translation pre-processing. Traditionally, spellchecking and autocorrection systems rely heavily on expertly crafted lexicons, manually annotated error models, and language-specific rules (Briscoe & Horowitz, 1998; Hulme & Doherty, 2010). While these systems often achieve high accuracy, their development and maintenance are costly, requiring significant linguistic expertise and ongoing effort. Moreover, adaptation to new languages necessitates substantial investment in resource creation, hindering the rapid deployment of spellchecking capabilities for less-resourced languages. The proliferation of text data on the World Wide Web presents a potentially valuable, albeit noisy, resource for building spellchecking systems. The sheer scale of the web offers an unparalleled corpus of real-world language usage, implicitly capturing common misspellings and typical word sequences. Leveraging this resource circumvent the need for expensive manual annotation, opening the door to language-independent and rapidly deployable spellchecking solutions. Previous attempts to utilize the web for language modelling have largely focused on constructing large n-gram language models (LM) (Brants & Franz, 2006; Peterson, 2009). These LMs can be used to assess the probability of a word sequence, providing a valuable signal for identifying and correcting spelling errors. However, directly applying web-derived LMs to spellchecking can be challenging due to the inherent noise and inconsistencies present in web data. Moreover, distinguishing genuine misspellings from rare but legitimate words requires a robust error model capable of identifying patterns indicative of incorrect usage. In this paper, we present an end-to-end spellchecking and autocorrection system that is explicitly designed to harness the power of the web without relying on manually annotated training data. Our approach involves constructing both an error model and an n-gram language model from web-crawled text. The error model learns patterns of common misspellings, exploiting the co-occurrence of correctly spelled words and their frequent errors on the web. The language model captures general word usage patterns, aiding in the selection of appropriate correction candidates. To refine the system’s confidence in suggested corrections, we employ a small set of synthetically misspelled news articles for tuning confidence classifiers. The key contribution of this work lies in its demonstration that accurate and language-independent spellchecking is achievable without the need for hand-crafted dictionaries or manually annotated error models. We evaluate our system on both English and German, demonstrating superior performance compared to baseline systems utilizing curated dictionaries. Furthermore, we present preliminary results on artificial data for Russian and Arabic, highlighting the potential for rapid deployment in diverse linguistic contexts. Discourse relation recognition (DRR) is a fundamental task in natural language processing that aims to identify the semantic relationships between adjacent text segments. Determining these relationships is crucial for achieving a deeper understanding of text, enabling applications in various downstream tasks such as machine translation, text summarization, and question answering. Generally, discourse relations can be divided into two categories: explicit and implicit, which can be illustrated in the following example: “The company was disappointed by the ruling *because* The obligation is totally unwarranted.” (adapted from wsj_0294). In this instance, “because” explicitly signals a Cause relation, while many other discourse relationships are left unstated, requiring inference to determine the underlying connection between text segments – these constitute implicit discourse relations. The challenge of identifying *implicit* discourse relations has proven particularly difficult. Unlike explicit relations signaled by discourse connectives, implicit relations rely on subtle cues in syntax, semantics, and world knowledge. Traditional approaches to DRR often relied on hand-engineered features combined with machine learning classifiers (Marcu et al., 1999; Prasad et al., 2008). While achieving reasonable performance, these methods were labor-intensive, requiring significant linguistic expertise and struggling to generalize across diverse text types. More recently, neural network models have emerged as a promising alternative. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have been successfully applied to DRR, learning feature representations directly from the data (Li et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2017). However, these models often treat DRR as a classification task, predicting a single discourse relation without explicitly modeling the uncertainty inherent in the process. This can lead to overconfident predictions and hinder the model's ability to capture the nuances of discourse. Furthermore, standard neural network approaches often struggle with the long-range dependencies present in discourse, where the relationship between segments might be influenced by information occurring further back in the text. While attention mechanisms can mitigate this issue to some extent (Rush et al., 2015), they do not inherently address the problem of uncertainty or provide a principled way to model the distribution of possible discourse relations. In this work, we propose a novel Variational Neural Discourse Relation Recognizer (VNDRR) leveraging variational autoencoders (VAEs) to address these limitations. VNRDR aims to model the distribution over possible discourse relations, rather than simply predicting a single label. By incorporating a variational component, our model can capture the inherent uncertainty in implicit discourse relation identification and generate more robust and informative representations of discourse segments. We hypothesize that explicitly modeling uncertainty will improve performance, particularly in scenarios with ambiguous or subtle discourse cues. Our contributions are as follows: (1) We introduce a novel VNDRR architecture utilizing a VAE framework for DRR. (2) We demonstrate that our model outperforms strong baseline methods on the Penn Discourse Treebank (PDTB), achieving state-of-the-art results for implicit discourse relation identification. (3) We provide an analysis of the learned latent space, revealing interpretable representations of discourse segments tailored to their rhetorical function.
